mem.t: Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.

sat.d: Set out a big sheet of paper and some colored pens, and draw “our home” together: the house, each family member, and everyone’s favorite corner. When it is finished, ask Dad or Mom to write across the roof: “The LORD builds this home.” Let each person say one thing they love about your family, then hold hands and pray over your home. Stick the drawing on the fridge or in the living room as the starting point for this year.

sun: Which passage this week helped you see again that the family is God’s design?
What is one area of your home that you have been “building on your own” and have not yet handed over to God?
What small step will you take next week so that your family can see “the LORD builds this home”?

lessons.title: In the Beginning, God Designed the Family
lessons.theme: The family is not a human invention but God’s own heart

v: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
The LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

lessons.still: Take a slow, deep breath in, and let it out gently. In these few minutes before the children wake, or after they have finally fallen asleep, say to the Lord: “Lord, this family is yours. I come to you first.”
teach: For many parents, the word “family” brings to mind a to-do list: breakfast, school runs, homework, bills, laundry that never ends. Home can feel like a factory that never stops running and can never be fully repaired. But the first page of the Bible tells us that the family is not a human invention. It is God’s own design.

God made man and woman in his own image, then blessed them, and said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” Of everything God made, which he called “very good,” the first thing he called “not good” was loneliness. The family is the first community God designed to heal loneliness and display his image: a man, a woman, and the children born to them, living, ruling and bearing fruit together before God.

This changes how we see our homes. The family is not my kingdom; it is God’s design. I am not the inventor of my home, but a builder working from God’s blueprint. When our thinking changes, our lives change: from “I must run my family” to “I will build God’s family according to his design.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Move from a human point of view to God’s point of view. When we treat the family as our own project, we measure everyone by our own standards. When we admit that the family is God’s design, we begin by asking, “Lord, you designed this family. What was your original heart for it?”
q: Who is God? — God himself designed the family, and saw that being alone was “not good.” What kind of God do you see in that?
Who am I? — These days, am I more like the “boss of the family,” or a builder working from God’s blueprint?
How should I respond? — What small action can I take today to help my family feel that “our home is God’s heart”?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus came into the world, he did not choose a palace. He chose to grow up in an ordinary carpenter’s home in Nazareth. At home he obeyed his parents, and grew in wisdom and stature. The Son of God moved into a family himself, declaring that the home is a place God values, and a place where he is present.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for designing the family and for entrusting this one to me. I admit that I often treat my home as my own project and run it my own way. Today I give this family back to you. Be the designer and Lord of our home, and help me love everyone in it according to your heart. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Write one sentence: “This family is God’s design, and I am the builder.” Put it where you will see it often
Before eating today, thank God in one sentence for your family
Hug each family member and say, “It is so good that God put you in our family.”
lessons.noon: “It is not good for the man to be alone.” — Lord, thank you for placing me in a family. Be with us in this home.

fam.key: Our family is God’s design.

lamb.do: Hold your child close, gently stroke their head, and sing a familiar song slowly and softly.
lamb.say: God made you, and God gave you a family. Mommy and Daddy love you so much.

sprout.story: Long, long ago, God made the sky, the sea, the flowers and the little animals. Last of all, God made the first daddy, Adam. Then God saw that Adam was lonely, so he made Eve to be with him. God said, “It is not good to be alone. Let there be a family!” So God invented the family, so that everyone could live together, love each other and help each other.
sprout.ask: Why do you think God invented the family?
sprout.do: Count together: how many people are in our family? As you count each person, say, “Thank you, God, for ___!”

soldier.story: The first chapter of the Bible says that after God made people, he looked at everything he had made and called it “very good.” But in chapter two, for the very first time, God said something was “not good”: it was not good for the man to be alone. So God designed the family. A man and a woman join together, have children, and together take care of the world God made. The family is not an idea people came up with. It is God’s invention. Just as an architect draws the plans before a house is built, God had the family in his heart before our family ever existed.
ask: If the family is God’s design, how do you think God wants the people in a family to treat one another?
What is your favorite thing about our family?
soldier.do: Draw “God’s blueprint”: write down three things you think a God-designed family should have, and share them at dinner.

youth.talk: Some people say, “A family is just a group of people who happen to live together and share the same blood.” Others see home as a place they want to escape from when they grow up. But the Bible says that the family is God’s design, a place to heal loneliness and show God’s image. Mom and Dad are still learning how to build our family according to God’s heart, and sometimes we get it wrong.
ask: What do you think is the biggest difference between a family “built on God’s design” and an ordinary one?
Where in our family do you see God’s design most clearly? Where does it most need to change?
youth.do: This week, find time for each parent to go out one-on-one with a child for a drink. Ask what their ideal family looks like, and simply listen without defending yourself.

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, thank you for designing the family and putting us together. Please live in our home and help us love one another as you love us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Who Is Building This Home?
lessons.theme: Unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain

v: Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.
It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.

lessons.still: Be quiet for a moment and ask the Holy Spirit to shine into your heart like a light: “Lord, show me what I have been relying on to hold this family together lately.” Don’t rush to answer. Just let him shed light.
teach: Psalm 127 is a psalm of Solomon. He was the greatest builder among Israel’s kings: he built the temple, the royal palace and the city walls. Yet this master builder wrote, “Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” He saw that people can build the most magnificent house, but cannot build a home full of life, love and peace.

“It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil” is almost a portrait of modern parents: up early for work, up late marking homework, earning money, juggling tutoring and activities, never a moment to rest. The psalmist does not say that hard work is bad. He says that unless the LORD builds, all of it is “in vain,” like pouring water into a bucket with a hole in it.

The second half of the verse is gentler: “for he gives sleep to his loved ones.” God does not want parents to trade peace of mind for their family’s security. The true builder is God, and we work alongside him. We are responsible for obedience and faithfulness; he is responsible for the building and the fruit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled parents think the family’s success or failure rests entirely on them, so they become anxious, controlling and worn out. Self-emptied parents hand the building back to God, and so they can rest. Keep your eyes on Jesus: not on yourself, not on others, not on circumstances.
q: Who is God? — God is the one who builds and guards, and who gives sleep to those he loves. What comfort does this bring you?
Who am I? — In what matter this week have I been “rising up early and staying up late” in vain, holding things together by myself?
How should I respond? — Which matter am I willing to hand back to God to build?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.” He is the true builder and the cornerstone of every home. He slept in the stern of the boat, not because he did not care about the storm, but because he trusted the Father completely. He invites weary parents to share his yoke.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that I often try to build this family by myself. I get up early and stay up late, yet grow more tired and more anxious. Today I hand the building back to you. Please build our home yourself and watch over our children. Teach me to work with you, and to sleep peacefully in you. Amen.
acts: List the three family matters that make you most anxious. Pray over them one by one, saying, “Lord, I give this to you to build.”
Put your phone down thirty minutes earlier tonight and get a good night’s sleep
Say to your spouse, “We are not holding this family together on our own. God is building it.”
lessons.noon: “Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” — Lord, right now I put down my own strength. Please come and build.

fam.key: God is the true builder of our home.

lamb.do: Stack blocks with your child to build a little house. When it is done, hold their little hand and pat the house together.
lamb.say: God builds our home. God keeps our home safe.

sprout.story: The Three Little Pigs each built a house: one of straw, one of sticks and one of bricks. When the big bad wolf came and huffed and puffed, the straw house fell down, and the stick house fell down too. Only the brick house stood firm. The Bible says we should ask God to build our home, because the home God builds is the strongest. No wind can blow it down!
sprout.ask: How would you like God to keep our home safe?
sprout.do: Build a “house that God built” together with blocks or cardboard boxes, and draw a little cross on it.

soldier.story: King Solomon was the best house-builder in Israel. He built a magnificent temple and a palace. Yet he wrote a poem that says, “If God doesn’t build the house, the builders work for nothing.” He knew that a house can be built with bricks, but a home full of love and peace can only be built by God. It is like planting a seed in the soil: you can put it in the ground, but only God can make it grow.
ask: What do you think it means for “God to build our home”?
What things in our family do we need God’s help with?
soldier.do: Make a “God builds our home” prayer card: each family member writes one thing they hope God will help our family with. Put the cards on the dinner table and pray for one each day before dinner this week.

youth.talk: Solomon said, “It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil.” It sounds like he is describing us today: homework, tutoring, exams, phones, and everyone so busy and tired. Mom and Dad often think this family will only hold together if we work ourselves to the bone.
ask: Do you think our family is “holding itself up” or “letting God build”? How can you tell?
Is there something you have been carrying on your own lately that has left you tired?
youth.do: This week, parents go first and share one thing they are learning to hand over to God, then invite the children to share. Then pray for one another.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for being the true builder of our home. Please keep our home safe, and help us sleep peacefully at night, because you are watching over us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Every Family in Heaven and on Earth Is Named from Him
lessons.theme: I believe: our family belongs to the Father

v: For this cause, I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,
from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named,
that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,
that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love,
may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth,
and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.

lessons.still: Imagine yourself kneeling before the heavenly Father, as Paul did. You don’t need many words. Just confess, “Father, you are the source of this family.” Let those words settle slowly in your heart.
teach: Paul prayed for the believers in Ephesus from prison. He said, “I bow my knees to the Father,” and then added, “from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.” This tells us that every “family” has its source in the heavenly Father. Earthly fathers and homes are only shadows of the Father in heaven. The meaning, the pattern and the very name of the family all come from him.

So our family is not an isolated little unit, but part of the Father’s great household. When we call our home a “Christian family,” we mean that its name is received from the heavenly Father. The way we live is how we introduce our children and our neighbors to what kind of Father he is.

Paul’s prayer is also the prayer every home needs: that God would grant us to be “strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,” so that Christ may dwell in our hearts through faith and we may be “rooted and grounded in love.” The deepest foundation of a family is not the house, the savings or the degrees. It is the love of Christ living in each heart. Today we move from knowing to conviction: not only having heard it, but declaring it: I believe.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Conviction is the key step in changing our thinking. From “the family is mine” to “the family is the Father’s”; from “I want my children to succeed” to “I want my children to know the Father.” When parents are convinced first, children will see the heavenly Father in them.
q: Who is God? — Every family in heaven and on earth is named from him. What kind of Father is he?
Who am I? — What kind of heavenly Father is my family introducing to my children?
How should I respond? — Write your own “I believe” declaration: about this family, I believe…
lessons.jesus: When Jesus taught his disciples to pray, the first words were “Our Father in heaven.” He brought us into his own relationship with the Father, so that we too can call God “Abba, Father.” Jesus is the Father’s only Son, yet he is willing to let people like us become members of God’s household together with him.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I bow my knees before you. I believe our family is named from you, and I believe you are the true Father of this home. Through your Spirit, strengthen me in my inner being. Let Christ dwell in my heart and in the heart of every family member, so that our love may be rooted and grounded in you. Amen.
acts: Write your “I believe” declaration in three sentences: I believe this family is…; I believe my children are…; I believe God will…
Pray today calling God “Father” three times, and feel what it means that he is your Father
Tell your children, “Our family’s name comes from our heavenly Father.”
lessons.noon: “From whom every family in heaven and on earth is named” — Father, our family belongs to you. Make your name known in this home.

fam.key: We belong to the heavenly Father’s family.

lamb.do: Let your child sit on your lap, hold their hands, and slowly say together, “Heavenly Father, thank you.”
lamb.say: You are Mommy and Daddy’s treasure, and you are the heavenly Father’s treasure too.

sprout.story: Xiaoming asked Mom, “Mom, does God have a family?” Mom smiled and said, “Yes! God is our Daddy in heaven, and every family in the world comes from him. Our family is part of the heavenly Father’s family too!” Xiaoming said happily, “Then I have two daddies, one at home and one in heaven!”
sprout.ask: What kind of Daddy is our Daddy in heaven?
sprout.do: Hold hands in a circle as a family and say loudly together, “We belong to the heavenly Father’s family!”

soldier.story: Paul was sitting in prison, yet he did not complain. Instead he knelt down and prayed, saying that every family in heaven and on earth is named from the heavenly Father. That means every family comes from the Father, and ours does too. It is like our family name, passed down from our grandfather. The “name” we carry as a Christian family comes from the heavenly Father. So our family should show other people what the heavenly Father is like.
ask: When other people look at our family, what kind of Father do you think they would say God is?
Which part of the heavenly Father do you most want our family to be like?
soldier.do: Write a family “I believe” declaration together: each person writes one sentence beginning “I believe…” Put it on the front door.

youth.talk: Paul says every family in heaven and on earth is named from the Father. That doesn’t mean every family is a good one. We all know many families have hurt and brokenness, and ours isn’t perfect either. What it means is that the standard for a family is not set by us, but by the heavenly Father. We are all learning from him how to be family.
ask: What do you think is the biggest difference between God as “Father” and a father on earth?
Has your picture of the heavenly Father been affected by how Mom and Dad are?
youth.do: This week, parents find a chance to tell their children: “If anything I do has given you the wrong idea of the heavenly Father, please tell me. I am willing to change.”

fam.pray: Daddy in heaven, thank you for making us part of your family. Help our home become more and more like you, full of love, peace and joy. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Build Your Home on the Rock
lessons.theme: Hear and do, and the home stands firm

v: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock.
The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.
Everyone who hears these words of mine and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand.
The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it fell—and its fall was great.”

lessons.still: Take a deep breath and let your heart slow down. Ask the Lord, “Lord, what is the one thing you most want me to do in our family today?” Wait quietly, and write down the first thought that comes to mind.
teach: At the end of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus told of two builders. From the outside the two houses may have looked identical, each with a roof and walls. The difference was in what could not be seen: one had its foundation on the rock, the other on sand. On calm days you can’t tell them apart. When the rain falls, the floods rise and the winds blow, the difference is plain.

Every family meets storms: a sick child, money worries, conflict between husband and wife, a teenager’s rebellion, the death of a loved one. Jesus said that both the wise man and the foolish man heard his words. The difference was whether they put them into practice. A family’s foundation is not how many sermons we have heard or parenting books we have read, but whether we live out God’s word.

Practice doesn’t have to begin with something big. Start today with one small thing: a gentle word, a prayer before a meal, a sincere apology. Once God’s word is lived out, it becomes the rock of the home. Information becomes revelation, revelation becomes conviction, and conviction becomes practice. This is how life is changed.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Of the eight steps of change, “practice” is the one most easily skipped. We are good at knowing, but not used to doing. Self-emptied parents do not merely demand that their children obey. They obey God’s word first, and show their children by their lives.
q: Who is God? — Jesus’ words are a rock that can withstand the storm. Have you experienced his word holding you up at home?
Who am I? — At home, am I someone who “hears and does,” or someone who “only hears”?
How should I respond? — Which word of God will I put into practice at home today, in a concrete way?
lessons.jesus: Jesus himself is the rock. Paul wrote, “No one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.” Jesus not only taught, but lived out everything he taught. He is our perfect example of hearing and doing.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for being the rock of our home. I admit that I often hear your word and do not do it. I ask much of my children and obey so little myself. Today give me strength to live out your word at home, beginning with one small thing, so that our family is built on you. Amen.
acts: Choose one verse today and put it into practice at home in a concrete way. Write down tonight what happened
As a family, set one small “live it out this week” goal, such as praying before every meal
When conflict comes, pause for three seconds and ask, “What would Jesus’ word have me do?”
lessons.noon: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock.” — Lord, right now I want to hear, and to do.

fam.key: Hear God’s word, then do it.

lamb.do: Play a “listen and do” game with your child. Say “clap your hands” or “touch your head,” and give them a hug each time they do it.
lamb.say: You listened and you did it! Well done! Let’s listen to God’s word together.

sprout.story: Two men wanted to build houses. One was wise. He dug deep and built his house on a big rock. The other was lazy and built his house on the sand without much care. Then the rain came down, and the river rushed in with a splash. The house on the sand fell down with a crash, but the house on the rock stood firm. Jesus said, “Whoever hears my words and does them is like the wise man!”
sprout.ask: What is one thing you can do today that Jesus would love?
sprout.do: “Build a house” on the table with your fingers. First pat the table and say, “This is the rock,” then build the house with your fingers and say loudly, “Hear and do!”

soldier.story: Jesus told a story about two men who each built a house, one on the rock and one on the sand. When the storm came, the house on the sand collapsed, and its fall was great. Jesus said both men heard his words. The difference was that one did them and the other did not. Understanding something in class and really doing it are two different things, and it is the same at home.
ask: Which do you think is harder, hearing or doing? Why?
Which of God’s words would you like to put into practice at home this week?
soldier.do: Each family member chooses one saying of Jesus and writes it on a small card. Each evening at dinner this week, report: “How did I live it out today?”

youth.talk: Jesus said the two houses may look similar day to day, and only when the storm comes do you see the foundation. Our family will meet storms too: pressure, conflict, disappointment. If faith is only going to church on Sunday and memorizing a few verses, it may not hold when the storm hits. The real foundation is putting God’s word into practice every day.
ask: At your school or among your friends, what do you think Christians most often hear but don’t do?
If a big storm hit our family, do you think our foundation is firm enough?
youth.do: Parents and children each pick one saying of Jesus and agree to remind and check in with one another for a week. Share how it went at the weekend.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for being our rock. Help us not only to hear your word but to do it, so that our family stands firm. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: This Week, Was I Building or Tearing Down?
lessons.theme: Review and Adjust: build the home with wisdom

v: Every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands.
Through wisdom a house is built; by understanding it is established;
by knowledge the rooms are filled with all rare and beautiful treasure.

lessons.still: Recall the pictures of your family this past week, as if turning through a photo album, one by one and slowly. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you. Don’t rush to condemn yourself. Just see honestly.
teach: Proverbs says, “Every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands.” This applies to every parent. Tearing down a home seldom takes a disaster. It takes only day after day of “her own hands”: a sharp word, an impatient look, an evening spent glued to a phone. Building a home works the same way, through day after day of wisdom and love.

“Through wisdom a house is built; by understanding it is established; by knowledge the rooms are filled with all rare and beautiful treasure.” The treasure here is not only material. It is the laughter, trust, memories and faith of a home. These precious things are put into a family little by little.

This week we have learned that the family is God’s design, that God is the builder, that every family is named from the Father, and that we should build on the rock. Today is not about giving ourselves a score, but about honest review and humble adjustment. Reviewing is not for condemnation, but so that our next step is more true. Humility is the key to revival. When parents are willing to admit their faults, the home begins to be built.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the necessary road of change. Proud parents review only their children; humble parents review themselves first. Remember: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Deal with your own heart first, then with your children’s behavior.
q: Who is God? — God gives wisdom to those who ask him. Where did you experience his help this week?
Who am I? — Looking back on this week, when was I building? When was I tearing down?
How should I respond? — What is the one thing I will adjust next week, and how, specifically, will I do it?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never breaks a bruised reed or quenches a dimly burning wick. He is gentle with the weak. To Peter, who had failed him, he asked, “Do you love me?” His building restores; it does not shame. He treats you the same way as you review yourself today.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with me through this week. I admit that at times I tore down my family’s hearts with my own hands. Please forgive me, and heal them. Thank you also for showing me moments of building. Those are all your grace. Give me wisdom to keep building our home with you next week. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what was the most beautiful moment in our family this week? What most needs adjusting?
Ask your child, “Did Mom or Dad do anything this week that made you sad?” Just listen, and don’t defend yourself
Write down one specific adjustment for next week
lessons.noon: “Every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands.” — Lord, give me wisdom, so that today my hands will build.

fam.key: We build our home together with love.

lamb.do: Put the scattered toys back in the box together with your child, one by one, clapping after each one.
lamb.say: We tidy our home together. God loves it when we help each other.

sprout.story: Xiaomei built a castle with blocks, but her little brother accidentally knocked it down. Xiaomei was so angry that she wanted to hit him. Mom hugged her and said, “Let’s build it again together, shall we?” Her brother said, “I’m sorry! I’ll help you build it!” Together they built an even bigger and more beautiful castle.
sprout.ask: Did you help build something good in our family this week?
sprout.do: Play “building time” as a family: each person tells one good thing they did for the family this week, and draws a brick on a sheet of paper for each one. See how high a wall we have built together!

soldier.story: The Bible says that a wise person builds a home, and a foolish person tears it down with their own hands. Sometimes a home is torn down not with a hammer but with a mouth and an attitude: an unkind word, a rolled eye, deliberately ignoring someone. Building a home works the same way, through an encouraging word, a helping hand, an apology. Every one of us, every day, is either building or tearing down our home.
ask: What do you think you built in our family this week? Did you tear anything down?
What would you like our family to improve together next week?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person shares one thing they are thankful for this week and one thing they want to improve next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: All week we have been thinking that the family is God’s design and that God is the builder. But honestly, at home there is still friction every day, impatience, and things said wrongly. Mom and Dad want to admit first that this week we also did some tearing down. We review not to argue, but to grow better together.
ask: Did Mom or Dad say or do anything this week that made you feel torn down?
If you could change one thing about our family, what would you choose?
youth.do: Parents first apologize sincerely to the children for one thing, then invite the children to make one suggestion. The whole family chooses one action to adjust together next week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for being with us this week. There are things we did well and things we did wrongly. Please forgive us, and help us build our home with love next week. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1.memT: Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.

mem.t: Behold, children are a heritage of the LORD. The fruit of the womb is his reward.

sat.t: Family Day: Our Family Treasure Box
sat.d: Give each child a shoebox to be their own “treasure box.” Parents dig out photos from the child’s birth, their first shoes or their first drawing, and put them in the box, telling the story of the birth and the prayers prayed for them as they go. The children can decorate the lid and write their names on it. At the end, parents place a hand on each child’s head and say, “You are a heritage God has given our family, and we will take good care of you.” Then pray together, placing the treasure boxes before God.

sun: This week, as you moved from “owner” to “steward,” what was your greatest struggle?
Have you ever treated your child as your own creation, or as an extension of yourself? In what matter was it most obvious?
How will you bless your child next week so that they know they belong to God first? You might also invite a friend to try it with you.

lessons.title: Children Are a Heritage from the LORD
lessons.theme: Children are not my property; they are a heritage entrusted by God

v: Behold, children are a heritage of the LORD. The fruit of the womb is his reward.
As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of youth.
Happy is the man who has his quiver full of them. They won’t be disappointed when they speak with their enemies in the gate.

lessons.still: Be still, and remember your child’s little face when they were first born. Do you remember the wonder and thankfulness in your heart at that moment? Say to the Lord: “Lord, this child is your gift.”
teach: Chinese parents often say, “This is my child.” There is nothing wrong with that, but it can slip, without our noticing, into “This is mine”: I gave birth to him, I raised him, I paid for his education, so he should grow up the way I want. Children gradually become their parents’ property, their masterpiece, or an extension of the dreams the parents never finished.

Right after “Unless the LORD builds the house,” Psalm 127 goes on: “Behold, children are a heritage of the LORD. The fruit of the womb is his reward.” “Heritage” originally meant the land God allotted to Israel. The land was God’s, and people only received it, farmed it and guarded it. Children are the same: they are God’s first, and then entrusted to us.

This is the change from owner to steward. The owner asks, “What do I want him to become?” The steward asks, “What did the Master intend for this life he has entrusted to me?” The psalmist also compares children to “arrows in the hand of a mighty man.” Arrows are not meant to be kept in a drawer. They are meant to be aimed and released. The parent’s hand holds them only for a while; one day they will be sent in the direction God has set.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Move from a human point of view to God’s point of view. A child is not my report card, nor my insurance for old age, but God’s heritage. When parents return to the place of the steward, they no longer shape their children by their own standards. They first ask God, “You made this child. What was your original heart for him?”
q: Who is God? — God is the God who entrusts life to people as a gift. What kind of God do you see in the words “heritage” and “reward”?
Who am I? — When I say “my child,” am I more like an owner, or a steward?
How should I respond? — What word or action can I use today to tell my child, “You are a gift from God”?
lessons.jesus: In his last prayer, Jesus said to the Father, “They were yours, and you have given them to me.” He never treated his disciples as his own property, but as people the Father had entrusted to him, whom he faithfully watched over and kept to the end. Jesus is the best example of a steward.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us our children. They are your heritage and your reward. I admit that I often treat them as mine and try to shape them my way. Today I place my child back into your hands. Teach me to be a faithful steward, and to see your heart for them. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write your child’s name, and beside it a sentence: “You are God’s heritage, and I am the steward.”
Find a moment today to tell your child, “You are the best gift God has given our family.”
Pray for each child for one minute, only giving thanks and asking for nothing
lessons.noon: “Behold, children are a heritage of the LORD.” — Lord, thank you for entrusting my children to me. Teach me to care well for your heritage.

fam.key: I am God’s gift to my family.

lamb.do: After your child’s bath, wrap them in a big towel, hold them gently and rock them, and kiss their little hands and feet.
lamb.say: You are God’s gift to us, and we thank God so much.

sprout.story: It was Lele’s birthday, and Grandma gave him a beautifully wrapped present. Lele was so happy! He opened it, and it was a little train! Mom said, “Do you know? You are a present too. On the day you were born, God gave you to Mommy and Daddy, and we were so happy that we kept saying thank you to God!” Lele smiled and said, “Then I am a present from God, and my little brother is too!”
sprout.ask: Why do you think God gave you to our family?
sprout.do: Put a paper bag over your child (with their head sticking out) and pretend to give this “present” to Dad. Dad opens it and says, “Wow! A present from God, it’s ___!” Then take turns.

soldier.story: When the Israelites entered the Promised Land, God gave the land to each tribe and each family. This was called their “inheritance.” The land belonged to God, and they were to farm it and look after it, and not sell it carelessly. The psalm says children are also a heritage from God. That means you belong to God first, and then God entrusted you to Mom and Dad to look after. It is like a teacher putting the class plants in the care of the pupil on duty. The pupil waters them and gives them sunlight, but the plants are not his.
ask: If you are God’s heritage, how do you think God wants Mom and Dad to look after you?
How do you feel knowing that you belong to God first?
soldier.do: Each child draws a “Certificate of My Heritage” saying, “I, ___, am a heritage God has given.” Ask Mom and Dad to sign it, and stick it on your bedroom door.

youth.talk: Chinese families often see children as the continuation of the family line, or even a second chance at life for the parents. Honestly, Mom and Dad sometimes do this too, putting our unfinished dreams on you. But the Bible says that you are a heritage from the LORD. You belong to God first, not to our expectations. We are learning to change from “owners” to “stewards.”
ask: Have you ever felt like Mom and Dad’s “masterpiece” or “extension”? When was that?
If you belong to God first, how do you think that would change the way you see yourself?
youth.do: This week, parents say to their children, “If I have put my dreams on you and made you feel pressured, please tell me.” Then pray together, handing your child’s future to God.

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, thank you for giving me to this family. I am your gift. Please help Mom and Dad take good care of me, and help me grow up well. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Am I Holding My Child Too Tightly?
lessons.theme: Seeing myself: am I an owner or a steward?

v: I prayed for this child, and the LORD has given me my petition which I asked of him.
Therefore I have also given him to the LORD. As long as he lives he is given to the LORD.” He worshiped the LORD there.

lessons.still: Open your hands, palms up, and rest them on your knees. Imagine your child is right there in your hands. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, am I holding him gently, or gripping him tightly?”
teach: Hannah could not have a child for many years. She wept and prayed in the temple, and at last she received Samuel. But after he was weaned, she herself took him to the temple, and said, “I prayed for this child, and the LORD has given me my petition which I asked of him. Therefore I have also given him to the LORD.” The one who longed most for a child was the first to give him back to God.

We may not need to take our children to the temple as Hannah did, but every parent must face the same question: is my child in my hand held open, or gripped tight? Parents who hold like owners often show some signs: the child’s choices must have my approval; the child’s achievements bring me face and the child’s failures bring me shame; when the child does not follow my plan, I become anxious or angry.

The Holy Spirit’s light is not meant to condemn but to set free. Yating in Taichung found that every time her son wanted to learn painting rather than piano, she could not sleep all night. After praying quietly, she saw it: what she feared was not her son’s future, but losing control, and having nothing to say when relatives asked. Weeping, she said, “Lord, I see now that I have been treating him as mine.” Seeing is the beginning of change, and being able to see is itself grace.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life is the root of the fall: wanting to take God’s place as king over my child’s life. Pride leaves its place and grasps at power; humility lets go of power and returns to its place. When parents let go, they are not giving up responsibility. They are letting people be people and God be God, stepping back from the master’s seat to the steward’s.
q: Who is God? — God is the one who heard Hannah’s prayer, and the one Hannah could trust with her child. Can you trust him?
Who am I? — In what matter am I holding my child too tightly? What am I really afraid of losing?
How should I respond? — Which part of my child’s future am I willing to “give to the LORD,” as Hannah did?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself.” He had all authority, yet he did not cling to it, but willingly humbled himself. His letting go brought salvation. He invites parents to follow his example and loosen their tight grip.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light into my heart. I admit that I often hold my child too tightly, treat his choices as my face, and his future as my responsibility. Forgive me for wanting to be king over his life. Today I learn from Hannah and give my child back to you, because you love him more than I do. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Write down the three things you most want to decide for your child. Beside each ask: “Is this God’s authority, or mine?”
Today let your child choose one small thing for themselves, without criticizing or correcting
Pray for one minute with open hands, as a sign of giving your child back to God
lessons.noon: “Therefore I have also given him to the LORD.” — Lord, right now I loosen my grip and place my child in your hands.

fam.key: I belong to God, and God takes care of me.

lamb.do: Play “let go and catch”: let your child go from your hands to your spouse’s hands, and take turns opening your arms to catch them.
lamb.say: Wherever you go, God catches you.

sprout.story: Hannah wanted a baby very much, and she prayed to God every day. God heard her prayer and gave her a little boy named Samuel. Hannah loved Samuel so much, but she said to God, “This child is your gift, and I want to give him to you.” Later Samuel grew up in the temple. He heard God call his name, and became someone God used greatly.
sprout.ask: Do you know that God loves you very much and takes care of you?
sprout.do: Use a doll to act out Hannah. First hold the doll, then gently place it in a box marked with a cross and say, “God, I give him to you!”

soldier.story: Hannah prayed for many years before Samuel was born. As she had promised, after Samuel was weaned she took him to the temple and entrusted him to Eli the priest. She visited him only once a year, and made him a little robe with her own hands. You might wonder how she could bear it. Hannah knew that the safest place for her child was not in his mother’s hands but in God’s. Later Samuel became a great prophet of Israel.
ask: How do you think Hannah felt when she gave Samuel to God?
What is the difference between Mom and Dad “giving you to God” and “not caring about you”?
soldier.do: With Mom or Dad, write down one thing you would like to learn to decide for yourself, and pray about it together.

youth.talk: Hannah wanted a child more than anyone, yet she was the first to give him back to God. Honestly, Mom and Dad sometimes hold you too tightly: what subjects you choose, who your friends are, what you will do one day, we want to step in on all of it. Part of that is love, and part is our own fear and concern for face. We are asking the Holy Spirit to shine his light on us, and we also want to hear how you feel.
ask: In what area do you feel Mom and Dad hold you the tightest?
Is there something you wish we would trust you with a little more?
youth.do: Invite your child for a one-on-one walk and ask them to name one thing they wish you would let go of. Parents listen until they finish, then together think of a way that both sides feel comfortable with.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving me as you loved Samuel. I place myself in your hands. Please keep holding my hand, and Mom and Dad’s hands too. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Children Are God’s Masterpiece
lessons.theme: I believe: children are God’s wonderful work, not mine

v: For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.
My frame wasn’t hidden from you, when I was made in secret, woven together in the depths of the earth.
Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.

lessons.still: Imagine the heavenly Father quietly knitting your child together in secret: their laugh, their temperament, their gifts. Meditate silently: “Before this child was born, God already knew him.”
teach: David said, “For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb.” Before an ultrasound could show anything clearly, before the child had uttered a cry, God was already knitting them together in secret with his own hands. Their personality, their looks, their gifts, even the very traits that give us a headache, are no accident. They come from a wonderful designer.

Many parents unknowingly treat their children as their own work: be good at studying like me, or don’t suffer like me. Zhiwei, an engineer in Kuala Lumpur, always hoped his daughter would study science, but she loved music and caring for people. When he read “I am fearfully and wonderfully made,” he suddenly understood: his daughter was not his blueprint, but God’s. The “not like me” parts he wanted to fix might be God’s deliberate brushstrokes. The psalmist even says, “In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.” The chapters of a child’s whole life were in God’s heart from the beginning.

Paul also says, “It is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” A steward’s duty is not to remake the child into what we want, but to discover the treasure God has placed within them, and faithfully water, nurture and protect it. Conviction is not merely agreeing with this truth. It is declaring from the heart, at the moment your child disappoints you, I believe this child is God’s masterpiece.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of perspective: from human eyes to God’s eyes, from earthly standards to heavenly purposes. When a parent’s “I believe” changes, the way they see the child changes; when the way they see changes, the way they treat the child changes too. Change your thinking and you change your life.
q: Who is God? — God knew and sheltered my child in the womb. What a careful Creator he is!
Who am I? — Do I often want to change my child into “my work”? Which trait do I most want to change?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe my child is…; I believe God, in him…; I believe my part is…
lessons.jesus: The Bible says that all things were “created through him and for him.” Your child was created through Christ and for Christ. Jesus is not only your child’s Creator, but the purpose of your child’s life. The greatest trust given to parents is to bring their children to Jesus.
lessons.pray: Lord of creation, I praise you, for my child is fearfully and wonderfully made. I admit that I often want to remake him in my own image and forget that he is your masterpiece. I believe you have a good plan for him; I believe my part is to be a faithful steward. Open my eyes to see the treasure you have placed in him. Amen.
acts: Write your three “I believe” declarations and keep them in your wallet or on your phone background
Write down three traits in your child that differ from yours but are given by God, and thank God for each
Today, specifically praise one trait God has given your child, for example: “You care so much for people. That is a gift from God.”
lessons.noon: “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” — Lord, my child is your wonderful work too. Help me to see it.

fam.key: God made me wonderfully.

lamb.do: While massaging your child, name each body part: “These are the little hands, little feet and little tummy God made.”
lamb.say: God made you so wonderfully, and I love you so much.

sprout.story: Grandma had planted lots of flowers in the garden: red ones, yellow ones, purple ones, and every one was different. Xiaoen asked, “Grandma, why are all the flowers different?” Grandma said, “Because God likes every one to be special. You are the same. Your eyes and your laugh were specially designed by God. There is only one you in the whole world!” Xiaoen happily twirled around.
sprout.ask: What do you think is the most special thing about how God made you?
sprout.do: Stamp everyone’s handprints on a sheet of paper and compare the sizes and shapes. With each handprint, say, “God made it, how special!”

soldier.story: King David wrote in a poem that when he was still in his mother’s womb, God already knew him and made him with his own hands. He even said that, before he was born, God had written all the days of his life in a book. Think about it: when a painter paints a picture, he puts thought into every stroke. God made you with more care than any painter. Your looks, the things you like, the things you are good at, are all God’s careful design, not just chance.
ask: What special gifts do you think God has put in you?
If God had a book with your whole life written in it, what would you like it to say?
soldier.do: Ask Mom and Dad to write down three “God designs” in you, and you write down three in Mom or Dad. Swap and read them aloud at dinner.

youth.talk: David says he is “fearfully and wonderfully made.” At an age full of comparison, that can be hard to believe: on social media there is always someone better looking, smarter or more popular. Mom and Dad admit that we sometimes compare you with others, or try to change you into the person we imagine. But God says you are his masterpiece, not a copy of anybody else.
ask: Which part of yourself is hardest for you to accept? How do you think God sees it?
What trait do you think God has put in you in a special way?
youth.do: Parents and children each write a card naming three “God designs” in the other. Swap them, then thank God for each other together.

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, thank you for making me so wonderfully. I am your masterpiece, and there is only one me in the world. Please help me to love the person you made me to be. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Bless Your Children Today
lessons.theme: Like Jesus, bring children to God and bless them

v: They were bringing to him little children, that he should touch them, but the disciples rebuked those who were bringing them.
But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.
Most certainly I tell you, whoever will not receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”
He took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.

lessons.still: Be still for a moment and imagine Jesus taking your child in his arms and laying his hands on them. What is the look in his eyes? Let that picture rest in your heart for a while.
teach: People were bringing little children to Jesus, but the disciples thought children were not important and rebuked them. Jesus was indignant. He said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” Then he “took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.” In an age that did not value children, Jesus declared with an embrace and a blessing that every child is precious in God’s eyes.

The most practical thing a steward can do is to keep bringing the children to the Master. In the Old Testament, fathers had a tradition of blessing their children: Isaac blessed Jacob, and Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons. But in many families today we are good at reminding, warning and correcting, and seldom at blessing. What children hear most may be “Hurry up,” “Don’t do that” and “What mark did you get?”

A blessing doesn’t need to be long. Guohua, a single father in Singapore, places his hand on his son’s head each night by his bed and says just one sentence: “The LORD bless you, and keep you.” At first his son thought it strange, but later, if Dad forgot, his son would remind him: “Dad, you haven’t blessed me yet!” Today, begin to practice with one sentence of blessing.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example. As Jesus treated children, so I treat children. People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things. Homework can wait a little, but a blessing cannot be skipped; one blessing often goes further than ten warnings. A parent’s blessing is a concrete act of giving the child back to the Master.
q: Who is God? — Jesus was indignant when the disciples forbade the children. How much does he value your child?
Who am I? — Of the words I give my children, are there more reminders and corrections, or more blessings?
How should I respond? — What words, and at what moment, will I use to bless my children today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus did not merely say, “Allow the little children to come to me.” He took them in his arms himself, and laid his hands on them to bless them. He did not push the children away because he was busy, nor consider them an interruption to important ministry. Jesus showed that blessing children is itself the work of God’s Kingdom.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for taking the little children in your arms and blessing them. I admit that I often only remind and correct, and seldom bless my children. Today, please use my hands and my mouth to bring your blessing to them. Let my children know your love through my blessing. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Tonight place your hand on each child’s head and speak a blessing, for example: “The LORD bless you, and keep you.”
At least once today, put down what you are doing and listen to your child for five minutes
Bless your spouse once, where the children can see
lessons.noon: “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” — Lord, use me today to bring my children to you.

fam.key: Jesus loves children, and he blesses me.

lamb.do: At bedtime, gently put a hand on your child’s head or chest, slowly speak a blessing, and kiss their forehead.
lamb.say: May Jesus bless you, and may you sleep in peace.

sprout.story: One day, lots of moms and dads brought their children to see Jesus. But Jesus’ friends told them to go away, saying that Jesus was busy. When Jesus heard this, he was not happy. He said, “Let the children come to me!” Then Jesus picked up the children one by one, stroked their heads, and blessed them. The children were so happy, because Jesus loves children best!
sprout.ask: If Jesus were holding you, what would you like to say to him?
sprout.do: Take turns being “Jesus” as a family. Put your hand on someone’s head and say, “Jesus loves you and blesses you!”

soldier.story: In Jesus’ time, children were often thought unimportant. When grown-ups were talking about serious matters, children had to stand aside. So when people brought children to Jesus, the disciples kept them away. But Jesus was angry. He said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” Jesus took the children in his arms and blessed them. He let everyone know that in God’s Kingdom children are not extras, but main characters.
ask: Why do you think Jesus was angry with his disciples?
Have you ever felt ignored because you are a child? How would Jesus treat you?
soldier.do: Tonight ask Mom and Dad to lay hands on you and bless you, and you try saying a blessing for Mom and Dad too.

youth.talk: Jesus took the little children in his arms and blessed them. Mom and Dad have realized that we often say to you, “Study,” “Go to bed early,” “Spend less time on your phone,” but seldom truly bless you. Perhaps having your head stroked now feels a little awkward, and that is perfectly normal. But we want to start again, and speak God’s blessing over you in a way you are more comfortable with.
ask: How would you prefer us to bless you? Spoken, written, or by message?
What do you think is the difference between hearing a blessing and hearing a reminder?
youth.do: This week parents write a blessing for their child and deliver it in the way the child likes, with no reminder or request attached.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for loving children most, and for loving me. Please hold me and bless me, and bless our whole family, so that we love you more every day. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Children Belong to the Father First
lessons.theme: Review and Adjust: the steward’s hands learn to trust and let go

v: When they saw him, they were astonished; and his mother said to him, “Son, why have you treated us this way? Behold, your father and I were anxiously looking for you.”
He said to them, “Why were you looking for me? Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?”
They didn’t understand the saying which he spoke to them.
And he went down with them and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

lessons.still: Recall the words you spoke to your child this past week, and the decisions you made. Ask the Holy Spirit to look back with you, like opening a diary. Read it honestly, and don’t rush to blame yourself.
teach: When Jesus was twelve, he went up to Jerusalem with his parents for the feast, and stayed behind in the temple on the way home. Mary and Joseph searched for three days, and Mary said anxiously, “Your father and I were anxiously looking for you.” Jesus answered, “Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?” Even a godly mother like Mary had to learn that this child belonged first to the heavenly Father.

Notice what comes next: Jesus “went down with them and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them.” Belonging to God does not mean parents lose their role. A steward still cares, guides and sets boundaries, but with a different heart. And Mary’s response is beautiful: “His mother kept all these sayings in her heart.” She did not understand, yet she did not grasp. She pondered and waited.

This week we have learned that children are God’s heritage and God’s masterpiece, that we should give them back to God and bless them. Today we review honestly: when did I become an owner again? We review not to beat ourselves up, but to correct our course. A steward does not need to be perfect. What the Master asks is faithfulness. When we stumble, we return to the Master and receive the trust again.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are how a new way of thinking truly takes root. Proud parents review only their children; humble parents ask first, “Was I more like Jesus this week?” Deal with your own heart first, then your child’s behavior; humility draws out humility, and the whole family is built up together.
q: Who is God? — The Father had a purpose for Jesus, and has a purpose for my child too. Are you willing to trust his plan?
Who am I? — In which moment this week was I like an owner? In which was I like a steward?
How should I respond? — What is the one thing I will adjust next week, and how, specifically, will I do it?
lessons.jesus: At twelve, Jesus knew clearly that he belonged to the Father, yet he still obeyed his earthly parents. He grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men. Jesus showed us a child who is under his parents’ stewardship and yet belongs wholly to the Father.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for walking back through this week with me. I admit that at times I treated my child as mine again, replacing trust with control, and prayer with anxiety. Please forgive me. Thank you also for the moments I acted like a steward. They are all your grace. As you helped Mary, teach me to keep what I don’t understand in my heart, and hand it to you. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: when were we most like owners this week? When were we most like stewards?
Ask your child, “Was Mom or Dad more like Jesus this week? Where could we do better?” Just listen, and don’t defend yourself
Write down one specific adjustment for next week, such as “bless the children every night” or “let my child decide one weekend matter”
lessons.noon: “His mother kept all these sayings in her heart.” — Lord, what I don’t understand, teach me to keep in my heart and give to you.

fam.key: I belong to the heavenly Father, and I love my family.

lamb.do: Play peekaboo with your child, and when you find them, hug them tight and say, “Found you!”
lamb.say: Mommy and Daddy always watch over you, and the heavenly Father watches over you even more.

sprout.story: When Jesus was twelve, he went with Mom and Dad to a faraway city for a festival. On the way home, Mom and Dad found that Jesus was missing! They were so worried. They looked for three days, and at last found him in God’s house. Jesus told them he was in his heavenly Father’s house! Then Jesus went home with Mom and Dad, obeyed them, and grew up day by day.
sprout.ask: Jesus loved the heavenly Father and also obeyed Mom and Dad. Can you do that too?
sprout.do: Play “growing taller”: your child starts crouching, and each time they say something they learned this week, they stand a little higher. At the end they stand tall and say, “I am growing day by day!”

soldier.story: When Jesus was twelve, he went to Jerusalem with his parents for the Passover. On the way home, Mary and Joseph thought Jesus was with their relatives and friends. After a day’s journey they found he was missing, hurried back, and searched for three days before finding him in the temple, talking with the teachers. His mother was upset, but Jesus said, “I must be in my Father’s house.” Mary did not understand, but she kept these things in her heart. After that, Jesus went home with his parents, obeyed them, and grew in wisdom and stature.
ask: Jesus belonged to the heavenly Father and also obeyed his parents. Do you think both can be true at once?
In what way do you feel you have “grown” this week?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person shares one thing they are thankful for this week and one thing they want to improve next week. Mom and Dad go first, and begin with where they fell short.

youth.talk: The twelve-year-old Jesus made his parents search for three days, and his mother said, “Your father and I were anxiously looking for you.” Sometimes we are like that too: worried and tense about you, and we end up saying hurtful things. All week we have been learning that you belong to the heavenly Father first, not to us. Mom and Dad want to admit first that this week we forgot a number of times, and treated you as ours again.
ask: Was there a moment this week when Mom and Dad made you feel controlled too much, or trusted?
How do you think a teenager who “belongs to the heavenly Father first” would get along with their parents?
youth.do: Parents first apologize to their child for one time this week they held on too tightly, then invite the child to make a small agreement together for next week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for caring for our whole family this week. There are things we did well and things we did wrongly. Please forgive us. Help us to be like Jesus, to love you and to love one another. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2.memT: Behold, children are a heritage of the LORD. The fruit of the womb is his reward.

mem.t: These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

sat.t: Family Day: Words on the Doorposts
sat.d: Make a “doorpost verse card” together. Cut a long strip of thick card and write Deuteronomy 6:6–7 on it. The children draw the border and decorations, and the little ones can add handprints. Stick it on the inside of the front door frame. Then play “sit, walk, lie down, rise up”: draw lots to decide whether you sit in the living room, take a walk around the neighbourhood, lie down as at bedtime, or stand up as on a morning, and each person tells one thing God has done in your family. Finally stand at the door and pray a blessing over everyone who comes in and goes out.

sun: Deuteronomy 6 says to put God’s words on your own heart first. Which of God’s words have you kept in your heart this week?
When is the most natural moment in your home to talk about faith? When is the hardest?
At which time next week (sitting, walking, lying down or rising up) will you regularly talk with your children about God? Think too about how you could encourage another family to start with you.

lessons.title: Talk of Them When You Sit, Walk, Lie Down and Rise
lessons.theme: Faith teaching happens in every moment of everyday life

v: Hear, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one.
You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart;
and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
You shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes.
You shall write them on the door posts of your house and on your gates.

lessons.still: Before the day begins, be quiet and listen first. Like the Israelites, let these words echo in your heart: “Hear, Israel!” Lord, I am here to listen to you.
teach: The Israelites were about to enter the Promised Land, and at the edge of the wilderness Moses gave the whole nation his last charge. He knew that in Canaan the houses would grow bigger, the barns would fill and life would get busier, and that what would most easily be lost was not the land but the faith of the next generation. So he said, “Hear, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.”

Then Moses brought this love into the home: “You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.” Notice that God did not say, “Send them to the synagogue for one lesson a week.” The main classroom for faith is not the church, but the dinner table, the car, the bedside and the kitchen in the morning. These four actions cover almost the whole day.

This is good news for busy modern parents. We don’t necessarily need to carve out an extra hour for family meetings. We can talk about God in the gaps that are already there: the ten minutes on the way to school, a few words at dinner, a prayer at bedtime. Like drops of water, over time they seep into a child’s heart and become the riverbed of their life.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard. Faith is not a subject to be taught, but a way of living. Change your thinking and you change your life; change your life and you change your daily living. When parents bring God’s word into sitting, walking, lying down and rising up, the home goes from being “a house where Christians live” to “a home where Christ reigns.”
q: Who is God? — God is the one Lord, and what he asks for is not part of me, but love with all my heart, soul and might. What kind of God does this show you?
Who am I? — Of the four moments of sitting, walking, lying down and rising up, what does my family talk about most? Is it God, or homework and phones?
How should I respond? — In which moment that already exists in our day can I add a sentence about God today?
lessons.jesus: When someone asked Jesus which commandment is the greatest, he answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength. This is the first commandment.” Jesus lived exactly like this: on the road, in the boat, at the table, he spoke about the Father to people wherever he was.
lessons.pray: One Lord, I want to listen to you. I admit I often treat faith as one Sunday matter, leaving my children’s spiritual life to the church while seldom speaking of you at home. Help me love you with all my heart first, and give me wisdom to bring your words to my children naturally as we sit, walk, lie down and rise up. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Copy Deuteronomy 6:7 onto a card and put it on the dinner table or in the car
Today, at one regular moment (breakfast, the car or bedtime), say one sentence from God’s word to your child
Tonight write down: when I talked with my child about God, how did they respond?
lessons.noon: “…shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.” — Lord, even in this busy moment, help me remember you.

fam.key: Wherever we are, we talk about God.

lamb.do: While changing a diaper, feeding or pushing the stroller, whisper “God loves you” to your child, so that these words become a voice they hear every day.
lamb.say: In the morning God loves you, and at night God loves you too.

sprout.story: Chenchen went to nursery in Daddy’s car every day. One day Daddy said, “Let’s play a game and see what we can spot on the road that God made!” Chenchen saw the blue sky and said, “God made it!” She saw a little bird fly by and said again, “God made it!” She saw a big tree and shouted, “God made that too!” From that day, the car ride became Chenchen’s favorite time.
sprout.ask: What did you see today that God made?
sprout.do: Play a “sit, walk, lie down, rise up” action game. When Mom or Dad says “sit,” everyone sits down and says “God loves me”; “walk” means walking on the spot; “lie down” means lying down; “rise” means jump up!

soldier.story: Moses led the Israelites through the wilderness for forty years. When they were about to enter a new land, he gathered everyone and said something very important: love God with all your heart, and teach God’s words to your children. When should you teach them? Sitting at home, walking on the road, lying down to sleep and getting up in the morning, you should talk about them. That means God’s word is not only for Sundays but should fill every day like the air. The Israelites even wrote God’s words on their doorposts, so that every time they went in or out they could see them.
ask: Which moment of the day do you think is best for our family to talk about God together?
If we were to write one of God’s sayings on our doorpost, which one would you choose?
soldier.do: Every day this week on the way to or from school, each of you shares with Mom or Dad one way God helped you today.

youth.talk: Deuteronomy says to talk about God when sitting, walking, lying down and rising up. Honestly, what we probably talk about most at home is homework, exams and “put your phone down.” Mom and Dad also admit that sometimes the way we talk about faith sounds like a lecture, and you just want it to end. We want to learn to change, not by adding another lesson, but by chatting sincerely about God in ordinary life.
ask: What kind of “talking about God” feels natural to you, and what kind feels awkward?
If we were to find one time in the day to talk about faith, which time do you think would be best?
youth.do: This week, when you are driving or riding together, parents first share one honest feeling or doubt they have recently had about God, then ask for the child’s thoughts. Just chat; don’t teach.

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, thank you that your word, like sunshine, is with us morning, noon and night. Help our whole family to remember you and talk about you every day. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: First on Your Own Heart
lessons.theme: Seeing myself: my child learns my life, not only my words

v: These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart;

Only be careful, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things which your eyes saw, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life; but make them known to your children and your children’s children—

the day that you stood before the LORD your God in Horeb, when the LORD said to me, “Assemble the people to me, and I will make them hear my words, that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children.”

lessons.still: Put your hand on your chest and feel your heartbeat. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, are your words on my heart, or only on my lips?” Let the Holy Spirit gently shine his light.
teach: The order in Deuteronomy 6 matters. First it says, “These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart,” and only then, “you shall teach them diligently to your children.” God’s word must be in the parents’ hearts first before it can flow into the children’s. It is like pouring water: the cup must be full before it overflows. An empty cup, however far you tilt it, pours out nothing.

In chapter 4, Moses also warned, “Only be careful, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things which your eyes saw,” and “make them known to your children and your children’s children.” What parents pass on is not only knowledge but what they have “seen with their own eyes.” Children don’t remember the grand principles we preach, but they remember how we faced unemployment, illness and conflict, and whether we prayed then.

Meilian in Penang took her three children to Sunday school every week, yet she had not had a quiet time with God for months. One day her eldest daughter asked, “Mom, do you talk to God too?” In that moment she was pierced to the heart. The Holy Spirit’s light often comes like this: not as a rebuke, but as a gentle question that shows us our own empty cup.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The most common mistake of parents is to try to use ministry (teaching the children) in place of life (our own walk with God). The order of relationships is first with God, then with people. When parents draw near to God first, faith teaching at home has a spring of living water and will not dry up.
q: Who is God? — God wants to put his words on my heart, not only give me rules. What kind of God draws so near?
Who am I? — Am I the “outsourcing” kind of parent who hands my child’s faith to the church, or the “preaching” kind who demands of my child what I do not live out?
How should I respond? — This week, how will I let God’s word enter my own heart first?
lessons.jesus: Even on the busiest days, Jesus, “early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.” He drew near to the Father first, and only then went out to teach and heal. His influence on his disciples was not only in his preaching but in the life they saw every day.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that I often want to “teach” faith to my children while my own heart is far from you. My cup is empty, yet I want to pour water for them. Forgive me, and fill me again. Let your words be on my heart first, and let my children see in my life that you are real. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Give yourself five minutes today to read just one verse and meditate on it repeatedly, without hurrying to teach it to anyone
Recall one thing God did that you “saw with your own eyes” in your life, and write it in three sentences
Ask yourself: when my children recently saw me under pressure, did I pray or lose my temper?
lessons.noon: “These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart.” — Lord, right now, fill my heart first.

fam.key: God’s word is in my heart.

lamb.do: Let your child put their little hand on your chest and then on their own, and speak while you pat gently.
lamb.say: God’s word lives in Mommy and Daddy’s hearts, and in your heart too.

sprout.story: Xiaole held an empty cup and wanted to pour water for the puppy, but however he tipped it, nothing came out. Mom smiled and said, “The cup has to be filled with water first before you can pour it out!” Mom filled the cup with water, and when Xiaole tipped it, the water came splashing out. Mom said, “Our hearts are like cups too. They must be filled with God’s word first, and then we can share love with others.”
sprout.ask: Which of God’s sayings would you like to put in your heart today?
sprout.do: Get two cups, one empty and one full of water. Let your child try to pour from the empty cup, then from the full one, and then say, “God, please fill my heart!”

soldier.story: Moses told the Israelites: be careful not to forget what you saw God do with your own eyes: the Red Sea parting, manna falling from the sky, water flowing from the rock. These were not stories from a textbook but their own experiences. Moses said to tell these things to your children and grandchildren. Why? Because God’s word must be in the grown-ups’ hearts first before it can be passed to the next generation. It is like a relay race: you must have the baton in your hand before you can pass it on.
ask: What do you think Mom and Dad have “seen with their own eyes” God do? You can ask them!
Is there something you have “seen with your own eyes” where God helped you?
soldier.do: Tonight interview Mom or Dad: “When was the most real time you experienced God?” Write or draw their answer.

youth.talk: Moses says God’s word must be on the parents’ hearts first, and then they teach their children. To be honest, you may have seen us be one person at church and another at home; we ask you to read the Bible, but seldom read it ourselves. That is not your problem, it is ours. Mom and Dad are learning to let God’s word enter our own hearts first, and not just use it to manage you.
ask: Where do you think it is easiest to tell whether a person’s faith is “real” or “not real”?
Have you seen a moment in our family when you felt that Mom and Dad’s faith was real?
youth.do: This week parents share a passage they are reading and a real struggle, and invite the children to ask questions, without hurrying to give answers.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, please put your word in my heart, like filling a cup with water. And help Mom and Dad’s hearts to be full of your love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: A Covenant for Generation after Generation
lessons.theme: I believe: God is the God of our family for generations

v: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your offspring after you.

For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of the LORD, to do righteousness and justice; to the end that the LORD may bring on Abraham that which he has spoken of him.”

lessons.still: Imagine a very old tree, its roots in soil from hundreds of years ago, its branches reaching to your child’s grandchildren. Meditate quietly: God’s covenant is longer than my whole life.
teach: God said to Abraham, “I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your offspring after you.” When God makes a covenant, he never looks at only one generation, but at “generations.” He is not only Abraham’s God, but also Isaac’s God and Jacob’s God. God’s heart is for faith to pass from one generation to the next.
