God also explained Abraham’s role in this covenant: “I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of the LORD.” God makes the covenant, and the power to keep it also comes from God, but the father is to take up the responsibility to instruct, teach and lead. God faithfully holds to his side, and parents faithfully hold to theirs.

This is a great comfort to Chinese Christian families. Some are the first generation in their family to believe, with no spiritual inheritance behind them; some have parents who believe while they themselves stumble along. In the New Testament, Peter declares, “For the promise is to you and to your children.” All who are in Christ are Abraham’s offspring. Your family’s story of faith can begin with your generation, and God’s covenant will continue in your children.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of perspective: from the temporary to the eternal, from one generation to many. If a parent’s eyes stop at this exam or this term, they become anxious; if they can see God’s covenant for generations, they can rest, and sow more faithfully. Building what belongs to God begins with the inheritance of one family.
q: Who is God? — God is the God of “generations,” and his covenant does not fail because of one generation’s weakness. What hope does this give you?
Who am I? — Which generation of faith am I in my family? What do I want to leave for the next?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe God is the God of our family for…; I believe God’s covenant will…; I believe my part is…
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus lifted the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.” The promise of the old covenant is fulfilled in Jesus. Our family can enter God’s covenant not by bloodline or effort, but by the precious blood of Jesus.
lessons.pray: Faithful God, thank you for being the God of every generation. I believe you are not only my God, but will be my children’s God, and my children’s children’s God. Help me to be faithful in my generation, as Abraham was, to command my household to keep your way, and to trust that you will fulfill your promise in the next generation. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations, for example: “I believe God is the God of our family for generations.”
Draw a simple family tree of faith: who was first to believe? Who has prayed for you?
Pray for one minute for your children’s future children, entrusting the third generation to God too
lessons.noon: “I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations.” — Faithful Lord, be the God of our family for generations.

fam.key: God is the God of every generation of our family.

lamb.do: Let your child look at a photo of the whole family and, pointing to Grandpa and Grandma, Mom and Dad and themselves, name each person.
lamb.say: God loves Grandpa and Grandma, God loves Mommy and Daddy, and God loves you too.

sprout.story: One night God took Abraham outside and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Abraham looked up and the whole sky was full of twinkling stars. God said his family would one day be as many as the stars! God said, “I will be your God, and also the God of your children, and your children’s children.” Our family is one little star in that great sky of stars too!
sprout.ask: Do you know who was the first person in our family to know Jesus?
sprout.do: Stick or draw lots of stars on black paper, write a family member’s name on each, and at the end write beside them, “God is our family’s God!”

soldier.story: God made a covenant with Abraham, like a promise that can never be canceled: God would be Abraham’s God, and also the God of his children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, from one generation to the next. God also said that Abraham was to teach his children and his whole household to follow God’s way. Later, Isaac came to know God, and Jacob came to know God too. Today, everyone who believes in Jesus has become part of Abraham’s spiritual family. This covenant has been passed all the way to our family.
ask: What do you think is the difference between faith “passed from generation to generation” and believing on your own?
Do you hope that your own family in the future will also be a family that knows God?
soldier.do: Interview Grandpa and Grandma (a video call is fine) and ask how they came to know God, or ask them to tell a family story, and then pray for them.

youth.talk: God told Abraham he would be God to his offspring “throughout their generations.” Some families have believed for several generations, some began with Mom and Dad, and in some only we believe in the whole family. We don’t want to pressure you, as if you must continue our faith; faith is between you and God. But we want to tell you that God’s promise is for you too. He is willing to be your own God, not just Mom and Dad’s God.
ask: What do you think is the difference between “Mom and Dad’s God” and “my God”?
Do you have any questions or thoughts about our family’s inheritance of faith?
youth.do: Parents and children draw a “family tree of faith” together, and parents honestly share how they came to believe, including their doubts and weakness.

fam.pray: Faithful heavenly Father, thank you for being Grandpa and Grandma’s God, Mom and Dad’s God, and my God too. Please let our family love you generation after generation. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Tell Your Children What God Has Done
lessons.theme: Today, tell one story of God in our family

v: We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.
For he established a covenant in Jacob, and appointed a teaching in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children;
that the generation to come might know, even the children who should be born; who should arise and tell their children,
that they might set their hope in God, and not forget God’s deeds, but keep his commandments,

lessons.still: Open the drawer of memory and find one thing God has done in your family: a provision, a healing, a turning point. Give thanks quietly, and let that feeling grow warm again.
teach: Psalm 78 says, “We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.” The most powerful tool for passing on faith is not a curriculum but a story. If God’s wondrous deeds are not told, the next generation will not know them; Judges records that another generation arose who “didn’t know the LORD, nor the work which he had done for Israel.”

The psalmist sees a chain of four generations: our fathers, ourselves, the generation to come, and their children. Each generation is to “arise and tell their children,” so that “they might set their hope in God, and not forget God’s deeds.” When children hear what God did for their parents, they will remember to look to the same God when they meet their own difficulties. Stories are like seeds: buried today, they sprout many years later.

Jianbang and Xiaowen, a working couple in Vancouver, decided to take turns telling a “God in our family” story at dinner every Friday: how, just after emigrating, they could not find work and brothers from church sent a box of vegetables; how, when their daughter was born early, the whole church prayed for her. What the children liked best was Dad telling how frightened he had been. A true story passes on faith better than a perfect sermon.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice is the key step of change. Parents need not only to know “we should pass it on” but to open their mouths today. Let Jesus receive all the glory: telling of God’s deeds gives the glory to God, not to our own efforts, and each time we tell it, our children come to know God a little more.
q: Who is God? — What wonderful thing has God done in your home? What did it show you of the kind of God he is?
Who am I? — Do I often tell my children about my achievements and hard work, or about what God has done?
How should I respond? — Which “God in our family” story will I tell my children today?
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus walked with two disciples on the road to Emmaus, and “beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.” Afterward they said, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way?” Jesus told of God’s deeds on the road, and set hearts on fire.
lessons.pray: Lord, you have done so many wonderful things in my life and in my family, and I have often not told my children. Today please help me open my mouth and honestly tell of your faithfulness, including my weakness and your grace. May my children hear it, set their hope in you and not forget your deeds. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: At dinner or bedtime today, tell one true “God in our family” story, in under five minutes
Start a “record of God’s deeds” notebook, and write down the first one, with the date
Ask your child, “What do you think God has done in our family lately?”
lessons.noon: “Telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.” — Lord, today give me an opportunity to tell my children about you.

fam.key: We tell what God has done.

lamb.do: Hold your child and look at their baby photos, and say simply one thing you thank God for.
lamb.say: When you were born, God took good care of you. Thank you, God!

sprout.story: At bedtime Grandpa said to Xiaoan, “When Grandpa was little, we lived in the countryside. One year a typhoon damaged our house, and we were all very scared. The uncles and aunties from church came to help, fixed the house with us, and brought rice for us to eat. That was when Grandpa knew that God was really looking after our family.” Xiaoan said, “Grandpa, I want to remember that God looks after our family too!”
sprout.ask: Do you remember something God did to help our family?
sprout.do: Take a little jar as a “thank-you jar.” Each person says one thing God has helped us with, draws it on a small slip of paper and puts it in.

soldier.story: The psalm writer says that we should not hide what God has done but tell it to our children, and when they grow up they should tell their own children. It is like a relay race, passing the baton from one runner to the next. The Bible also has a frightening example: after Joshua’s generation passed away, the next generation did not know God, or what God had done for Israel. Why? Perhaps because the grown-ups forgot to tell them. That is why every story of God deserves to be told.
ask: Which story of God would you most like to hear Mom and Dad tell?
If you have children in the future, which thing God did for you would you tell them?
soldier.do: Start a family “record of God’s deeds” notebook, and you do the illustrations. Tonight, write down the first story Mom or Dad tells.

youth.talk: Psalm 78 says to tell God’s deeds to the next generation. We have realized that we seldom tell you the real stories of our faith, especially the parts about fear, failure and doubt. Perhaps we were afraid you would see our weakness. But we want to tell you that God helped us most truly in our weakest moments.
ask: What would you like to know about Mom and Dad’s journey of faith? You can ask anything.
Is there something in your own life so far that you could call a “deed of God”?
youth.do: This week each parent tells a story of a time in their life when God truly stepped in, and then invites the children to ask questions, anything at all.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for doing so many things for our family. Help us remember, and tell your stories to others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: When Your Child Asks: What Does This Mean?
lessons.theme: Review and Adjust: let your child’s questions be a door to passing on faith

v: When your son asks you in time to come, saying, “What do the testimonies, the statutes, and the ordinances, which the LORD our God has commanded you mean?”
then you shall tell your son, “We were Pharaoh’s slaves in Egypt. The LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand;
and the LORD showed great and awesome signs and wonders on Egypt, on Pharaoh, and on all his house, before our eyes;
and he brought us out from there, that he might bring us in, to give us the land which he swore to our fathers.
The LORD commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the LORD our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive, as we are today.
It shall be righteousness to us, if we observe to do all these commandments before the LORD our God, as he has commanded us.”

lessons.still: Look back over this week. What questions did your child ask you, about God, about life, about themselves? Recall them slowly, and ask the Holy Spirit to look with you at how you responded in those moments.
teach: Moses foretold a scene: “When your son asks you in time to come, saying, ‘What do the testimonies, the statutes, and the ordinances, which the LORD our God has commanded you mean?’” God expected children to ask questions, and treated the child’s question as the doorway for passing on faith. The parent’s answer is not a list of rules but a story: “We were Pharaoh’s slaves in Egypt. The LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.”

Chinese parents often treat a child’s questions as a challenge to authority: “Why so many whys? Just do as you’re told!” But in Deuteronomy a child asking “why” is a good thing. It shows they are beginning to think, and their faith is about to move from their parents’ to their own. We don’t need perfect answers, but we do need an honest attitude: “This is what I have lived, and this is what God did for us.”

This week we learned to talk about God when we sit, walk, lie down and rise up, to keep God’s word on our own hearts first, to believe that God is God for generations, and to tell of God’s deeds. Today we review honestly: did I talk with my child about God this week? When my child asked questions, did I open the door or close it? Don’t condemn yourself. Just find one thing you can adjust next week.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the necessary road to a changed way of thinking. Humble parents are not afraid of their children’s questions, nor of saying, “I don’t know. Let’s find the answer together.” When parents are humble, children are willing to open up. Humility draws out humility, and the whole family grows together.
q: Who is God? — God expected children to ask questions, and put the answers in the story of his salvation. What kind of teacher is he?
Who am I? — When my child asked questions this week, did I open the door or close it? What kind of question do I fear most?
How should I respond? — What is the one thing I will adjust next week, and how, specifically, will I do it?
lessons.jesus: Thomas asked Jesus honestly, “Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?” Jesus did not rebuke him, but gave the most precious answer: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” Jesus welcomes sincere questions, and answers them with himself.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for going back through this week with me. I admit that sometimes when my child asks questions I find it annoying, or close the door with “just do as you’re told.” Please forgive me. Thank you also for the times I was able to talk with my child about you. They are all your grace. Give me patience and wisdom, so that every question my child asks becomes a door to knowing you. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: when was “talking about God” most natural in our family this week? When did we miss it most?
Ask your child, “Was Mom or Dad more like Jesus this week? Is there a question you have wanted to ask but haven’t?” Just listen, and don’t defend yourself
Write down one specific adjustment for next week, such as “pray together every day when I take the children to school”
lessons.noon: “We were Pharaoh’s slaves in Egypt. The LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand” — Lord, prepare my heart to answer my child’s questions with the story of how you saved me.

fam.key: I can ask, and God loves to answer.

lamb.do: When your child makes a sound or points at something, crouch down, look into their eyes, respond seriously, and say the name of the thing.
lamb.say: You are talking to me, and I love to listen. God loves to listen to you too.

sprout.story: Xiaoyu kept asking, “Mom, why do we pray before we eat?” Mom didn’t say, “Just do as you’re told.” She crouched down and said, “Because our family used to be very poor and often had nothing to eat, and God kept providing for us. So every time we eat, we thank God.” Xiaoyu nodded and said, “Then today I’ll thank God out loud!”
sprout.ask: Is there a question about God that you want to ask Mom and Dad?
sprout.do: Play “question treasure box”: each person thinks of a question about God, Mom and Dad help write it on paper and put it in the box, and every day you pick one to talk about together.

soldier.story: Moses said that in the future your children will ask, “Why do we have to keep these rules?” When that happens, don’t say, “Just do as you’re told.” Tell them a story: we used to be slaves in Egypt, and God rescued us with his mighty hand and brought us to this good land. So we keep God’s word, not because we are afraid, but because we are thankful. It turns out that behind God’s rules is always God’s love.
ask: Is there a rule that seems strange to you, and you would like to know why?
What do you think is the difference between obeying because you are afraid and obeying because you are thankful?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person shares one thing they are thankful for this week and one thing they want to improve next week. Mom and Dad go first, then let the children ask one “why” question and talk about it together.

youth.talk: Deuteronomy says that when a child asks, “What does this mean?” the parent is to tell a story of God’s rescue. We admit that sometimes when you ask questions about faith we get nervous, as if you were doubting something, and we hurry to give the standard answer, or even get a little angry. In fact, it is a good thing that you are willing to ask. This week we also want to review whether we have made you feel safe to ask.
ask: Is there a question about faith you have kept in your heart and not dared to ask?
When Mom and Dad answer questions, which way makes you most willing to keep talking?
youth.do: Parents first apologize to their child for one response this week that “closed the door,” then arrange a time when the child can ask anything about faith, and look into it together.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you love us to ask questions, and love to answer us. Please forgive what we did wrongly this week, and help us love you more and love one another more next week. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

3.memT: These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

mem.t: If it seems evil to you to serve the LORD, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

sat.t: Family Day: Our Family Vision Banner
sat.d: Get an old piece of cloth or a large sheet of paper, colored pens and stickers, and design “our family vision banner” together. Write the family vision statement you set this week in the middle, and let each person draw a picture around it that stands for your family, such as a dinner table, a cross, an open door or a pair of hands. The little ones can add handprints. Hang it in the living room, then stand in front of it and read Joshua 24:15 aloud together, and pray over the vision. You could also take a photo and send it to a friend’s family to share your vision.

sun: Joshua said, “as for me and my house.” In what matter this week do you need to make a clear choice for your whole family?
What did your family vision statement say? What did you discover, as a couple or as parent and child, while writing it?
How can your family become an “outpost” of God’s Kingdom among your neighbors? Which family would you like to invite for a meal or for prayer next week?

lessons.title: As for Me and My House
lessons.theme: Every family serves something; parents must choose for the whole household

v: “Now therefore fear the LORD, and serve him in sincerity and in truth. Put away the gods which your fathers served beyond the River, in Egypt; and serve the LORD.

If it seems evil to you to serve the LORD, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”

lessons.still: Be still, as if standing at a fork in the road. On the left is the voice of the world; on the right is the voice of God. Say to the Lord: “Lord, today I choose you once again.”
teach: When Joshua was old, he gathered all the tribes of Israel at Shechem and looked back over how God had led them from Abraham to the entry into Canaan. Finally he set a choice before everyone: “Choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell.” The options were not only the LORD. There were also the gods of their ancestors and the idols popular in the land.

While the people were still hesitating, Joshua spoke first: “But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” He did not wait for the whole nation to decide before he followed, and he did not say, “Let’s see what the children choose later.” As head of his household, he set the direction for his family. A family’s direction is often decided by one clear choice made by its parents.

Chinese families today face the same fork in the road: the values handed down from our ancestors (bringing honor to the family, getting ahead) and the popular culture of the place we live (success, pleasure, comparison). Every family serves something, whether or not they say so aloud. God invites every pair of parents to say clearly, as Joshua did: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The two cores: let Jesus reign; let Jesus receive all the glory. If a family does not choose Jesus as king, something else will take the throne: grades, money, face, or the parents themselves. Building what belongs to God begins with the parents’ clear choice.
q: Who is God? — Joshua made his choice after looking back at how God had led them. In your family’s history, how has God proved he is worth serving?
Who am I? — If someone watched our family for a month, what would they say we serve?
How should I respond? — Today, in one sentence, I will tell my spouse or my children the choice I have made for this family.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” His whole life had one direction: to serve the Father. In the wilderness he refused the glory of all the kingdoms of the world, and in Gethsemane he chose the Father’s will. Jesus is the perfect example of someone who makes a clear choice.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that our family often wavers between two roads, saying with our lips that we serve you while our hearts chase other things. Today I choose, as Joshua did: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. Give me strength to lead this family, and be the Lord of our home. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” and read it aloud three times
Find a moment today to tell your spouse, “I want to lead this family with you in serving God.”
List the three things our family spends the most time and money on, and honestly look at what they say
lessons.noon: “But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” — Lord, right now I choose you once again.

fam.key: My family and I will serve God.

lamb.do: Carry your child around each room of the house, and softly say in each one, “God, this place belongs to you.”
lamb.say: Our home is God’s home, and we all love Jesus.

sprout.story: Grandfather Joshua was a brave leader. One day he called everyone together and asked whom they would choose to follow. Everyone looked at one another and said nothing. Grandfather Joshua stood up and said loudly, “As for me and my family, we will serve the LORD!” When the people heard it, they said they would follow God too!
sprout.ask: Would you like to choose to follow God, like Joshua?
sprout.do: Stand in a line as a family. Mom or Dad calls out, “Whom will our family follow?” and everyone raises their hand and shouts together, “Follow Jesus!”

soldier.story: Joshua led the Israelites to many victories and into the land God had promised. When he was old, he gathered everyone and said: choose whom you will serve. The idols your ancestors worshiped, the false gods of the people in this land, or the LORD? While everyone was still thinking, Joshua spoke first: “As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” He did not wait for others. He decided first for himself and his family. Whom a family follows matters very much.
ask: Why do you think Joshua said his choice “first”?
At school or among friends, what makes it hard to choose to follow God?
soldier.do: Copy Joshua 24:15 onto a card, decorate it, and put it on your desk. Read it aloud once a day this week.

youth.talk: Joshua said, “As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” We want to say honestly: choosing to follow God is a decision Mom and Dad have made for ourselves, and the direction we want to set for this family. But we know that your faith cannot be chosen for you by us. We will do our best to live it out, and we want to hear what you really think, including your doubts.
ask: What do you think is the biggest rival to “following God” for your generation?
What do you think our family actually values most right now? Is it the same as what we say?
youth.do: Parents honestly share why they first chose to follow Jesus, then ask their child, “How do you think you would make this choice now?” Just listen; don’t comment.

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, we choose to follow you. Be the king of our family, and help us love you and listen to you every day. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: What Is Our Family Really Serving?
lessons.theme: Seeing myself: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also

v: for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.

lessons.still: Open your phone’s calendar or your budget book, and quietly look at where last month’s time and money went. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you: “Lord, what do these numbers say about where my heart is?”
teach: Jesus said, “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” He also said, “No one can serve two masters,” and “You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” Jesus did not say we “should not” serve two masters, but that we “can’t.” The heart has only one throne. Either God sits on it, or something else does.

Many Christian parents say with their lips that “God comes first,” but their calendars tell a different story: weekends are packed with tutoring and activities, Sunday worship is often missed, and in the family budget education and the mortgage take up most of it, leaving only crumbs for giving and serving. We may not bow to ancestral tablets, but we may unknowingly make our children’s future, the family’s security or other people’s opinion the god we actually serve.

Jiahao and Peishan in Singapore did a calculation and found that their family spent more than ten hours a week on tutoring runs, but less than ten minutes praying together. They did not blame themselves. They knelt down together and said, “Lord, we see it.” The Holy Spirit’s light is meant to bring us back before the right throne, not to crush us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your eyes on Jesus: not on yourself, not on others, not on circumstances. A self-ruled family seems to be centered on the children, but is really centered on the parents’ anxiety and expectations. Only when we see what we truly serve can we humbly give the throne back to Jesus and bring the family back into right order.
q: Who is God? — God will not share our hearts with other masters, because he knows only he can satisfy us. What kind of love is this?
Who am I? — Judging by our family’s time, money and emotions, what is really sitting on the throne?
How should I respond? — In what matter am I willing to give the throne back to Jesus?
lessons.jesus: The devil showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their glory and asked him to fall down and worship him. Jesus answered, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.” He refused the shortcut and the glory and served the Father wholeheartedly. Jesus overcame temptation, and he can help us overcome the idols in our home.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light on our home. I admit that we say with our lips that you come first, yet in practice we often put grades, security and face before you. Forgive us, and tear down the idols in our hearts. We are willing to give the throne back to you. Be the Lord of our family again. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Write down the three things our family spent the most time on this week, and beside each write: “Is this what I serve?”
Choose one activity you can cut back, and replace it with ten minutes of family prayer or conversation
Share with your spouse one “little idol” in your own heart, and pray for each other
lessons.noon: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” — Lord, be the only treasure in my heart.

fam.key: Jesus is number one in our family.

lamb.do: Put your child’s favorite toy to one side, open your arms, and let your child choose to crawl to the toy or into your embrace, then hold them tight.
lamb.say: You are a treasure, and Jesus is our greatest treasure.

sprout.story: Xiaojie had a dinosaur toy he loved more than anything. He took it everywhere, hugged it to eat and hugged it to sleep, and even played with it while he prayed. Mom said gently, “Xiaojie, the dinosaur is cute, but it can’t listen to your prayers or keep you safe. Jesus is the one who loves you most!” Xiaojie thought for a moment, put the dinosaur to one side, closed his eyes and said, “Jesus, I love you!”
sprout.ask: What is your favorite thing? Is Jesus your favorite too?
sprout.do: Play “number one”: line up a few toys, put a card with a cross on it at the front, and say together, “Jesus is number one!”

soldier.story: Jesus said that no one can serve two masters at once. It is like a soccer player who cannot wear two teams’ shirts in the same match: at some moment he has to decide which goal to kick toward. Jesus also said, where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. If what a person loves most is games, pocket money or match results, their heart will keep thinking about those things. God wants us to love him most, because only he will never let us down.
ask: What do you think your heart thinks about most these days?
What do you think our family thinks about most?
soldier.do: Make a “pie chart of my time”: draw a circle and divide up how much of your day goes to school, homework, play, screens and God. Look at it together with Mom and Dad.

youth.talk: Jesus said, where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Honestly, when Mom and Dad looked back at our family calendar and spending, we found that we say God is most important, but what takes the most time and money is tutoring, grades and your future. What does that make you feel is most important? We want to admit this gap, and think again together.
ask: What do you think is really “number one” in our family? It’s okay to be honest.
Is there something in your own heart that is often more important than God?
youth.do: Parents and children look at a week’s calendar together, each choose one thing that could be cut back, and replace it with some family time or one-on-one time.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, you are our greatest treasure. Help us love you most, more than toys, phones or anything else. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Write the Vision on Tablets
lessons.theme: I believe: God has a heart for our family, and we will write it down

v: The LORD answered me, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it.
For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it, because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
Where there is no revelation, the people cast off restraint; but one who keeps the law is blessed.

lessons.still: Imagine an evening ten years from now. Your children are grown, and the whole family is sitting around the dinner table. What do you hope your family is like then? Ask the Lord quietly: “Lord, what is your heart for our family?”
teach: Proverbs says, “Where there is no revelation, the people cast off restraint.” To “cast off restraint” means to lose all discipline and scatter in every direction, like sheep without a shepherd. If a family has no shared direction, everyone is busy on their own: parents with work, children with homework and phones. They live under the same roof, but their hearts are scattered, like people in one boat each rowing their own way.

God said to the prophet Habakkuk, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it.” A vision should be written down, simple and clear, so that even a child can read it. God also said, “Though it takes time, wait for it, because it will surely come.” A family vision is not fulfilled overnight. It is a direction that pulls the whole family back on track, again and again, through long days.

A family vision statement need not be long. Three or five sentences are enough. For example: “We are a family where Jesus reigns. We love each other and forgive each other. We open our door and bless our neighbors.” It is not to look good hanging on a wall, but to declare a conviction: I believe God has a heart for our family; I believe this home is an outpost of God’s Kingdom on earth.
lessons.light: 321 Light: One purpose: build what belongs to God. The smallest unit of change in the church, the workplace and society is the family. A vision statement says clearly why our family exists. When we move from a human point of view to God’s, the family is not only for living well ourselves, but for the Kingdom of God.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who gives the vision and also fulfills it. What might his heart be for your family?
Who am I? — Is our family a family with direction right now, or a family where everyone is busy on their own and “casting off restraint”?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe God’s heart for our family is…; and try writing a three-sentence draft of a family vision statement.
lessons.jesus: Jesus, “for the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, despising its shame.” He knew his mission clearly throughout his life, and so he could endure to the end. People with a vision can survive hardship, because what they see is not only what is in front of them, but the future God has promised.
lessons.pray: God who gives vision, I believe you have a good heart for our family. I admit that our family often has no direction and everyone is busy on their own. Place your heart clearly in mine, so that I can write it down, speak it out and live it. Though it takes time, I am willing to wait, because what you have promised will surely come. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” sentences, for example: “I believe God will use our family to bless our neighbors.”
Try a three-sentence draft of a family vision statement, and discuss it with your family tomorrow
Share with your spouse: when our children grow up, what kind of family do we most want them to remember?
lessons.noon: “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it.” — Lord, write your heart for our family clearly on my heart.

fam.key: God has a wonderful plan for our family.

lamb.do: Take your child to the window or balcony, point to the distant sky, a tree or a house, and slowly speak your blessing over them.
lamb.say: God has a wonderful plan for you, and Mommy and Daddy can’t wait.

sprout.story: Xiaoxin and Daddy were going to the park. Daddy drew a little map: start at the front door, pass the shop, turn at the big tree, and there is the park! Xiaoxin held the map and didn’t get lost at all. Daddy said, “God gives our family a map too, showing us which way to go: love God, love our family, and help others.” Xiaoxin said, “Then our family won’t get lost!”
sprout.ask: Where do you think God wants our family to go?
sprout.do: Draw “our family’s map” together: start from home and draw the places we want to go, such as “love God,” “love our family” and “help our neighbors.”

soldier.story: God told the prophet Habakkuk, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it.” This means God’s plan should be written down so clearly that even someone running past can understand it at a glance. Many sports teams have a slogan, and schools have a motto, to remind everyone what they are working for. A family can have its own “family motto” too, to remind everyone: why does our family exist? What kind of family do we want to be?
ask: If our family had a motto, what would you like it to be?
What do you think is most special about our family, and what would you most like others to see?
soldier.do: Each person writes one sentence for “our family motto.” Tomorrow the whole family will join everyone’s sentences into one vision statement.

youth.talk: Proverbs says, “Where there is no revelation, the people cast off restraint.” We have noticed that we seldom talk about “what kind of family we are,” and more often talk about what mark you will get or which school you will go to. Mom and Dad would like to try writing a family vision statement, but we don’t want to write it ourselves and then tell you to follow it. Your voice matters, because this is your home too.
ask: What kind of family do you hope ours will become? Describe it in three words.
Is there a family you really admire? What is special about them?
youth.do: Parents show their child their draft vision statement and invite them to change it, delete something, or add a sentence in their own words.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for having a wonderful plan for our family. Lead us on your way so that we don’t get lost, and we can love you and love others together. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Light for the Household and for Our Neighbors
lessons.theme: Today, let our home be an outpost of God’s Kingdom

v: “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

lessons.still: Imagine a lamp burning by the window at night, where everyone passing by can see it. Meditate quietly: Lord, whom can our family’s lamp light up today?
teach: Jesus said, “Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.” In ancient Jewish homes there was usually only one room, and a lamp set on a high place lit the whole household. The first circle of light is “all who are in the house”: our family members are the first to see whether we really follow Jesus. If we serve zealously outside but come home cold and short-tempered, the lamp is covered by the basket.

But Jesus went on, “Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” A Christian home is not a closed castle but “a city located on a hill,” an outpost of God’s Kingdom on earth. Neighbors, classmates and colleagues often notice a family first, and only then become curious about that family’s God.

Shufen, a single mother in Ipoh with two children, doesn’t have an easy life. Her family’s vision is “a home with an open door”: each month they invite an elderly person who lives alone to a simple dinner, and the children set the table and say grace. The light does not depend on how big or perfect the home is, but on whether we are willing to put the lamp on the stand. Today, let the whole family settle the vision together and do one small thing to light up someone else.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory. The purpose of good works is not for others to say, “What a lovely family,” but for people to “glorify your Father who is in heaven.” When a family lives out God’s heart, it is building what belongs to God: one family influences another, one generation influences the next.
q: Who is God? — God is light, and he makes our home light. Whom does he want to light up through your family?
Who am I? — Is our family’s lamp on the stand, or often covered by a “basket” (busyness, weariness, fear of trouble)?
How should I respond? — What small thing can the whole family do together today to light up someone else?
lessons.jesus: Jesus went into the house of Zacchaeus, the tax collector everyone looked down on, and he was changed because of Jesus and was willing to give back what he had taken wrongly. Jesus said, “Today, salvation has come to this house.” When Jesus enters a home, that home becomes a light, and even lights up the whole city.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the light of the world. Thank you for making our home a light too. I admit that we often hide the lamp and care only for our own home. Today please help us put the lamp on the stand, lighting up first everyone in our home, and then our neighbors, so that people glorify our Father because of our family. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Tonight, as a whole family, discuss and finalize the family vision statement, and have everyone sign it
As a family, do one small thing to light up a neighbor: send a card, a snack, or pray for a neighbor
Take a photo of the vision statement and use it as the wallpaper on the family’s phones, or stick it by the door
lessons.noon: “Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.” — Lord, today make our family a light.

fam.key: Our family is a lamp for God.

lamb.do: Switch off the lights and turn on a small flashlight. Let the light shine on your child’s little hands, then on each family member’s face, calling each name in turn.
lamb.say: Jesus is the light, and you are Mommy and Daddy’s little light.

sprout.story: One night the power went out, and the house was pitch dark. Little sister was so scared that she cried. Big brother quickly found a little candle, and Mom lit it, and at once the whole room was bright and everyone could see. Mom said, “Jesus says we should be like this candle, so that our home and our neighbors can see the light.” Little sister stopped crying and smiled. “I want to be a little candle too!”
sprout.ask: How can you be our family’s little candle?
sprout.do: As a family, make a “love card” to give to a neighbor or the building caretaker. The children do the drawing.

soldier.story: Jesus said, “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.” In the old days there were no street lights, and a traveler at night only had to see the lights of a city on a hill to know which way to go. Jesus also said that nobody lights a lamp and covers it with a basket. They put it up high to light the whole house. Our family is a lamp too: when we love one another at home and are kind to our neighbors, others will see it, and want to know why we live like this, and then come to know our Father in heaven.
ask: How do you think our family can “light up” our neighbors or classmates?
If our family’s lamp were “covered,” what might be the reason?
soldier.do: As a family, finalize our family vision statement and have everyone sign it, then choose a neighbor’s or friend’s home and do one thing for them this week.

youth.talk: Jesus said a city on a hill can’t be hidden. Actually, our family has always been seen: neighbors, your classmates, and our colleagues are all watching what a Christian family is like. To be honest, sometimes our family does not look attractive, and Mom and Dad share the responsibility. But we would like to try together to make our home a place with an open door, where people feel warmth.
ask: Do you have a friend who needs a warm place or a meal?
Are you willing to work with us to make our home a place friends can come to? What do you think would need to change?
youth.do: As a family, finalize the vision statement, and ask your child to invite a friend to dinner at home this month. Parents prepare, and the child decides the menu.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, you are the light of the world. Please make our family a lamp too, lighting up the people at home and our neighbors. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Set Up a Stone as a Witness
lessons.theme: Review and Adjust: remember the covenant, and keep walking

v: The people said to Joshua, “We will serve the LORD our God, and we will listen to his voice.”
So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and made for them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem.
Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God; and he took a great stone, and set it up there under the oak that was by the sanctuary of the LORD.

Joshua said to all the people, “Behold, this stone shall be a witness against us, for it has heard all the LORD’s words which he spoke to us. It shall be therefore a witness against you, lest you deny your God.”

lessons.still: Look back over this week: from Joshua’s choice, to seeing the idols in your home, to writing the vision, to lighting up your neighbors. Slowly turn through the pictures of these days, and ask the Holy Spirit to help you see honestly.
teach: The people answered Joshua, “We will serve the LORD our God, and we will listen to his voice.” Joshua was not content to leave it there. He wrote these words in the book of the law of God, and set up a great stone, saying, “Behold, this stone shall be a witness against us.” A choice needs to be remembered, because people forget so easily. Today’s zeal may be washed out by tomorrow’s busyness.

The stone was a visible reminder. In the days that followed, every time the Israelites passed Shechem and saw that great stone, they would remember: we once made a covenant before God. A family needs a “witness stone” too: a vision statement on the wall, a notebook recording God’s deeds, a regular family prayer time. They cannot make us holy, but they can pull us back to our first choice, again and again.

The Bible records: “Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, and had known all the work of the LORD, that he had worked for Israel.” One person’s choice influenced a whole generation. Today we review this week: is our family’s choice clear? Have we written down the vision? Is there anywhere that needs adjusting? Don’t condemn yourself. Just find the next step.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition, and finally multiplication. If a family’s vision is not reviewed regularly, it slowly fades; if it is remembered, adjusted and lived out again and again, it will influence the next generation, and even other families. Humble parents review themselves first, then invite the whole family to adjust together.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who makes covenants and faithfully keeps them. Where did you experience his faithfulness this week?
Who am I? — Did our family live out “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” this week? Where did we drift?
How should I respond? — What is the one thing I will adjust next week? What kind of “witness stone” will our family set up?
lessons.jesus: In his last prayer Jesus said to the Father, “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.” He was faithful from his first choice to the very end. Jesus is not only our example but our strength: when we fall, he lifts us up so that we can keep going to the end of the road.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for walking with our family through this week. I admit that our choices are sometimes clear and sometimes waver. Forgive our drifting, and thank you for being faithful even in our weakness. Help us remember the covenant we made before you, and return again and again to our first choice. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what progress has our family vision made this week? What most needs adjusting?
Ask your child, “Was Mom or Dad more like Jesus this week? Was our family more like what the vision statement says?” Just listen, and don’t defend yourself
Write down one specific adjustment for next week, and decide where our family’s “witness stone” will go
lessons.noon: “We will serve the LORD our God, and we will listen to his voice.” — Lord, today I answer you in this way once again.

fam.key: We remember our promise to God.

lamb.do: Let your child touch a smooth, big stone (too big to go in their mouth), and hold their hand as you put it together on a shelf at home.
lamb.say: This stone reminds us: we love Jesus.

sprout.story: Joshua and everyone agreed to follow God together. So that nobody would forget, he found a very, very big stone and set it up under a tree, so that the stone would help everyone remember today’s promise. After that, every time people passed and saw the big stone, they remembered: “That’s right, we are going to follow God!”
sprout.ask: What would you like to promise God today?
sprout.do: Find a small stone at the park or downstairs, wash it, draw a heart or a cross on it, and keep it at home as our family’s “remembering stone.”

soldier.story: The Israelites said, “We will serve the LORD our God, and we will listen to his voice.” Joshua wrote this covenant in a book and set up a great stone under the oak as a witness. Why a stone? Because people forget easily, but a stone stands there and keeps reminding them. It is like an important day you circle on the calendar, or a medal from a match: when you see it you remember what happened that day.
ask: Did our family do what our vision statement says this week? What did we do best?
What could our family use as a “witness stone” to remind us to follow God?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person shares one thing they are thankful for this week and one thing they want to improve next week, with Mom and Dad first. Then the whole family chooses something to be our family’s “witness stone.”

youth.talk: This week we thought together about the choice of “my house and me,” and wrote a vision statement. But honestly, writing it down is easy and living it out is hard. Mom and Dad also noticed several times this week when what we said and what we did were different. Joshua set up a stone as a witness, and we also want to find a way to keep our family from forgetting this choice, a way that you agree with too.
ask: Which line of our family vision statement do you think is hardest to live out?
Was there anything Mom or Dad did this week that did not match what we say?
youth.do: Parents first apologize to their child for one time this week when their words and actions did not match, then decide together on a time each month to review the vision statement, and write it in the family calendar.

fam.pray: Faithful heavenly Father, thank you for always remembering us. Help us to remember our promise to you, and to follow you together as a family. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

4.memT: If it seems evil to you to serve the LORD, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

mem.t: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

sat.t: Family Day: Give the Crown to Jesus
sat.d: Using card and gold paper, each person makes a paper crown. Put it on and take turns saying one thing “I most want to decide for myself” (for example, how long to use the tablet, what to eat, how to plan the weekend). Parents go first. Then tie two sticks into a cross and set it on the table. One by one, each family member places their crown before the cross and says, “Jesus, you are the king of our family.” Finally, Mom and Dad act as “servants”: pour each child a drink and hand out snacks so that the children experience being served, and then pray together.

sun: At what moment this week did you most clearly see “I want to be king at home”?
In your relationship with your children, how does “leaving your place and grasping at power” usually happen?
What act of serving your family will you choose next week to show that “Jesus is the king”? Think too about how you might share this grace with another parent.

lessons.title: Wanting to Be King Is the Root of the Fall
lessons.theme: The self-ruled life, trying to take God’s place, is the source of everything broken

v: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?”
The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden,
but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’”
The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die,
for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.

lessons.still: Be still and admit one thing: “Lord, there is also a me in my heart who wants to be king.” You don’t need to rush to fix it. Just say it honestly before the Lord.
teach: Nothing was lacking in Eden, yet the serpent’s temptation went straight to the deepest desire of the human heart: “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” The problem was not only a piece of fruit but a thought: I don’t want to be a created being any more. I want to decide for myself what is good and what is bad. I don’t want God to be king. I want to be king myself. This is the self-ruled life: putting self at the center, trying to take God’s place.

The self-ruled life is the root of the fall, and the root of the family’s brokenness. As soon as the first family fell, blame-shifting appeared: Adam blamed Eve, Eve blamed the serpent, and then Cain killed Abel. When everyone wants to be king, the home becomes a battlefield. Parents want to be their children’s king, children want to be their own king, pride stirs up pride, and in the end everyone loses.

A parent’s kingship is often dressed respectably: “I’m doing this for your own good.” “I have eaten more salt than you have eaten rice.” We want children to study, make friends and choose a major the way we would, and even decide what they should feel. Love is often mixed with control. This week God wants us to see honestly: who is king in our home?
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life (putting self at the center, wanting to be king, trying to take God’s place) is the root of the fall. Pride leaves its place and grasps at power; humility lets go of power and returns to its place. Let people be people and God be God. Parents are not the king of the home. Jesus is. Parents are only stewards entrusted by the King.
q: Who is God? — God is the only one worthy to be king, and the God who came looking for people even after they fell.
Who am I? — In what kind of matters at home do I most often “want to be king”?
How should I respond? — In which small matter today am I willing to hand the decision back to God?
lessons.jesus: The first Adam said in Eden, “I will decide for myself.” The last Adam, Jesus, prayed in Gethsemane, “Not what I desire, but what you desire.” One garden brought the fall, and another garden opened salvation. Jesus healed the human sickness of wanting to be king by his obedience.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit there is a me in my heart who wants to be king. I often think I know best what is good for my children, and I take my will for yours. Forgive my pride in trying to take your place. Today I give the throne back to you. Be the true king of our family. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one sentence you often say to your children that sounds like “being king,” for example, “Just do as I say.”
Today, on one small matter, ask your child’s opinion and respect their choice
Add one sentence to your prayer before meals: “Lord Jesus, you are the king of our family.”
lessons.noon: “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” — Lord, I don’t want to be my own god. Be my king.

fam.key: Jesus is the king of our family.

lamb.do: Make a little crown from paper or a towel, put it on your child’s head and take it off again, and place it beside a picture of Jesus.
lamb.say: Jesus is King, and Jesus loves you so much.

sprout.story: God made a beautiful garden for Adam and Eve to live in. God said they could eat the fruit of all the trees in the garden except one. But a serpent tricked Eve, saying, “You will be like God!” Eve thought, I want to be like God and decide for myself! So she ate the fruit, and Adam ate it too. From that day they were not happy, because they had not listened to God.
sprout.ask: Why is listening to God better than deciding for yourself?
sprout.do: Play “who is king”: one person wears a paper crown and everyone else does what they say. After a while, put the crown on a picture of the cross, and everyone says, “Jesus is the King!”

soldier.story: Adam and Eve lived in the beautiful Garden of Eden, and had everything. But the serpent told them that if they ate the fruit of that tree, they would be like God and know good and evil. They thought, why should we listen to God? We will decide for ourselves! So they ate the fruit. As a result they began to hide from God, and blamed one another. The thought “I want to decide for myself” is like a bad seed that has been passed down to this day, and it is in every heart.
ask: When do you think the thought “I want to decide for myself” most often pops up at home?
Do Mom and Dad ever “want to be king”? You can say so honestly.
soldier.do: This week, watch yourself: each time you notice “I want to be king,” draw a little crown in a notebook, and share it with the family on Friday.

youth.talk: The temptation in Eden was “you will be like God.” Honestly, Mom and Dad sometimes act at home as if we wanted to be God: deciding everything for you, and saying it is for your own good. We also know that at your age you very much want to decide for yourself, and that is normal. But the Bible says the problem is not who has the power, but that each of us wants to take God’s place. We want to admit our own problem first.
ask: In what way do you think Mom and Dad are most like “being your king”?
Do you think “deciding for yourself” and “letting Jesus decide” can exist together? Why?
youth.do: This week, parents first name one area where they were too forceful and apologize to their child, then ask, “How would you like me to change in this?”

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, you are the king of our family. Help me listen to you and not only want to decide for myself. Help Mom and Dad listen to you too. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: What Kind of King Am I?
lessons.theme: Seeing myself: a parent who lords it over, or a parent who serves

v: Jesus summoned them and said to them, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.still: Recall a conversation with your child this morning or last night. What was your tone, your expression, your volume? What kind of person did you sound like? Ask the Holy Spirit to be like a mirror, so that you can see yourself gently.
teach: James and John asked Jesus to let them sit one at his right and one at his left in his kingdom, and when the other disciples heard it they were indignant. Jesus called them together and said, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you.” In God’s Kingdom, greatness is turned upside down: “whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.”

Many parents do not feel they are “lording it over” anyone. But ask the Holy Spirit to light up a few signs: when my child talks back, my first feeling is “offended,” not “what is wrong with him?”; I often end a discussion by saying “I am your father” or “I am your mother”; I demand that my child apologize, but seldom apologize myself; I am gracious and polite outside, but at home I become a tyrant. These are what the “rulers over the nations” look like at home.

Bohan in Taipei has four children. He considered himself a responsible father, until his eldest son wrote in an essay: “My father is like an officer.” He was sad for days, and later understood in prayer: what his children needed was not an officer but a father willing to stoop down. Seeing yourself hurts, yet it is the beginning of grace.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride stirs up pride, and both lose; humility draws out humility, and both win. When parents suppress with power, children learn to rebel or to please; when parents lead by serving, children learn respect and love. People matter more than tasks. Don’t win an argument at the cost of losing your child’s heart.
q: Who is God? — The King of kings said, “The Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve.” What kind of king is this?
Who am I? — In my children’s eyes, am I more like a “ruler who lords it over,” or a “servant”?
How should I respond? — What one habit of “lording it over” do I most need to change?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart.” He had all authority, yet he never used it to crush people. Children could come near him, and sinners dared to ask him for help. Jesus’ authority was used to serve and to save.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, shine your light on me. I admit that at home I often act like a ruler who lords it over, using my voice, my face and my power to make my children obey, while seldom stooping down to serve them. Forgive me. I want to learn from you, gentle and humble, to be a parent who serves. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Notice the volume and tone of your voice today, and deliberately soften it at least once
When you hear yourself say “because I’m your dad/mom,” stop and explain the reason instead
Ask your spouse, “Which of my habits in front of the children sounds like an officer?” Listen humbly
lessons.noon: “The Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve.” — Lord, today teach me to be someone who serves my family.

fam.key: In Jesus’ Kingdom, the greatest is the one who helps.

lamb.do: Crouch down to your child’s height, look into their eyes, and help them put on their shoes or wipe their hands, slowly and gently.
lamb.say: Mommy and Daddy love to help you, because Jesus helps us too.

sprout.story: Two of Jesus’ friends secretly told him they wanted to be the greatest! The other friends were very angry when they heard. Jesus called everyone over and said: in my Kingdom, the greatest is not the one who tells others what to do, but the one who helps others. Jesus himself is like that. He came to help everyone.
sprout.ask: How can you help someone at home today?
sprout.do: Play a “little helper” game: each person draws a slip of paper with one way to help the family (for example, setting the table or fetching slippers). Each one you do today earns a sticker.

soldier.story: James and John wanted to sit in the highest seats in Jesus’ Kingdom, and when the other disciples heard, they were angry, and everyone started arguing. Jesus said that the kings of the world like to boss people and give orders, but in Jesus’ Kingdom it is the opposite: whoever wants to be great must first be a servant. It is like a team. The best captain is not the one who shouts the loudest, but the one who is most willing to pass the ball and help teammates. Jesus himself is that kind of king. He came to serve, and even gave his life for us.
ask: Which do you think is harder, being the boss or being a servant? Why?
At home, do you think Mom and Dad are more like a “boss” or a “servant”?
soldier.do: Every day this week, secretly do one small act of service for a family member, without letting them know it was you, and reveal it on Friday.

youth.talk: Jesus said that the rulers of the nations lord it over people, but in his Kingdom it is not so. Mom and Dad have been reflecting these days that we sometimes act at home like an “officer,” using our position and our volume to shut you up instead of listening to you. That is not how Jesus is. We want to learn another way to lead this family, and we need your help to remind us.
ask: In your mind, what is an adult like who has authority but whom people willingly follow?
When is it easiest for our family to turn into a “power struggle”?
youth.do: Parents invite their child to point out a moment when “I felt you were like an officer,” just listen and don’t defend, then say, “Thank you for telling me. I will learn to change.”

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for being the best king, who came to help us. Help our whole family to follow your example and help one another. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: No Longer I, but Christ
lessons.theme: I believe: the old self was crucified with Christ, and Christ lives in me

v: For I through the law died to the law, that I might live to God.

I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

lessons.still: Imagine yourself standing at the foot of the cross, placing the “me” who wants to be king, to control and to be respected on Jesus’ cross. Quietly say: “Lord, I give this me to you.”
teach: Paul said, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” This does not mean we should destroy our personalities, nor that parents should become weak and without principles. It means that the “old self,” which was centered on itself and wanted to be king, has died together with Christ. Now the one who rules my life is Christ.

For parents, this is very practical. Grandma Xiuying in Kuala Lumpur raised her grandson, and when he talked back, the “I” in her would leap up: “I raised you all this time, and you dare speak to me like this!” She learned to whisper at that moment: “No longer I, but Christ.” She found that when the old self was no longer in a hurry to defend its dignity, there was room for Christ’s gentleness.

Conviction is not gritting our teeth and enduring by willpower. It is believing a fact: “That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.” We can lay down the right to be king because we are deeply loved by the King who gave himself up for us. A person who is loved doesn’t need to prove herself by controlling others. Today, write down your “I believe.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life: no longer I, but Christ lives in me. The self-emptied life overcomes Satan, because Satan’s greatest weapon is the self-ruled life. A parent’s self-emptiness does not mean having no self, but letting Christ sit at the center. When Christ reigns, parents can truly return to the steward’s place.
q: Who is God? — The Son of God “loved me and gave himself up for me.” How does his love enable me to lay down the right to be king?
Who am I? — At home, when does the “old self” most often leap out to defend itself?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe the old self has…; I believe Christ in me…; I believe at home I can…
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” He himself is that grain of wheat, who died for us and brought much life. When a parent’s old self dies on the cross, a family bears the fruit of life.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, who gave yourself up for me, I believe that my old self has been crucified with you; I believe it is no longer I who live, but you who live in me. When I want to be king at home, to rage, to fight for face, remind me: I am deeply loved by you, and I don’t need control to prove myself. Live out your life in me. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” sentences, stick them on the bathroom mirror, and read them morning and evening
Today, when the old self wants to leap out, whisper: “No longer I, but Christ.”
Write down one thing you most want to “win” against your child, and write beside it: “This I give to Christ.”
lessons.noon: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” — Lord, right now, live in me.

fam.key: Jesus lives in my heart.

lamb.do: Let your child put an ear against your chest to hear your heartbeat, and then gently touch their little chest.
lamb.say: Jesus lives in my heart, and wants to live in your heart too.

sprout.story: A glove cannot move by itself, but lies soft on the table. But when Mom puts her hand inside, the glove can wave, clap and pick things up! Mom said, “We are like the glove. When Jesus lives in our hearts, it is like a hand going into a glove. Jesus helps us to love, to share and to say sorry.” Little sister looked at the glove and said, “Then Jesus is waving inside me!”
sprout.ask: Now that Jesus lives in your heart, what good things will he help you do?
sprout.do: Take a glove and let your child see it lying still, then put your hand in and make it wave, and say together, “It’s not me, it’s Jesus in me!”

soldier.story: Paul said that his old self had been crucified with Jesus, and that it was no longer he who lived, but Christ who lived in him. What does that mean? Imagine a glove. A glove cannot move by itself, but once a hand goes inside it can write, pick things up and shake hands. We are like the glove: when Jesus lives in us, we can do what we could not do ourselves: forgive someone who has hurt us, say sorry first, and not fight to be first.
ask: Is there something you find hard to do, like sharing or saying sorry?
If Jesus is in you, how do you think he would help you?
soldier.do: Write “No longer I, but Christ” on a glove and keep it in your school bag. This week, when you feel like getting angry or arguing, touch it and remember that Jesus lives in you.

youth.talk: Paul said, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” It sounds as if we are asked to give up ourselves, but really it is a kind of freedom: no more proving ourselves by winning, by face or by control. Mom and Dad have noticed that many of our arguments at home happen because that “I” will not give way. We want to learn to let Christ reign, and we would love to know what you think of this verse.
ask: Does “no longer I” sound to you like losing yourself, or finding freedom? Why?
In your life, where is the place where “I” is least willing to give way?
youth.do: Parents and children each write their own three “I believe” sentences, swap and read them, and then pray for each other once.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for loving me and dying for me on the cross. Please live in my heart and help me to love, to share and to say sorry. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Today, Stoop Down
lessons.theme: Like Jesus washing feet, serve instead of lording it over

v: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.

lessons.still: Look at your hands. These hands will do many things today. Quietly give them to the Lord: “Lord, today please use my hands to serve the people in my home.”
teach: John specifically notes that before Jesus washed the disciples’ feet, he knew “that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God.” Jesus knew perfectly well who he was and what authority he had. Precisely for that reason he had nothing to prove, and could rise from supper, lay aside his outer garments, wrap a towel around his waist, and kneel to wash his disciples’ feet, which was a task for the lowest servant.

Security decides whether we can serve. A parent who is unsure of her identity clings to authority and fears being looked down on by her children; a parent who knows he is God’s beloved child can stoop down without fear of losing dignity. Jesus said, “I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.”

“Washing feet” today can be very concrete: being the first to apologize, clearing the table the children have messed up when they have no time, crouching down beside a child during an emotional storm, preparing a late-night snack for a teenager without a sermon attached. Zhiming, a single father in Johor Bahru, says that the first time he knelt to tie his daughter’s shoelaces, she was stunned for a moment, and then hugged him tightly. Serving often opens a child’s heart faster than commanding.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example. Humility is not weakness, but letting go of power and returning to one’s place; serving is not losing authority, but using authority to build people up. When parents stoop first, children learn to stoop; humility draws out humility, and the home changes from a power struggle into mutual service.
q: Who is God? — The Lord, with all things in his hands, knelt to wash his disciples’ feet. What kind of God does this show you?
Who am I? — Where at home am I “unwilling to stoop”? Am I afraid of losing my dignity?
How should I respond? — What concrete action will I take today to “wash the feet” of my family?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was the disciples’ Lord and Teacher, yet he washed their feet with his own hands, even those of Judas who would betray him. He said, “I have given you an example.” Jesus’ greatness lies not in being high above, but in being willing to humble himself. What he washed was not only feet but our hearts.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you knew that the Father had given all things into your hands, yet you stooped down to wash your disciples’ feet. I admit I often refuse to stoop, afraid of losing dignity in front of my children. Give me security in your love, so that today I can lay down my status and serve my family with my hands. Let my children see your example in me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Do one concrete act of service for each child today: pour water, tidy up or prepare a snack, with no demands attached
If there is something to apologize for, be the first to speak today
With your spouse, do one “foot-washing” act for a child, such as sorting out their school bag or cleaning their shoes
lessons.noon: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” — Lord, today help me to stoop down and serve.

fam.key: Jesus stooped down, and we serve one another too.

lamb.do: Wash your child’s feet or hands, gently massaging as you wash, and dry them slowly with a towel.
lamb.say: Jesus loves us so much, and we love you so much.

sprout.story: Before dinner, Jesus stood up, tied a towel round his waist and poured water into a basin. He knelt down and washed his friends’ feet one by one! The friends were so surprised: Jesus is our teacher. How can he wash our feet? Jesus said: I do this so that you will help each other this way too.
sprout.ask: Whom in the family would you like to do something for?
sprout.do: Prepare a basin of warm water and a towel. Mom and Dad first wash their children’s feet, then let the children wash Mom and Dad’s hands.

soldier.story: In Jesus’ time people wore sandals and walked along dusty roads, so their feet were very dirty. Before a guest came into a house, the lowest servant usually washed his feet. On the day of the Last Supper there was no servant, and none of the disciples wanted to do it. But Jesus stood up, tied a towel round his waist, knelt down and washed the disciples’ feet one by one. Peter was shocked and refused to let Jesus wash his. Jesus said that if he, the Teacher and Lord, was willing to wash their feet, they should wash one another’s feet too.
ask: If you were a disciple and saw Jesus kneel to wash your feet, how would you feel?
In our family, what is most like “washing feet,” something nobody wants to do but somebody needs to?
soldier.do: Today, offer to do something at home that nobody wants to do, such as taking out the trash or washing up, and don’t tell anyone.

youth.talk: Jesus knew who he was, so he could kneel and wash his disciples’ feet. Mom and Dad have realized that sometimes we are unwilling to apologize first or to stoop down because we are afraid of losing our dignity in front of you. But Jesus shows us that true authority is willingness to serve. Today we want to try doing something different, and you don’t need to respond in any way.
ask: Do you think an adult who is willing to stoop down earns more respect from you, or less?
Among friends or family, have you ever tried “stooping first”? What happened?
youth.do: Today parents do one act of service for their child that they will like (such as preparing their favorite late-night snack or sorting out a hassle for them), with no sermon or demand attached.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for stooping down to wash your disciples’ feet. Help our whole family to be willing to help and serve one another. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Lay Down the Crown at the Cross
