lessons.theme: Review and Adjust: confess honestly, and receive grace with boldness

v: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.
Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.

lessons.still: Look back over this week, at the moments you wanted to be king, to control, to win. Let them come up one by one. Don’t hide and don’t blame yourself. Just say to the Lord, “Lord, you saw it all. Here I am.”
teach: After the fall, Adam and Eve’s first reaction was to hide. God called in the garden, “Where are you?” God did not lack knowledge of where they were. He was inviting them to come out. In reviewing our own self-rule, the greatest temptation is to hide: to defend ourselves, to blame the child for being hard to teach, to blame a spouse for not cooperating, or simply not to think about it.

John says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” And, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” We confess not to knock ourselves down, but to be cleansed. Hebrews adds that we have a high priest who can be “touched with the feeling of our infirmities,” so we can “draw near with boldness to the throne of grace.”

This week we have seen that wanting to be king is the root of the fall; that we often act like rulers who lord it over; that the old self has been crucified with Christ; and that we can learn from Jesus to stoop and serve. When we see our problems, we must also see the grace of the cross. Today, lay down your crown at the cross, review honestly, and then take that grace with you and write down one adjustment for next week.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility overcomes pride. Proud parents see only their children’s faults; humble parents first see their own. Pride makes people hide; humility lets them walk into the light. Deal with your own heart first, then with your child’s behavior. When parents apologize first, the family begins to be restored.
q: Who is God? — God is faithful and righteous to forgive, and a high priest who sympathizes with our weakness. What grace of his do you need this week?
Who am I? — At which moment this week did I most want to be king? Did I hide, or come into the light?
How should I respond? — What is the one thing I will adjust next week, and how, specifically, will I do it?
lessons.jesus: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Jesus did not wait for us to get better before loving us. On the cross he wore a crown of thorns, so that we could lay down our own crowns and enter his grace.
lessons.pray: Lord, you saw it all. Several times this week I wanted to be king at home, crushing people with power and hurting them with my concern for face. I will not hide any more. I confess my sin, and ask you to forgive me and cleanse me. Thank you for sympathizing with my weakness, so that I may come boldly to your throne of grace. I lay my crown before your cross. Be the King of our family. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: where did each of us most want to be king this week? When did we learn to stoop down?
Ask your child, “Was Mom or Dad more like Jesus this week? Was there a time when I seemed too bossy?” Just listen, and don’t defend yourself
Write down one specific adjustment for next week, and formally apologize to your child for one thing
lessons.noon: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins.” — Lord, thank you that your grace is greater than my sin.

fam.key: Say sorry, and Jesus forgives.

lamb.do: After your child has fallen or been upset, pick them up, gently pat their back, and kiss them once they have calmed down.
lamb.say: It’s all right. Mommy and Daddy love you, and Jesus loves you.

sprout.story: Xiaoyu broke Mom’s vase. He was so scared that he hid under the bed. Mom found him, crouched down and said, “Xiaoyu, will you come out? Mom isn’t going to scold you. Mom wants to give you a hug.” Xiaoyu crawled out and said softly, “Sorry.” Mom hugged him tight and said, “I forgive you. Jesus is the same. When we say sorry, he forgives us.”
sprout.ask: When you do something wrong, do you want to hide, or say sorry?
sprout.do: Play “sorry hugs” as a family: each person thinks of one thing they did wrong this week and says, “Sorry.” The one who hears it answers, “I forgive you,” and gives a hug. Mom and Dad start.

soldier.story: After Adam and Eve disobeyed God, they heard the sound of God walking in the garden and hid behind the trees. God called to Adam, “Where are you?” God actually knew where they were. He was inviting them to come out and face it. Often when we do something wrong, our first thought is also to hide and find excuses. But the Bible says that if we confess our wrongs, God is faithful and will certainly forgive us. Confessing is not shameful. It is returning to God’s arms.
ask: When you do something wrong, what is your most common way of “hiding”?
Do you think Mom and Dad need to say sorry to you for anything this week?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person shares one thing they are thankful for this week and one thing they want to improve next week. Mom and Dad go first, and begin with one time this week they “wanted to be king.”

youth.talk: All week we have been looking at “who is king at home.” Honestly, Mom and Dad became the king of the house again several times this week: raising our voices, not listening to your explanations, demanding that you do as we say. We don’t want to hide, or make excuses that work has been tiring. We want to apologize to you, and to tell you we are learning to give the throne back to Jesus.
ask: Was there a moment this week when you felt Mom and Dad were really changing?
Was there a moment when you felt we had gone back to our old ways?
youth.do: Parents apologize to their child for one specific thing this week, saying clearly what they did wrong, and then ask, “Next week, what would you like me to do to make it better?”

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, thank you for forgiving us when we say sorry. Help our whole family to be willing to admit our wrongs and to forgive others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

5.memT: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

mem.t: casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

sat.t: Family Day: Watch the Birds, Count the Flowers
sat.d: Take the whole family on a picnic to a park, the seaside or a green space in your neighbourhood. Start with a contest: who can spot the most kinds of birds and flowers? Take photos or draw them. Then sit down and ask someone to read Matthew 6:26. Next, each person writes or draws one worry on a small slip of paper (parents write for little ones), folds it into a paper boat, and floats it in a basin of water you have brought along. Say together: “Our heavenly Father cares for us.” Finally, each person shares one thing they saw today that made them thankful to God. Take the paper boats home and drop them in the recycling bin, to show that the worries have been handed over.

sun: This past week, what most often triggered your need to control, or your anxiety?
What is the hardest part of handing your children’s future back to God?
Next week, what one concrete way will you use to turn worry into prayer? You might also think of an anxious parent near you whom you could pray with.

lessons.title: Cast Your Worries on God
lessons.theme: The way out of control and anxiety is to humble ourselves under God’s mighty hand

v: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,
casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

lessons.still: Notice how your shoulders and chest feel right now. Are they tight? Breathe in slowly and out slowly, and say to the Lord, “Lord, I am carrying so many burdens. Right now I want to put them down.”
teach: Peter says, “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” The word “casting” means to throw a heavy load onto someone else, like heaving the luggage you have carried all the way onto the back of an ox. God does not ask us to pretend we have no worries. He invites us to hand the whole worry over, because he cares for our children even more than we do.

Many people skip the verse before it: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God.” Peter puts humility and casting our worries side by side because behind anxiety there is often a hidden pride. I tell myself my child’s whole life is in my hands, and that if I work hard enough, watch closely enough and plan well enough, I can guarantee his safety and success. Control and anxiety are two sides of one coin: both reach for authority that belongs to God.

The controlling parent grips tightly; the anxious parent cannot let go of the worry. Both are exhausted, and both leave children gasping for air. The way out is not to try harder but to be humble: to admit I am not God, and that my child’s future is not in my hands but under God’s mighty hand. When parents return to their proper place, they can move from “I must guarantee” to “I entrust.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our proper place to grab power. Anxious parents often grab, without realizing it, an authority that belongs only to God: ruling over their children’s future. Humility is laying down that power and returning to our place: let people be people, and let God be God. Use your heart and rely on the Holy Spirit; do not use your head and rely on yourself. The heart brings joy; the head brings worry.
q: Who is God? — God is the one who “cares for you,” and his mighty hand holds your child. What comfort does that bring you?
Who am I? — Am I more the controlling type (gripping tightly) or the anxious type (unable to let the worry go)? Or a bit of both?
How should I respond? — Which specific worry about my child will I cast on God today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.” The safest place for our children is not within our control but in the hand of the good shepherd. His hand is bigger and steadier than ours, and he loves them more.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father who cares for me, I admit that I often live carrying worries about my child, thinking that if I hold on tightly enough he will be safe. In truth I have been reaching for your authority. Please forgive me. Today I humble myself under your mighty hand and cast all my worries on you, because you care for him more than I do. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Write down the three things you worry about most for your child. Beside each one, write: “God cares for him.”
Choose one worry today and pray with open hands, as a sign that you are casting it on God.
Notice how many times today you say, “I’m so worried.” Each time, turn it into a short prayer.
lessons.noon: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” — Lord, right now I hand this worry over to you.

fam.key: My heavenly Father cares for me, so I don’t need to be afraid.

lamb.do: When your child is crying or frightened, hold him close and breathe slowly, so he can feel the steady rise and fall of your chest.
lamb.say: Don’t be afraid, don’t be afraid. God is here, and Mommy and Daddy are here too.

sprout.story: Little brother was carrying a very heavy school bag. He was puffing and panting, and his face was red. Daddy saw him and said, “Come, give me your bag!” Little brother handed it over and at once felt so light that he could skip all the way. Daddy said, “You can give your worries to your heavenly Father just like that bag. He is the strongest, and he loves you the most!”
sprout.ask: Is there something in your heart that you are worried about and would like to give to your heavenly Father?
sprout.do: Let your child walk a few steps with a backpack full of books, then hand it to Mom or Dad. Say together, “Give the worries to God!”

soldier.story: Peter used to be very impulsive, and he was easily frightened. Once he walked on the water toward Jesus, but when he saw the wind and waves he got scared and began to sink. Later, when he was grown and mature, he wrote to Christians who were suffering and told them to cast all their worries on God, because God cares for them. “Casting” means throwing a heavy load onto someone else, like handing a very heavy box to a strong person. Peter used his own experience to tell everyone that God can be trusted.
ask: Is there something you have been really worried about lately? Can you tell us?
After you cast your worry on God, do you think there is anything you still need to do?
soldier.do: Write a “worry card.” Write down what you are worried about, pray over it with Mom or Dad, and then put the card into an envelope marked “Given to God.”

youth.talk: Peter says to cast all our worries on God. As your parents, we need to admit that we often turn our worry about you into control: asking again and again, reminding, checking. That is really our own anxiety, yet it makes you feel we do not trust you. We are learning to hand our worries to God instead of pouring them onto you, and we would like to hear how you feel.
ask: Which of our worries puts the most pressure on you?
Is there anything you are worried about lately that we don’t know about?
youth.do: Parents and child each share one recent worry. Offer no advice; simply pray together and give both worries to God.

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, thank you for caring for me. I give you the worries in my heart. You are the strongest and you love me the most. Help me not to be afraid. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Martha-Style Parents
lessons.theme: Seeing ourselves: anxious and troubled about many things

v: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus sitting in your living room while you are still busy in the kitchen. Gently he calls your name twice. Be still, and listen to how he calls you.
teach: Martha welcomed Jesus out of love. But she “was distracted with much serving,” and in the end she could not help complaining to Jesus: “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone?” Her anxiety turned into control. She did not just want to be busy herself; she wanted to direct others to be busy too, and even tried to direct Jesus.

Many parents are “Martha-style”: we love our children but are crushed under the weight of that love. Our calendars are packed, the group chats never stop, and one comparison article follows another. When our child is a little slow, we rush; when another child learns one more thing, we panic. Anxiety keeps us doing, and control makes us demand that everyone keep to our pace. We say, “It’s all for the family,” yet inside we often feel, “None of you care.”

Jesus answered, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed.” He called her name twice, and the tone was tender, not a rebuke. The Holy Spirit’s light is gentle in the same way. If you find that you have long-term sleeplessness or a racing heart, or anxiety is affecting your daily life, please do not carry it alone. Seek professional counseling and the company of your pastor.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Martha put ministry before life: she was busy serving in front of Jesus but never sat down to listen to him. Using your head and relying on yourself brings worry; using your heart and relying on the Holy Spirit brings joy. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on tasks, not on other people, and not on circumstances.
q: Who is God? — When Jesus said, “Martha, Martha,” what was in his heart? How does he see your busyness?
Who am I? — Where am I “anxious and troubled”? What demand on my family does my anxiety often turn into?
How should I respond? — For my family, what is the “one thing needed”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said to busy Martha, “One thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” He did not reject Martha’s serving; he invited her to sit down first. Jesus does not only want us to work for him. He longs for us to be with him.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you see my busyness. I admit that I am often anxious and troubled about many things, that I turn my anxiety into demands on my children and spouse, and that I resent others for not caring. Please call my name gently, so that I stop and sit at your feet. Teach me to choose the one thing that is needed. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: List the three things that have made this week most hectic, and ask yourself, “Is this the one thing needed?”
Drop or postpone one unnecessary task today, and use that time to sit quietly before the Lord.
Say to your family, “I’ve been too anxious lately and I keep rushing you. I’m sorry.”
lessons.noon: “but one thing is needed.” — Lord, right now I put down my busyness and choose to sit at your feet.

fam.key: The most important thing is being with Jesus.

lamb.do: Put down your phone and the housework, sit on the floor and play with your child for five minutes. Do nothing else; just look at him and smile.
lamb.say: I’m not doing anything else right now. I’m just with you.

sprout.story: Jesus came to visit Martha’s house. Martha was rushing around in the kitchen, cooking, chopping vegetables and setting out bowls. She was so tired. But her sister Mary sat beside Jesus, listening to his stories. Martha grumbled and asked Jesus to tell Mary to come and help. Jesus said gently, “Martha, Martha, you are too busy. Sitting down to be with me is the most important thing.”
sprout.ask: Do you like rushing about, or sitting down to talk with Jesus?
sprout.do: Play “Pause.” Everyone walks around the living room, and when you hear “Stop!” you sit down, close your eyes and say, “Jesus, I want to be with you.”

soldier.story: Jesus visited the home of Martha and Mary. Martha was busy preparing a huge meal, and the busier she got, the more upset she became. Her sister Mary just sat at Jesus’ feet, listening to his teaching. At last Martha could not stand it and ran to complain to Jesus, asking him to tell Mary to help. But Jesus called her name twice, “Martha, Martha,” and told her that she was worried about many things, yet only one thing really mattered. There was nothing wrong with Martha’s serving. The trouble was that her heart was full of busyness and had no room for Jesus.
ask: Why do you think Martha got angrier the busier she became?
Have you ever been so busy that you felt upset inside? What did you do then?
soldier.do: Look at this week’s schedule with Mom and Dad and find a “Mary time”: ten minutes with no homework and no screens, just reading a Bible passage or chatting together.

youth.talk: Jesus said to Martha, “You are anxious and troubled about many things.” It feels as if he is describing us, your parents: often busy, often in a hurry, always pushing you, so that the mood at home gets tight. Many times the problem is not that you did something wrong, but that we ourselves are anxious inside. We want to stop first, and we would also like to know whether you have been feeling tired too.
ask: When do you think our home is most “Martha”?
In your own life, are there many things that make you anxious and troubled?
youth.do: Parents and child list each other’s most hectic things this week, and each drops one. Then set a phone-free “Mary time.”

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for loving to be with me. Please help our family not to be too busy, but to sit down often and listen to you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Looking at What Is Unseen
lessons.theme: I believe: what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal

v: For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory,
while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,” says the LORD, “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.

lessons.still: Imagine twenty years from now, when your child has grown up. What do you most hope he will have? Qualifications, income, or a heart that loves God and others? Answer quietly before the Lord.
teach: Paul says, “we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” Most parental anxiety comes from “the things which are seen”: report cards, rankings, school entry, certificates for talents, how other people’s children are doing. These can be seen and compared, but they are all temporary.

What God values is unseen but lasting: our child’s character, faith, ability to love, and relationship with God. Junjie and Jiaxin, a Chinese couple in Melbourne, once lost a whole night’s sleep when their son failed to get into an elite high school. Later they asked themselves: twenty years from now, what will we most want him to remember? That one failed entrance exam, or how his parents held him and prayed with him that day? When their viewpoint shifted, the anxiety loosened its grip.

Through Jeremiah God said, “For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,” says the LORD, “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.” These words were first spoken to people in exile who could see no way forward, yet God had a long-term plan. Our children are also in God’s long-term plan. Conviction means that even when we cannot see the outcome, we still declare: I believe God’s thoughts are better than my plans.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your viewpoint, from the temporary to the eternal, from earth to heaven, from human views to God’s. Anxious parents live under the pressure of “it must happen now”; trusting parents live in the peace of “there is hope for eternity.” Only when parents’ vision changes can children be freed from the report card.
q: Who is God? — God is the one whose thoughts toward us are “thoughts of peace,” and he sees the future that I cannot see.
Who am I? — Is the thing I worry about most among “the things which are seen” and temporary, or “the things which are not seen” and eternal?
How should I respond? — Write down your “I believe”: I believe God’s thoughts toward my child are … ; I believe the eternal is more than the temporary …; I believe I can let go of …
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “In my Father’s house are many homes,” and “I am going to prepare a place for you.” Jesus always looks to eternity. What he prepares for us is not only success in this life but a place in the Father’s house for ever. With an eternal hope, today’s anxiety has its limits.
lessons.pray: Eternal God, I admit that I often look only at what can be seen: my child’s grades, rankings and future job, and I let anxiety fill my heart. I believe that what is seen is temporary, and what is unseen is eternal. I believe the thoughts you have toward my child are thoughts of peace. Please open my eyes to see my child with an eternal perspective. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” sentences, for example: “I believe God’s thoughts toward my child are thoughts of peace.”
Write down one “temporary” thing about your child that worries you most, and beside it one “eternal” thing you would rather nurture.
Today, praise your child for a quality of character, not for grades or performance.
lessons.noon: “the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” — Lord, help me today to see my child with eternal eyes.

fam.key: What we cannot see matters more than what we can see.

lamb.do: Play peekaboo with your child: cover your face with a towel and then take it away, so he learns that even when he cannot see you, you are still there.
lamb.say: You can’t see me, but I’m still here. God is always here too.

sprout.story: The wind cannot be seen, but Xiaoyun saw the leaves swaying and the kite flying, and she knew the wind was blowing. Mommy said, “God’s love can’t be seen either, but we can feel it, just like the wind. There are many other things we can’t see, like love, courage and kindness, and they matter more than toys!” Xiaoyun said, “Then I will keep these unseen treasures in my heart!”
sprout.ask: What do you think is something we cannot see but is very important?
sprout.do: Blow on a sheet of paper together and watch it flutter. Say, “The wind we can’t see is so strong! God’s love is too!”

soldier.story: Paul went through many hardships in his life: beatings, prison and shipwreck. But he said these were temporary and light, because he was not looking at what is seen but at what is unseen; what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal. Think about it: your certificates will get old, your toys will break and your marks will be forgotten. But your honesty, courage and love, and your relationship with God, will stay with you for ever.
ask: Do you think what you care about most is “seen” or “unseen”?
Ten years from now, which unseen treasure would you like to have?
soldier.do: Draw a line down a sheet of paper. On the left write “Seen (temporary)” and on the right “Unseen (eternal).” Each family member writes three things for each side. Stick it on the fridge.

youth.talk: Paul says, “the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” Honestly, we parents often fix our eyes on what can be seen: your grades, rankings and school entry. Sometimes we forget to ask whether you are happy, whether your heart is at peace, and how your relationship with God is going. We want to admit that our anxiety has put a lot of pressure on you. We want to learn to look at you with a longer view.
ask: What do you think we care about most in you? What do you wish we cared about more?
In your own opinion, what in life is truly “eternal”?
youth.do: Parents write a card to their child listing only three “unseen treasures” (character, faith, kindness) they see in him, with no mention of grades or performance.

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, thank you for seeing what is in my heart. Help our family to value love, honesty and faith more, because these last for ever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Turn Your Worry List into a Prayer List
lessons.theme: Bring every worry to God today

v: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Put a sheet of paper in front of you. Do not write yet. Just be quiet for a moment and say to the Lord, “Lord, you know every worry in my heart. Now I will tell you about them one by one.”
teach: Paul says, “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.” He does not say, “Just don’t think about it.” He gives a concrete direction: turn worry into prayer. Anxiety keeps a problem circling in our own heads; prayer sets the problem before God and entrusts it to him.

It is interesting that after “prayer and petition” Paul adds “thanksgiving.” Anxious parents often see only what is lacking and dangerous; thanksgiving turns our eyes back to what God has already done. The result: “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” “Guard” was originally a military word for soldiers keeping watch over a city. God’s peace stands like a sentry at the gate of our hearts.

Let us practice today. Write down your worries about your child one by one, and beside each add a line of prayer and a line of thanks. For example: “Worried he will fall in with the wrong friends.” Prayer: “Lord, give him wisdom to discern, and one or two good friends.” Thanks: “Thank you that he is willing to tell me about school.” In this way the worry list becomes a prayer list.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Of the eight steps for changing our thinking, practice is the most crucial. It is easy to know that we should entrust our worries to God; actually handing them over one by one takes practice. Use your heart and rely on the Holy Spirit; do not use your head and rely on yourself. Every time you turn a worry into prayer, you give the throne back to Jesus once more.
q: Who is God? — God hears prayer and gives a peace that surpasses understanding. Have you experienced his peace?
Who am I? — Do I tend to keep my worries circling in my head, or bring them to God in prayer?
How should I respond? — Which three worries will I write down today, and turn into prayer and thanksgiving?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane, facing the cross, Jesus was “in agony” and “prayed more earnestly.” He did not pretend not to be afraid; he brought his deepest pain to the Father. After praying, he rose calmly and walked toward the road ahead. Jesus shows us that entrusting is not suppressing our feelings but bringing them to the Father.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for inviting me to make everything known to you in prayer. Now I bring before you every worry about my child: his health, his friends, his studies, his faith. Please watch over him, and thank you for all you have already done for him. Let your peace, which surpasses understanding, guard my heart and my thoughts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Make a “worry into prayer” chart: worries in the left column, prayers in the middle, thanks on the right, at least three rows.
Whenever anxiety rises today, pray one sentence and then say one thank you.
At bedtime, share with your child one worry and one thank you each, and give them to God.
lessons.noon: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.” — Lord, right now I turn my worry into a prayer and give it to you.

fam.key: When I am worried, I pray.

lamb.do: When your child is unsettled, hold his little hand, say a simple prayer very slowly, and kiss his palm.
lamb.say: Jesus, please stay with the baby. Thank you!

sprout.story: One night there was thunder, boom, boom! Xiaozhe was so scared that he hid under the covers. Mommy sat on the bed and said, “Shall we talk to Jesus?” Xiaozhe whispered, “Jesus, I’m scared of the thunder. Please keep me safe.” Mommy said, “Let’s thank Jesus too!” Xiaozhe said, “Thank you, Jesus, for my warm blanket and for Mommy being here.” After that, his heart felt so peaceful, and he slowly fell asleep.
sprout.ask: When you are scared, what can you say to Jesus?
sprout.do: Make a “prayer hand.” Trace your child’s hand, write “worry” on the thumb and “thank you” on the other fingers, and look at it when you pray.

soldier.story: When Paul wrote to the church in Philippi he was locked in prison, not knowing whether he would be sentenced to death the next day. Yet he wrote: in nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, make your requests known to God. He was not free of worries. He turned every worry into prayer and added thanks. As a result, God’s peace stood guard over his heart like a sentry. If even a man in prison could do this, we can try it when we face exams, matches or arguments with friends.
ask: What is a worry of yours lately that you can turn into a prayer?
What can you thank God for in this situation?
soldier.do: Make your own “worry into prayer” chart: write one worry, one prayer and one thank you, and share it with your family at dinner.

youth.talk: Paul wrote “In nothing be anxious” from a prison cell. He is not telling us to “stop overthinking”; he is telling us to turn worry into prayer and add thanksgiving. We, your parents, admit that many of our worries about you have never become prayers. They have only become nagging and checking. Today we want to do it differently and bring our worries to God, not pour them out on you.
ask: What difference do you see between “praying” and “just not thinking about it”?
Is there something you are worried about lately that you would let us pray over with you?
youth.do: Parents show their child their own “worry into prayer” chart (the parts that are suitable to share), then invite the child to write one too, and pray for each other for a week.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, when I am worried you know it. I give my worries to you, and thank you for always keeping us safe. Please give me peace in my heart. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Quiet as a Weaned Child
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: from control back to rest

v: LORD, my heart isn’t arrogant, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me.
Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.
Israel, hope in the LORD, from this time forward and forever more.

lessons.still: Picture a well-fed child lying quietly in his mother’s arms, neither crying nor fussing. Quietly ask the Lord, “This week, has my heart been quiet like this?”
teach: Psalm 131 is very short but very deep: “LORD, my heart isn’t arrogant, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me.” David admits that some things are beyond his ability and understanding, and he does not grasp at them. This is not giving up; it is humbly admitting: I am not God, and some things I cannot control.

Then he says, “Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother.” A nursing baby clamors for milk the moment his mother is near. A weaned child rests in his mother’s arms not to get something but because he trusts her and is content. Mature faith does not mean getting every outcome we want through prayer. It means that even when the outcome is unclear, we can rest quietly in God’s arms.

This week we have seen the pride behind control and anxiety, seen Martha-style busyness, learned to look at eternal things, and turned our worry list into a prayer list. Today let us review honestly: how many times this week did I grab back God’s authority? How many times did I learn to entrust? Do not condemn yourself. Simply find one adjustment for next week, and once more return quietly to God’s arms.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjust, repeat. Moving from control to trust is not learned in one go; it means returning to our place again and again. Humble parents say with David, “nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me,” and so they can let people be people and let God be God. The atmosphere at home loosens too.
q: Who is God? — God is like a mother who lets us rest quietly in her arms. Where did you experience his steadiness this week?
Who am I? — In which moment this week did I grab back control? In which moment did I learn to entrust?
How should I respond? — What one thing will I adjust next week, and how will I do it concretely?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.” His peace does not depend on smooth circumstances; it comes from being with the Father. Jesus leaves this peace to every anxious parent.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with me through this week. I admit that several times I grabbed back your authority and treated my family with control and anxiety. Please forgive me. Thank you also for the times I was able to entrust and to rest; they were all your grace. Make my heart calm and quiet, like a weaned child with his mother. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what was our family’s most anxious moment this week? What was our most peaceful moment?
Ask your child, “This week, have Mom and Dad been more like Jesus? Have I been rushing and bossing you less?” Just listen; do not defend yourself.
Write down one concrete adjustment for next week, for example, “Every night before bed I will give one worry to God.”
lessons.noon: “Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.” — Lord, right now I rest quietly in your arms.

fam.key: I am so quiet in God’s arms.

lamb.do: Let your child lean against you, rock him gently, and be quiet together for a minute, listening to each other breathe.
lamb.say: So quiet, so safe. God is holding you, and I am holding you too.

sprout.story: When a baby is hungry, he cries loudly. But when he has had enough to eat, he rests quietly in Mommy’s arms and makes no fuss at all. King David said, “My heart is like a baby who has had enough, resting quietly in God’s arms.” Whatever is happening outside, God is holding us.
sprout.ask: When do you feel safest?
sprout.do: Play “One Quiet Minute” as a family: sit close together, close your eyes and say nothing for a minute. At the end say together, “God is holding us!”

soldier.story: David was a very capable king who won many battles. Yet he wrote a very short psalm saying: my heart is not proud, and I don’t force myself to do things that are too big or too hard. My heart is quiet, like a weaned child leaning against his mother. A baby clamors for milk as soon as he is near his mother, but an older child leans on her simply because he likes being there and feels safe. David says being with God is this kind of safety.
ask: Was there something this week that you really wanted to control but could not? What happened in the end?
When do you think your heart is the most quiet?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person shares one thing to be thankful for this week and one thing to improve next week. Mom and Dad go first, and begin with one time this week when they were “too anxious.”

youth.talk: All this week we have been learning to lay down God’s authority. Honestly, we, your parents, found that we were more anxious than we thought, and much of it turned into pressing and checking you. We want to say sorry. We are also learning, like David, to admit that some things are not ours to control, including your future. We want to trust God more, and trust you more.
ask: This week, did you feel your parents were a bit more relaxed? What stayed the same?
How do you think we could show our care without making you feel controlled?
youth.do: Parents apologize to their child for one time this week when they were “too anxious and too controlling,” then work with the child to make a “trust agreement” for next week.

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, thank you for holding us the way a mother holds her child. Please make our whole family quiet inside and unafraid, because you are beside us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

6.memT: casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

mem.t: ‘But the LORD said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.”

sat.t: Family Day: I See Your Heart
sat.d: Give everyone a few small cards. For each family member, write (or draw) one “good quality I see in your heart,” such as honesty, courage, willingness to share, or caring for others. There is only one rule: no marks, no looks, no prizes. When the cards are ready, take turns sitting on the “heart chair” while the others read their cards aloud to that person, one by one. Finally, Dad or Mom reads 1 Samuel 16:7 and lays hands on each person to bless them: “God sees your heart, and so do we.” Put the cards into an envelope, write the date on it, and keep it as a family treasure.

sun: In the family you grew up in, what kind of “face” mattered most? How do those expectations shape the way you see your own children today?
Among marks, talents, looks and manners, which one makes it easiest to compare your child with others? What are you really afraid of underneath?
What one sentence or action will you use next week to let your child know, “You are not my report card”? You could invite another parent in your group to practice with you and remind each other.

lessons.title: God Looks at the Heart
lessons.theme: Man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart

v: When they had come, he looked at Eliab, and said, “Surely the LORD’s anointed is before him.”

But the LORD said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.”

Samuel said to Jesse, “Are all your children here?” He said, “There remains yet the youngest. Behold, he is keeping the sheep.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send and get him, for we will not sit down until he comes here.”
He sent, and brought him in. Now he was ruddy, with a handsome face and good appearance. The LORD said, “Arise! Anoint him, for this is he.”

lessons.still: Rest your hand gently on your chest and feel your heartbeat. God sees this heart clearly. Say to the Lord, “Lord, today please look at me with your eyes, and teach me to look at my child with your eyes.” Be quiet for a while, with nothing to hurry toward.
teach: The prophet Samuel was sent to Jesse’s house in Bethlehem to anoint a new king. As soon as the eldest son, Eliab, walked in, Samuel reached a conclusion: “Surely the LORD’s anointed is before him.” Tall, steady and the firstborn: in today’s terms, he was probably the one with straight A’s, a piano competition trophy, and the praise at every family gathering. If even a prophet was persuaded by appearances, how much more are we parents, who live every day in a culture of comparison?

God corrected Samuel at once: “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature,” and, “I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.” Seven sons passed by, one by one, and God had chosen none of them. So Samuel asked, “Are all your children here?” Only then did Jesse remember: “There remains yet the youngest. Behold, he is keeping the sheep.” The boy who had not even been called to the sacrificial meal was the one God had chosen. What the father had not seen, God had seen all along.

Chinese culture places great weight on face. Our children’s marks, schools, talents and manners are like medals pinned on a parent’s chest. But when God measures a child, he does not look at the medals; he looks at the heart. This does not mean that marks do not matter. It means that marks are not our child’s worth. When parents begin to learn to see their children with God’s eyes, they turn from the human viewpoint to God’s viewpoint. When the way we think changes, the atmosphere in the home changes too.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change the way you think and you change your life. The idea of face tells us, “If my child does well, then I have worth.” God’s idea tells us, “Your child is my inheritance entrusted to you, and what I value is his heart.” When parents’ focus turns from other people’s eyes back to Jesus, they no longer trade their children for their own face.
q: Who is God? — God looks at the heart; even the youngest son whom his father forgot to call, he saw. What does this show you of God that is new?
Who am I? — When others praise or criticize my child, is my first reaction concern for my child’s heart, or concern for my own face?
How should I respond? — In which child will I deliberately look for a good quality that is not on the report card today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus grew up in Nazareth, where his neighbors said, “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?” He had no famous family and no impressive résumé. Yet before he had done a single miracle, the Father spoke from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” Jesus’ worth did not come from his performance but from the Father’s love, and the same is true of our children.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you that you look at the heart. I admit that I often look at appearances, marks and what others say, and I measure my child by them, and myself too. Please open my eyes to see my child’s heart as you saw David’s. Help me stop trading my child for face, and instead walk beside him as he becomes the person who pleases you. In the name of Jesus, Amen.
acts: Today, find one good quality in each child that is “not on the report card,” and tell him about it specifically.
Notice how many times today you say something about marks or performance, and note it on your phone.
In a parents’ group chat or at a gathering of relatives, hold back once from either boasting about your child or putting him down.
lessons.noon: “For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.” — Lord, give me your eyes to see my child’s heart.

fam.key: God sees my heart.

lamb.do: Hold your child and gently touch his chest with a finger, then touch your own, and speak slowly while looking into his eyes.
lamb.say: God sees your heart. Your heart is so precious.

sprout.story: Jesse had eight sons. When the prophet Samuel came looking for a new king, the eldest was tall and handsome, and Samuel thought, “It must be him!” But God said to Samuel, “Not him. I look at the heart.” Seven brothers walked past, one by one, and none was the one. At last they ran to the field and called back the youngest, David, who was looking after the lambs. God said, “That’s him!” God had seen David’s heart of love for him all along.
sprout.ask: What do you think God sees in your heart?
sprout.do: Play “Hidden in the Heart.” Each person draws on a paper heart something good inside them (like loving to help or sharing), sticks it on their chest, and lets the family guess what it is.

soldier.story: Samuel went to Bethlehem to anoint a new king. Jesse’s eldest son, Eliab, came out tall and handsome, and Samuel thought, “This must be the one!” But God said, “Man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.” Seven brothers passed by, one after another, and none was chosen. Finally the youngest son, David, whom even his father had not thought to call, was brought in from the sheep, and God said he was the one. At school, we often compare who got the highest marks, who is best-looking, and who has the newest trainers. But God measures a person by his heart: Is he honest? Does he help others? Does he love God?
ask: What do you think people in your class compare most? How does that make people feel?
If God looks at your heart, what do you hope he will see?
soldier.do: This week be a “heart detective.” Each day, find one unseen but precious quality in a classmate or family member, and report it at dinner, saying how you discovered it.

youth.talk: Honestly, sometimes we care about your marks not only for your sake but for our own face. When relatives ask or colleagues compare, we want to have something to show. This week we read how God told Samuel that man looks at the outward appearance but the LORD looks at the heart. We want to admit first that sometimes we have looked at your marks more than at your heart.
ask: Do you ever feel that your worth at home is tied to marks or performance? When is it most obvious?
In your circle of friends or on social media, what do people get compared on most? How do you handle that?
youth.do: This week, find a quiet moment and say one thing to your child that has nothing to do with marks: “I admire your ____, because I see your heart.” After you say it, do not add a “but.”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for seeing our hearts. Please make our hearts clean, kind and full of love for you, and help us see each other with your eyes. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Whose Eyes Do I Care About?
lessons.theme: Loving the praise of men, or loving the praise of God

v: Nevertheless, even many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they didn’t confess it, so that they wouldn’t be put out of the synagogue,
for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.
How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God?

lessons.still: Settle down and ask the Holy Spirit to take you back to the most recent family gathering, parents’ group chat, or moment at the school gate. At that moment, whose eyes mattered most to you? There is no need to defend yourself; just let him shine his gentle light.
teach: John records a heartbreaking scene. Many of the rulers actually believed in Jesus, “but because of the Pharisees they didn’t confess it, so that they wouldn’t be put out of the synagogue.” Then John puts his finger on it: “for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.” It was not that they did not know the truth; they could not let go of other people’s eyes. Face can sometimes direct a person’s steps more than truth does.

Parents’ face often wears the coat of “it’s for the child’s good.” When our child does not greet people at a gathering, we are embarrassed. When his marks drop, we dread the relatives’ questions. When he chooses an unusual subject, we worry what others will think. Mrs. Lin in Singapore said that what she dreaded was not really her child doing badly. It was seeing other parents post their children’s results in the group chat when she had nothing to post. At that moment she realized that what she cared about was herself.

Jesus asked, “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God?” The culture of face is an exchange market of “receive glory from one another”: you praise my child, I praise yours, and we trade applause for our children’s performance. That glory is fragile; it is here today and gone tomorrow. God invites parents to leave this market, come back to him, and receive an acceptance that no report card can rewrite.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Behind face is the self-ruled life: I want to be respected, I want to win. Pride is leaving our proper place to grab power, even using our children as our own stage. Letting Jesus receive all the glory means I no longer need my child to bring me honor; my child and I together give the glory to him.
q: Who is God? — He is the only God who can give people true glory. When have you experienced his approval?
Who am I? — What kind of parent am I: one who scolds a child for fear of embarrassment? One who pushes a child to bring me honor? Or one who often compares my child with others?
How should I respond? — In which setting will I put down other people’s eyes and choose to stand beside my child?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I don’t receive glory from men.” When the crowd wanted to seize him and make him king, he withdrew alone to the mountain. When the religious leaders mocked him as a friend of tax collectors and sinners, he went on sitting at table with them. He lived his whole life without needing people’s applause, caring only about the Father’s pleasure. Precisely because he did not need face, he was free to love those whom others would be ashamed of.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light on me. I admit that I often love the praise of men more than your praise. My child’s performance has become my face, and his failure has become my shame. Forgive me for placing my child on my stage. Let me find my security in your acceptance, and no longer need my child to prove who I am. Amen.
acts: Recall the last time you scolded your child because of “embarrassment,” and write down what you were really afraid of.
Today, pause once the urge to post your child’s marks or certificates in a parents’ group or on social media.
Say to your child, “If I have ever scolded you because I was afraid of what others would think, I’m sorry.”
lessons.noon: “for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.” — Lord, today I want to care only about your eyes.

fam.key: God loves me, not because I do well.

lamb.do: When your child cries in public or accidentally spills something, kneel down first and hold him, and speak in a calm voice. Do not rush to apologize to those nearby.
lamb.say: It’s all right. Mommy and Daddy are here, and God loves you too.

sprout.story: Xiaoan was very shy at the family gathering. She did not dare to greet her uncles and aunties and kept hiding behind Mommy. One auntie said, “Why is this child so rude?” Mommy’s face went red, and she really wanted to scold Xiaoan. But Mommy thought of Jesus, knelt down and said softly, “You’re scared, aren’t you? I’m here with you.” On the way home, Xiaoan hugged Mommy and said, “Next time I want to try waving.”
sprout.ask: When you are scared, how do you want Mom and Dad to be with you?
sprout.do: Practice a “brave little wave.” Take turns pretending to be uncles and aunties so your child can practice waving or nodding hello, and clap together when it works.

soldier.story: When Jesus was on earth, some important rulers actually believed in him, but they were afraid of being laughed at or put out of the synagogue, so they pretended not to know him. The Bible says they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise, which means they cared more about people’s approval than about what God thought. It is the same at school. Sometimes we join in making fun of a classmate just because we are afraid of being left out. Sometimes we don’t dare say we are Christians, for fear of being thought odd. Caring about other people’s eyes is normal, but God invites us to care even more about his.
ask: Have you ever done, or not done, something because you were afraid of being laughed at?
Has there been a time when your parents made you feel they cared more about what other people thought?
soldier.do: Write a little card and keep it in your schoolbag: “Today I will care what God thinks of me.” This week, note one time you chose God’s view, and share it with your family at the weekend.

youth.talk: Many adults, ourselves included, often say, “I’m only doing this for your good.” This week we read in John that some people believed in Jesus but did not dare confess it, because they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise. We want to be honest: sometimes we control you because we fear others will say we don’t know how to raise children. You also live in a world that cares a lot about likes and followers, so we are all learning the same lesson.
ask: What effect do you think “likes” on social media have on how you see yourself?
Do you ever feel your parents get especially tense about your performance in certain settings? How do you feel then?
youth.do: Do a small experiment together: this week, each choose one day when you post nothing and do not check likes, then share at the weekend what felt different in your heart that day.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us, not because we do well but because we are your children. Help us not to fear being laughed at, and to want only to please you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Wonderfully Made, Not a Report Card
lessons.theme: I believe: God defines my child’s worth

v: For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.
My frame wasn’t hidden from you, when I was made in secret, woven together in the depths of the earth.
Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.

lessons.still: Imagine the first time you held your newborn child. He could do nothing yet, but your heart was full of thanksgiving. Find that look again, and say to the Lord, “Lord, this child is your making.” Let those words rest in your heart for a while.
teach: When a child is born, no parent holds the baby and compares: “Look, the baby in the next bed cries louder.” At that moment we are simply thankful: he has arrived safely, and all his fingers and toes are there. But at some point, numbers begin to pile up around our children: height percentiles, the month of the first steps, exam rankings, competition places. Slowly the child turns from “God’s gift” into “the parents’ report card.”

David says, “For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb.” He says, “I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” Before the child had done anything, God’s “eyes saw” him, and “in your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me.” A child’s worth is settled before the first report card appears, and it is defined not by the school, nor by relatives, nor even by parents, but by the God who made him with his own hands.

Paul warns that those who measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves “are without understanding.” Comparison leaves us without understanding because it uses the wrong ruler to measure a unique life. God did not make two children alike, and he did not give every child the same running track. Today we move from knowing to conviction and write our own declaration: I believe my child is wonderfully made; I believe he is not my report card.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your viewpoint, from the human ruler to God’s ruler, from earthly rankings to the book in heaven, from temporary marks to eternal worth. Only when parents are convinced themselves can they still look at their child with the same warm eyes on the day he fails an exam.
q: Who is God? — He saw and covered my child before he was formed. How does this God see your child?
Who am I? — What ruler do I use in my heart to measure my child? Who handed it to me?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe my child is …; I believe his worth comes from …
lessons.jesus: The disciples scolded those who brought children to Jesus, thinking the children unimportant. But Jesus “was moved with indignation and said to them, ‘Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.’” He took them in his arms and blessed them. Those children had achieved nothing, yet Jesus counted them precious. This is how God sees our children.
lessons.pray: God who made me and made my child, I give thanks to you, for we are fearfully and wonderfully made. I admit that I have measured my child by marks, rankings and other people’s children, and made him feel he is not good enough. Today I declare: I believe he is your masterpiece, and his worth is defined by you. Let this belief flow from my heart to my mouth, and to my eyes. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations: I believe my child is …; I believe his worth comes from …; I believe God has prepared for him …
Find a photo of your child as a baby, recall the thankfulness of that time, and write a sentence to him as he is now.
When you talk with your child today, do not mention the name of any other child.
lessons.noon: “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” — Lord, let my child know that he is your wonderful work.

fam.key: I am God’s wonderful work.

lamb.do: While bathing or dressing your child, gently stroke his little hands and feet and count slowly: “One, two, three …”
lamb.say: God made your little hands and feet. You are so wonderful!

sprout.story: Xiaoyu asked Daddy, “Why does my big sister run faster than me and draw better too?” Daddy picked up two leaves and said, “Look, are these two leaves the same?” Xiaoyu looked closely. “No! One is round and one is pointy.” Daddy said, “God made every leaf different, and he made every child different too. You don’t have to be like your sister. You are Xiaoyu, specially made by God!”
sprout.ask: What special thing did God give you when he made you?
sprout.do: Go outside and pick up a few leaves. Compare them as a family and look for differences. Each time you find one, say together, “What God made is wonderful!”

soldier.story: David wrote in a psalm that God made him in his mother’s womb, and that God’s eyes saw him before he was born. Think about it: there are over eight billion people in the world, and no two have the same fingerprint. God does not make children from a factory mold; like an artist, he makes each one by hand. So comparing yourself with others is like comparing a landscape painting with a poem to see which is better. You can’t, because both are the artist’s heart and soul.
ask: Who do you most often compare yourself with? How do you feel afterward?
If you believed you were made by God’s own hands, how would you see your weaknesses?
soldier.do: As a family, press your fingerprints onto the same sheet of paper and compare everyone’s patterns with a magnifying glass. Write beside them, “I am fearfully and wonderfully made,” and stick it above your desk.

youth.talk: Many of us parents grew up among rankings and comparisons: what place in the monthly test, which school we got into, how many A’s. We thought helping you win was how to love you. But reading Psalm 139, we found that before you had any results, God had already written your days in his book. We want to tell you: you are not our report card; you are God’s work.
ask: How much of your sense of worth do you think is built on marks or other people’s opinions?
If one day you do very badly in an exam, how would you most like us to respond?
youth.do: Parent and child each write an “I believe” card: parents write “I believe you are …” for the child, and the child writes “I believe I am …” for themselves. Swap and read, and say only “thank you,” with no comments.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father who made us, thank you for making each of us different and wonderful. Help us not to compare ourselves with others, and to love the way you made us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: He Must Increase, but I Must Decrease
lessons.theme: Let Jesus receive the glory, not our face

v: They came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.”
John answered, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.
You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’
He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore my joy is made full.
He must increase, but I must decrease.

lessons.still: Be quiet for a moment and ask the Lord, “Lord, in our home today, in which corner am I grabbing the stage?” Hand that picture over to him and ask him to make Jesus great there.
teach: John the Baptist’s disciples were distressed: “everyone is coming to him.” The crowds who had gathered around John were now going to Jesus. In our place, we would probably feel outdone and lose face. But John calmly said, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” He knew his own role, and he knew who the star of the stage was.

John compared himself to the friend of the bridegroom: the bridegroom is the center of the wedding, and the friend’s joy is to stand nearby and hear the bridegroom’s voice. Then he said those famous words: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” This is not low self-esteem; it is the freedom of returning to our proper place. Once a person no longer needs to be the star, there is no need to be anxious, to compare, or to fight for the spotlight.

Our homes have a stage too. At our children’s graduations, competitions, performances and even baptisms, we often step into the spotlight without noticing, wanting others to admire “me, the parent.” Today’s practice is very concrete: at home, deliberately let Jesus be great, let your child’s heart be seen, and let your own face decrease. When you celebrate, thank God first. When you praise, praise character. When you share with others, speak of God’s grace and not how well you taught.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Letting Jesus receive all the glory is one of the two cores of the 321 vision. When parents decrease, they do not lose authority; they return to their place as stewards. When Jesus increases, the family has a true star. Children also learn from their parents that life is not for being seen but for letting him be seen.
q: Who is God? — Everything is given from heaven, including our children’s gifts. What does the God who gives deserve?
Who am I? — When I face my child’s achievements, am I more like John the Baptist, or like those anxious disciples?
How should I respond? — What concrete action will I take today to let Jesus be great in our home?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus performed miracles, he often told people not to spread the news. He said, “I don’t receive glory from men.” His whole purpose on earth was to glorify the Father. Even facing the cross, his prayer was, “Father, glorify your name!” Jesus is the fullest fulfillment of “He must increase, but I must decrease.”
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you deserve all the glory. I admit that I often want to gain glory through my child and treat his achievements as my medals. Today I am willing to say, like John the Baptist, he must increase, but I must decrease. Please be made great in our home, so that my child sees not a parent who wants face but a parent who lifts you high. Amen.
acts: At dinner tonight, change the first question from “How did you do in the test?” to “Where did you see God’s grace today?”
For your child’s latest achievement, first lead the family in thanking God, and then praise his effort and character specifically.
When you speak to friends about your child, deliberately say, “This is God’s grace,” rather than “This is how I taught him.”
lessons.noon: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” — Lord Jesus, today in my home, may you be the star.

fam.key: Let Jesus be the star of our home.

lamb.do: Hold your child and look together at a picture book with Jesus in it. Point to Jesus, then lift your child’s little hand up high.
lamb.say: Jesus is the greatest, Jesus is the best!

sprout.story: John was the one who prepared the way for Jesus. Many people came to hear John speak, but when Jesus came they all ran to Jesus. John’s friends said unhappily, “Nobody is coming to you any more!” But John smiled and said, “That’s wonderful! Jesus is the most important. I only want everyone to know him.” John was like a signpost, with his finger always pointing to Jesus.
sprout.ask: How can you be a signpost pointing to Jesus?
sprout.do: Play “signpost” as a family. One person asks, “Who is the greatest?” and everyone points a finger upward and shouts, “Jesus is the greatest!”

soldier.story: John the Baptist was very famous, and people came from far and wide to hear him preach and be baptized by him. When Jesus began his ministry, the crowds gradually moved over to Jesus. John’s disciples were upset and came to complain. But John said he was like the bridegroom’s best friend at a wedding: seeing the bridegroom celebrated, he was just so happy. He said, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Think about it: if you were the most popular person in your class and one day a new student got more attention than you, what would you think? John’s secret was that he knew his job was to help people see Jesus.
ask: Why was John not angry but glad when he saw everyone going to Jesus?
At school or at home, how can you help others see Jesus and not just you?
soldier.do: This week make a “Grace Wall” as a family. Whenever someone does something good or gets good marks, write “Thank you, God, for …” on a paper on the wall, so that the glory goes first to God.

youth.talk: You may have seen some parents post their children’s certificates and acceptance letters on social media, and we have wanted to do that too. John the Baptist said, “He must increase, but I must decrease,” which makes us ask: do we often want to shine through you? This week we want to celebrate your efforts differently, not to give us face but to thank God together and truly appreciate you as a person.
ask: Do you like it when we mention you in front of others? What kind of mention makes you uncomfortable?
What could “letting Jesus receive glory” look like for you at school or online?
youth.do: Agree on a house rule with your child: before you publicly share a photo, mark or story about him, you ask him first. Start this week with one such question.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the most important one in our family. Help us to do everything so that others see you, not ourselves. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Letting Go of Empty Glory
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: has the way I look at my child changed this week?

v: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.

lessons.still: Start from the moment Samuel walked into Jesse’s house, and recall your way through to today. Ask the Holy Spirit to go through this week’s moments with you: when did I see my child’s heart? When did I slip back into face?
teach: Paul wrote to the church in Philippi: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit.” Older translations speak of “vain glory,” which means empty, with no weight. Face is just like that: it seems very important, but in the hand it is empty. A compliment in a parents’ group chat or a little envy at the relatives’ dinner table is forgotten in a few days. But how our child felt in those moments, compared, shown off or put down, may stay with him for a lifetime.

Paul goes on: “in humility, each counting others better than himself.” And “let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.” This gives parents two directions for review. First, have I compared my child with others so that he feels he is never good enough? Second, have I compared myself with other parents and then passed that pressure on to my child? Comparison is often a chain pulling from the parent’s heart all the way to the child’s shoulders.

Zhihao, a single father in Kuala Lumpur, said his biggest breakthrough this week came when his son failed a math test. His first sentence was not “What did the others get?” but “How did you feel during the exam?” His son was startled, and his eyes reddened. Review is not about giving ourselves a mark. It is about seeing small changes and writing down the next step. To have the mind of Christ Jesus is to return from face to love, again and again.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjust and repeat are the last steps in changing the way we think. Humble parents do not only ask where their child falls short; they first ask where their own way of seeing needs to be renewed. Humility leads to humility: when parents admit they love face, children learn they do not have to prove themselves through performance.
q: Who is God? — God never compares us with others; he treats us with the heart of Christ. Where did you experience his acceptance this week?
Who am I? — Did I compare my child with others this week? Did I compare myself with other parents?
How should I respond? — What one phrase or habit will I adjust next week, and how will I do it concretely?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never compared his disciples with one another. When Peter saw John and asked Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?” Jesus answered, “What is that to you? You follow me.” He has a unique calling for each person, and he treats each person with unique love. His heart is the heart we are to learn.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with me through this week. I admit that I still often grasp for empty glory and compare my child with others, and myself too. Thank you for letting me see some small changes; they are all your grace. Give me the mind of Christ, and next week help me keep learning to value my child’s heart over my own face. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: which sentence this week sounded most like “comparison”? When did we truly see our child’s heart? (Single parents can invite a spiritual companion to review with them.)
Ask your child, “This week, has the way Mom or Dad looks at you been more like Jesus?” Just listen; do not defend yourself.
Write down next week’s adjustment, for example: not mentioning any other child’s marks for a whole week.
lessons.noon: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself” — Lord, set me free from face.

fam.key: We don’t compare; we appreciate one another.

lamb.do: Hold your child and look in the mirror together. Point at him in the mirror, then at yourself, and give him a big hug.
lamb.say: You are you, and Mommy and Daddy like you so much.

sprout.story: Two brothers each drew a picture. The older brother drew an airplane, and the younger brother drew a bunch of colorful circles. When the younger one saw his brother’s picture, he cried and said, “Mine is so ugly!” Grandma came over, stuck the two pictures side by side on the wall, and said, “The airplane is so cool, and the rainbow circles are so happy. God loves that you both draw!” The little brother wiped his tears, picked up his pen again, and drew another picture to give to his big brother.
sprout.ask: What do you like best about each person in your family?
sprout.do: Play “Praise Circle.” Sit in a ring as a family and take turns saying, “I appreciate ___, because …” No talking about marks or looks!

soldier.story: Paul reminded the church not to compare themselves with one another for empty glory, but in humility to count others better than themselves. There is a fable about a forest choosing its most useful animal. The eagle said he flew highest, the rabbit said he ran fastest, and the fish said he swam best. The more they compared, the more each thought the others could not match him, and the unhappier they all became. Then the owl said, “The forest needs every one of you. Comparing only stops you seeing each other’s good.” It is the same at home, among brothers and sisters and classmates: instead of competing over who is best, learn to appreciate.
ask: Did you compare yourself with others this week? How did you feel afterward?
Do you think your parents have changed this week in how they compare?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting. Each person shares one thing they appreciated about a family member this week, and one place where they want to compare less next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: All this week we have been learning one thing: you are not our report card. It is easy to say but hard to do. Several times these past days we almost asked, “So what did so-and-so get?” and once we really did. We would like to hear how you felt: did we seem a little different this week, or no different at all? Your answer matters to us, and we will listen seriously without getting angry.
ask: This week, was there a moment when you felt compared again by Mom and Dad?
How would you like us to talk about marks so that you don’t feel pressured?
youth.do: Parents apologize to the child for a comparing remark, and then ask the child to help write “our family’s guidelines for talking about marks” and stick them on the fridge.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us this week to see one another’s hearts. Forgive us for comparing, and help us appreciate and encourage one another, as Jesus does. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

7.memT: ‘But the LORD said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.”

mem.t: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

sat.t: Family Day: Graduation Picnic for the “Vision” Stage
sat.d: This is the last week of the “vision” stage. Take a picnic blanket to the park, or simply spread it out on the living-room floor, and prepare your children’s favorite snacks. Bring out the family verses from the past eight weeks, the cards on the fridge, and the “Our Family” picture drawn in week one. Look at them one by one, and ask everyone to say, “Over these eight weeks, the biggest change in our family is …” Mom and Dad first thank the children for coming along on the journey, and say sorry for one thing. Finally, read James 4:6 together, hold hands, and pray for the next stage, “life.”

sun: Looking back over these eight weeks, which change in thinking has affected you most deeply? Moving from the human viewpoint to God’s, what have you changed concretely at home?
Did you say “I’m sorry” to your child this week? What was hardest about saying it? How did your child respond?

In your family health check, which area most needs God’s grace? As we enter the “life” stage next week, how would you like your group to watch over you? Which family could you walk beside as they begin this journey?

lessons.title: God Gives Grace to the Humble
lessons.theme: Pride is resisted by God; humility receives grace

v: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

lessons.still: Let your body relax and rest your hands palms up on your knees, like an empty vessel. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I come empty. Please put your grace into me.” Stay quietly for a while.
teach: James chapter 4 begins with a question: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?” The answer: from the desires within us. The wars at home are the same: who has the final say, who is right and wrong, who should give way. Adults and children each guard their own city walls. James does not teach us how to win. He points to a way out: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

The word “resists” is strong. Proud parents do not only set themselves against their children; they place themselves in opposition to God, because pride is leaving our place to grasp the authority that belongs only to God. Humble people, on the other hand, are not weaker; they are standing where grace flows down. Just as water always runs to the lowest place, God’s grace always flows to those willing to lower themselves.
