James gives a concrete path to humility: “Be subject therefore to God,” “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you,” and “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.” Over these eight weeks we have walked from the family as God’s design, to who reigns at home, to control and anxiety, to face and comparison, and every road points to the same answer: parents must return to their place as stewards. Let people be people and let God be God. That is humility.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility overcomes pride. Pride stirs up pride: the harder the parent, the harder the child, and in the end both lose. Humility draws out humility: when parents bow first, children learn to be soft too, and the home wins together. Humility is not giving up a parent’s responsibility; it is laying down a throne that was never ours.
q: Who is God? — God resists the proud but gives even more grace to the humble. How have you experienced this God?
Who am I? — In what kind of matters do I most often refuse to give an inch at home?
How should I respond? — In what matter will I choose today to bow first and draw near to God?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane, facing the cup of suffering on the cross, Jesus prayed, “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” He is the Son of God, yet he submitted completely before the Father. Jesus’ humility was not forced; it was a choice made out of love. We learn humility not by gritting our teeth but by drawing near to this Lord who obeyed to the end.
lessons.pray: Lord, you resist the proud and give grace to the humble. I admit that at home I often harden my neck, wanting to win, to be right, to have the final say. Today I am willing to submit to you, draw near to you, and humble myself in your sight. Please put me back in my place as a steward, and pour your grace on our home. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Recall the last argument you had with your child or spouse and ask yourself: was I holding on to the truth, or to my own face and power?
Deliberately give way today in one small matter, for example letting your child choose tonight’s dinner or the weekend activity.
Read James 4:6–10, change “you” to “I,” and pray it slowly once.
lessons.noon: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” — Lord, I am willing to come down low and stand where your grace flows.

fam.key: God gives grace to the humble.

lamb.do: Crouch down or lie on the floor so your eyes are level with your child’s, and play the game he wants to play for a while.
lamb.say: Mommy and Daddy come down low to be with you. Jesus loves us like this too.

sprout.story: A big rainstorm fell on the mountain, and the rain rushed down, splash, splash. At the high mountaintop not one drop could stay, but in the low valley there were streams and flowers and little fish. Mommy said, “God’s grace is like the rain and flows to low places. People who are willing to say ‘I need God’ and willing to let others go first are like the valley, and can be filled with God’s grace.”
sprout.ask: Would you rather be a high mountaintop or a low valley? Why?
sprout.do: Do an experiment with a cup and a plate: pour water on the bottom of an upside-down cup and into a flat plate, and see which one holds water. Say together, “Come down low, and be filled with grace!”

soldier.story: In ancient Babylon there was a very powerful king named Nebuchadnezzar. One day, as he walked on the roof of his palace, he said proudly, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built … by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” Before he had finished speaking, God took away his senses. He left the palace and ate grass in the fields like an ox for a long time. Then he lifted his eyes to heaven and admitted that God was the true King, and God restored him. He said that God is able to bring down those who walk in pride. Pride makes people think they are king; humility puts them back in their place.
ask: Why does God not like pride? How do proud people treat others?
At home or at school, when is it hardest for you to be humble?
soldier.do: This week be a “Bow-Low Warrior.” Each day look for one chance to give way first, help first, or say “I was wrong” first, and at night draw a star on the calendar.

youth.talk: Let’s talk about something very practical: when we argue in our family, who usually gives way first? Honestly, Mom and Dad often think, “I’m the adult, so I must be right.” But James says God resists the proud. We want to learn humility, not by giving up our responsibility as parents but by admitting we are not the king of this home. Jesus is.
ask: Who do you think needs to “win” most often in our family? What effect does that have on the atmosphere at home?
What do you think is the difference between humility and weakness? Is there a humble person around you whom you admire?
youth.do: Parent and child each choose a small thing that often causes arguments (such as phone time or a tidy room), sit down together, and each begin by saying what they got wrong in it, before discussing it together.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, you love the humble. Help us not to be proud or quarrel, but to be willing to give way first, help first and say sorry first. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Pharisee or Tax Collector?
lessons.theme: What kind of parent am I: self-righteous, or asking the Lord for mercy?

v: “Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed by himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to lead you into the temple and let you stand beside the two men who are praying. Listen to their voices, and then listen to the voice in your own heart. Do not rush to answer; simply listen quietly.
teach: Jesus told this parable to people who “convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others.” The Pharisee stood and prayed, and every sentence was about “I”: I am not like the rest of men, I fast, I give. His prayer was really a résumé, and he did not forget to add a comparison: I am not like this tax collector either. The tax collector stood far away, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!”

Parents too can easily live as Pharisees: I am not like those parents who let their children do whatever they like. I take my child to Sunday school every week. I have sacrificed so much for this family. All of that may be true. But when these things become our reason for standing before God, and the ground for looking down on our children, our spouse or other families, we have taken the Pharisee’s place. Junhong and Wanting, a dual-income couple in Taichung, found that the sentence they said most often when they argued was, “I’ve already done enough.”

Jesus’ conclusion is surprising: the tax collector “went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.” Today let the Holy Spirit shine his light: in front of my children, am I a Pharisee who is always right, or a tax collector willing to admit that I too need grace? The place where we admit we need mercy is exactly where our home begins to be changed by grace.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled parents live in comparison and self-righteousness, measuring others’ faults by their own goodness. Self-emptied parents live in grace, knowing that every bit of good in them was freely given. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on your own performance and not on others’ failures.
q: Who is God? — God values a chest-beating plea for mercy more than a beautiful spiritual résumé. What new thing does this show you about God?
Who am I? — What kind of parent am I? In front of my children, spouse or other families, what is the “I am not like them” that I most often say in my heart?
How should I respond? — What one thing will I admit to God today with the tax collector’s prayer?
lessons.jesus: Jesus often ate with tax collectors and sinners, and the Pharisees criticized him for it. But Jesus said, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.” He is not approving of sin; he knows that only those who admit they are sick will let the doctor heal them. Today he sits beside parents who admit they are not good enough.
lessons.pray: Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner. I admit that I am often like the Pharisee, counting up how much I do for my family, blind to my own pride and looking down on my child’s weaknesses. Today I no longer bring my résumé before you; I come only with a heart that needs mercy. Please forgive me and renew me, so that at home I live as one changed by grace. Amen.
acts: Write down three “I am not like …” sentences you often say in your heart, and hand them to God one by one.
Today, when your child makes a mistake, first pray silently, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner,” and then speak.
Tell your spouse about one thing you have seen them do for the family recently that you have never thanked them for.
lessons.noon: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” — Lord, before my children and before you, I need your mercy.

fam.key: We all need God’s mercy.

lamb.do: When your child falls or cries, pick him up, gently pat his back and rock him slowly.
lamb.say: Ouch, ouch. Mommy’s got you. God holds us like this too.

sprout.story: Two men went to the temple to pray. The first stood up very straight and said loudly, “God, I’m the best! I’m better behaved than everybody!” The second hung his head and said very softly, “God, I did wrong. Please have mercy on me and forgive me.” Jesus said God liked the second man’s prayer, because he told the truth. God loves it most when we tell him the truth.
sprout.ask: If you did something wrong, how would you tell God?
sprout.do: Play “True-Heart Prayer.” Each person says one honest sentence to God, such as “God, I was mean to my brother today. I’m sorry.” Mom and Dad go first.

soldier.story: Jesus told a parable about two men who went to the temple to pray. The Pharisee was thought a good man by everyone, and in his prayer he kept saying how good he was: I am not as bad as other people, I fast twice a week, I give a tenth of my income to God, and I am not like that tax collector over there. Tax collectors were regarded then as greedy, bad people, and this one stood far away, did not dare lift his head, and beat his chest, saying, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” Jesus said God counted the tax collector as right with him, because he was honest and humble. Before God, what matters most is not how good we are, but whether we are willing to admit we need him.
ask: What do you think was the Pharisee’s problem? Were the things he did bad?
Have you ever said in your heart, “I’m better than him”? What was happening then?
soldier.do: This week, when you notice yourself wanting to say “I’m better than him,” pray silently instead, “God, I need you too.” At the weekend, share one time you did this.

youth.talk: Jesus told this parable to people who thought they were righteous and looked down on others. Honestly, Mom and Dad are sometimes like that. We think we are more serious than other parents and wiser than you, so we seldom admit we are wrong. This week we want to learn from the tax collector and admit honestly, before God and before you, that we need mercy.
ask: Have you met “Pharisee” types at church or school? How did they make you feel?
When do you think we are most like the Pharisee? You can tell us honestly.
youth.do: Parents first share one thing from this week in which they were self-righteous, then invite the child to share, and finally pray for each other with the tax collector’s prayer.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, we all need your love and mercy. Thank you for accepting those who tell the truth. Help us not to be proud, and to be honest with you always. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Have the Mind of Christ
lessons.theme: I believe: humility is not weakness; it is returning to our place

v: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.

lessons.still: Read slowly, “but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” Imagine the King of kings taking off his royal robe and tying on an apron. Look at him quietly and say, “Lord, I am willing to learn your way.”
teach: Many parents worry: if I am humble, apologize to my children and give way, will I lose my authority? Will my children climb over my head? Behind this worry lies an idea that authority comes from standing high above. Philippians 2 shows us a different kind of authority: Christ, “existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped.” He had authority, yet he did not clutch at it.

He “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and “humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death.” Jesus’ humility was not weakness but the greatest strength: the lower he went, the higher God raised him. True authority is not won by volume, punishment or the silent treatment; it is built on character and love. What a child will respect in the end is not a parent who never admits a mistake but one whose words and actions agree, and who dares to admit when wrong.

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” Pride is leaving our place to grab power; humility is laying down power and returning to our place. Parents are not God and cannot decide their children’s whole lives. Neither are they slaves, who must be held hostage by their children’s moods. Parents are stewards, loving and guiding their children under God’s authority. Today, write your “I believe”: I believe humility is not weakness; I believe that when I let God be God, I can be a good human being.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let people be people, and let God be God. When parents try to be their children’s god, they control, they worry, and they love face. When parents return to the human place, they can be humble, rest and be real. Shift from the human viewpoint to God’s: true height is being willing to go low, like Christ.
q: Who is God? — Christ was in the form of God and yet willingly emptied himself. How does this God’s humility touch you?
Who am I? — Do I believe in my heart that “once parents admit a mistake, they lose their dignity”? Where did that idea come from?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe humility is …; I believe my place at home is …
lessons.jesus: Before the Last Supper, Jesus knew “that the Father had given all things into his hands,” yet he rose, wrapped a towel around his waist, knelt and washed the disciples’ feet. Then he said, “I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” He held all things in his hands, yet he bent down to serve. That is having the mind of Christ.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you were in the form of God, yet you emptied yourself to become a servant and died on the cross for me. I admit that I often fear losing my authority as a parent and hold tightly to power. Today I declare: I believe humility is not weakness, and I believe that when I let you be God, I can be a good parent. Please give me your mind as my own. Amen.
acts: Write down your “I believe” declaration: I believe humility is not weakness; I believe that when I let God be God, I can be a good human being; I believe my place at home is …
Do one “servant’s task” for your family today: take out the trash, wash the dishes, or polish your child’s shoes, without a word of complaint.
When you want to raise your voice to gain control, stop first and speak softly instead.
lessons.noon: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” — Lord Jesus, today at home, give me your mind.

fam.key: Jesus is King, yet he is willing to serve.

lamb.do: When you wash your child’s hands and feet, slow down, and smile at him as you wash.
lamb.say: Jesus loves us so much. He even washed people’s feet!

sprout.story: Jesus and his friends were about to have supper. Everyone’s feet were dirty and smelly after walking all day, but nobody wanted to wash them. Then Jesus stood up, took a basin of water and a towel, knelt down and washed his friends’ feet one by one! His friends were amazed: Jesus is the greatest, so why is he washing our feet? Jesus said he did this to give an example, so that we would serve one another too.
sprout.ask: How can you serve someone in your family today?
sprout.do: Play “Little Servant” as a family. Each person draws a family member’s name, secretly does one helpful thing for that person today, and at bedtime guesses who helped them.

soldier.story: Jesus is the Son of God, the King of kings. Yet the night before he was crucified, he did something that astonished his disciples: he took off his outer garment, tied a towel around his waist, poured water into a basin and washed the disciples’ feet, which in those days was a servant’s job. Peter said, “Lord, do you wash my feet?” Jesus told them he was giving them an example. Paul later wrote that Christ, being in the form of God, emptied himself and took the form of a servant. True greatness is not having others serve you but being willing to serve others.
ask: When a king kneels down to wash feet, do you think people respect him more or less? Why?
At home, what “servant’s jobs” could you take up on your own?
soldier.do: This week choose one chore nobody likes (such as cleaning the toilet or emptying the food waste), and take turns doing it as a family. When you finish, say, “I’m learning to serve like Jesus.”

youth.talk: Many people think that to have dignity, parents must never admit a mistake or show weakness in front of their children. We used to think so too. But reading in Philippians that Jesus, in the form of God, willingly emptied himself and took the form of a servant, we began to wonder whether true authority might not be never bowing, but having power and still being willing to bend down, as Jesus did. We are still learning, and we would like to hear your view.
ask: What is a respected adult like in your mind? Have they ever admitted a mistake in front of you?
In your generation, is “humility” admired or seen as weakness?
youth.do: Together find a humble person you both admire (from church, school or history), talk about what in them is like Jesus, and try to learn one thing from them this week.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, you are King, yet you bent down to serve others. Teach us to be like you, to serve and love one another at home. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: A Parent’s First “I’m Sorry”
lessons.theme: Humility begins with a sincere apology

v: “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to remind you: has there been a moment recently when your child’s eyes grew dim, and you know it was because of you? Do not turn away from that picture. Ask the Lord for courage to be reconciled today.
teach: Jesus said that if you are offering your gift at the altar and remember that your brother has anything against you, “leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” God puts reconciliation before worship. This cuts parents deeply: we may take our children to church every week and lead devotions at home, yet never have said sorry for the day we shouted at them, the time we blamed them wrongly, or the promise we did not keep.

Many Chinese parents never heard their own parents say sorry, so these words are especially hard to say. We fear that if we apologize, our children will take advantage, or that it means admitting we are failed parents. In fact it is the opposite. Xiulan, a mother of three in Penang, apologized to her eldest son for the first time. He was silent for a long time, then said, “Mom, I was wrong too.” Pride stirs up pride, and humility draws out humility; children learn to admit mistakes, often, by watching their parents admit theirs.

A good apology is simple but specific. Say what I did, for example, shouting at you yesterday. Acknowledge the child’s feelings, for example, you must have been scared and hurt. Do not add “but.” Say how I am willing to change. Finally ask, “Will you forgive me?” James says, “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed.” An apology mends more than one incident; it heals a relationship. If your home has deeper harm, such as physical violence or long-term cold treatment, please be sure to seek help from your pastor and from professionals.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than things, and relationships matter more than possessions. A parent’s first “I’m sorry” lays down “I must be right” and lifts up “let us be reconciled.” Deal with your own heart first, then with the child’s behavior; life first, then relationships. A sincere apology is often the first brick in the revival of a family.
q: Who is God? — God counts reconciliation more important than offering a gift. What does this show you of his heart?
Who am I? — When did I last say “I’m sorry” to my child? What kept me from saying it?
How should I respond? — For what specific matter will I apologize today, and to which child (or my spouse)?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never sinned and had no need to apologize to anyone, yet he willingly carried the cross for our sins. Because he has already paid the price for our wrongs, we can say “I’m sorry” without relying on face and without fearing embarrassment. In him, admitting a mistake is not failure; it is the beginning of healing.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for reconciling me to God on the cross. I admit that I owe my children several apologies that, out of pride and fear, I have never been able to say. Today please give me courage to be reconciled with my child first and then come before you. Heal the wounds between us, and let my child see your grace in my apology. Amen.
acts: Today, apologize to your child for one specific thing: say what I did, acknowledge his feelings, do not say “but,” and ask whether he is willing to forgive.
If your child is small, kneel down and hold him, and say, “Just now Daddy/Mommy was too harsh. I’m sorry.”
After you apologize, do something relaxing with your child, such as having a snack or going for a walk, so the relationship can warm up again.
lessons.noon: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” — Lord, give me courage to be reconciled first today.

fam.key: Saying sorry is brave.

lamb.do: If you were short with your child today, pick him up, look into his eyes, speak gently, and give him a long hug.
lamb.say: Mommy was too loud just now. I’m sorry. I love you.

sprout.story: One evening Xiaojie knocked over his milk, and Daddy scolded him loudly. Xiaojie ran to his room crying. After a while Daddy knocked on the door and sat down on the bed. “Xiaojie, Daddy was too harsh just now. I’m sorry. You spilled the milk by accident, and Daddy shouldn’t have shouted. Can you forgive me?” Xiaojie nodded and hugged Daddy. “I forgive you! I’ll help wipe the floor too.” And the two of them laughed together.
sprout.ask: If someone says sorry to you, what will you say?
sprout.do: Practice the “Three Steps of Sorry”: say what I did, say sorry, ask “Can you forgive me?” Act it out as a family with toys.

soldier.story: Jesus taught his disciples: if you bring a gift to the altar to offer to God, and remember that someone is upset because of you, put down your gift, go and make peace with him, and then come back and offer it to God. Why? Because God cares about our relationships with people as much as our relationship with him. Think about it: you can sing many songs to God and still be angry with your little brother, or go to Sunday school and still not have said sorry to a classmate. Jesus says, go and make peace first. Saying “I’m sorry” takes courage, but it can join a broken relationship back together.
ask: Why is it often so hard to say “I’m sorry”?
Is there anyone you need to make peace with this week?
soldier.do: Write a “peace card” to someone you need to make peace with (a family member or classmate): write what I did, I’m sorry, and how I want to change. Give it to them in person this week.

youth.talk: We want to do something we seldom do: apologize to you. (Parents, here name one specific thing, for example: Last month I criticized you in front of your friends, and it embarrassed you badly. I’m sorry.) We are not asking you to apologize straight away, or to say right away that it’s okay. We just want to do what Jesus said and be reconciled first. You can take your time, and say whatever you want to say.
ask: Since you were little, has there been something you have always wanted us to apologize for?
What do you think is the difference between a sincere apology and a half-hearted one?
youth.do: This week parents take the initiative to invite their child out for a meal or a walk, listen carefully without defending themselves, and if the child raises something that needs an apology, apologize sincerely on the spot.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for forgiving us. Give us courage to say sorry, and soft hearts to say “I forgive you,” so that our family is often reconciled. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Eight-Week Review and Family Health Check
lessons.theme: Return to our place as stewards, and prepare to enter the renewal of life

v: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.
See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.
Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.

lessons.still: Bring your notes, cards or the stickers on your fridge from these eight weeks in front of you. Ask the Holy Spirit, like a gentle doctor, to look through them from the beginning with you. Say to him, “Search me, God, and know my heart.”
teach: In the ruins of a shattered home and a destroyed temple, Jeremiah wrote, “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.” We search not to condemn ourselves but to return. Eight weeks ago we began with the family as God’s design. We saw that children are an inheritance from the LORD, that faith is to be passed down through the generations, and we wrote down the vision: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” That was the first half of the vision stage: turning from the human viewpoint to God’s.

Then we went deeper: who reigns at home? We saw that the self-ruled life is the root of the fall, and that control and anxiety, face and comparison are all parents wanting to sit in God’s place. This week we found the way out: humility, letting people be people and God be God, returning to our place as stewards, beginning with one “I’m sorry.” Every week we went through information, revelation, conviction, practice, and review and adjustment. Only by repeating the cycle does a new way of thinking take root.

Today you are invited to do a “family health check.” A medical check-up is not meant to frighten us but to let us take care of things early. A family health check likewise lets us see clearly where the family stands before entering the next stage, “life.” Husband and wife each (single parents can invite a spiritual companion) give a score from 1 to 5 for eight areas: the family belongs to God, children are an inheritance, faith is passed on, the whole family has a vision, Jesus reigns at home, children are entrusted to God, no comparing but seeing the heart, and parents humble themselves first. A low score is not failure; it is where God will renew us next.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change the way you think and you change your life; change your life and you change the way you live. The vision stage is over, but the change has only begun. In the next stage we move from knowing to being renewed: parents first remain in the Lord and bear the fruit of the Spirit at home. The result of your family health check is the prayer list you take into the next stage.
q: Who is God? — Over these eight weeks, when did God speak to you most truly? What kind of God did you see?
Who am I? — Compared with eight weeks ago, in which way of thinking have I changed? Which has stayed where it was?
How should I respond? — For the lowest-scoring area in the family health check, what concrete adjustment will I write down for next week?
lessons.jesus: After his resurrection, on the shore Jesus prepared a charcoal fire and breakfast for Peter, who had denied him three times, and asked him three times, “do you love me?” He did not dig up the past; he gently led Peter to face himself and then entrusted him: “Feed my sheep.” Jesus’ reviews always lead to restoration and sending, and he leads you this way now as you look back over eight weeks.
lessons.pray: God, search me and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way. Thank you that these eight weeks have changed how I see my home, my children and myself. I place the results of our family health check in your hands. Give your grace where we are weak, and bring our whole family into the renewal of life. Amen.
acts: Complete the “family health check”: score the eight areas from 1 to 5: the family belongs to God, children are an inheritance, faith is passed on, the whole family has a vision, Jesus reigns at home, children are entrusted to God, no comparing but seeing the heart, and parents humble themselves first.
Talk with your spouse (or a spiritual companion): compare your scores, choose the area most needing adjustment, and write down one concrete action for next week.
Ask your child, “Over these eight weeks, have Mom and Dad been more like Jesus? What has been most different?” Just listen; do not defend yourself.
lessons.noon: “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.” — Lord, I look back and I return; lead us forward.

fam.key: We look back together and go forward together.

lamb.do: Open the photos of your child from the past two months on your phone, hold him, and look at them one by one, saying a thank you for each.
lamb.say: Thank you, God, that you have grown so much. We love you so much.

sprout.story: Xiaobao stood by the door frame to be measured, and Mommy drew a line above his head, next to the line she had drawn two months before. Xiaobao shouted in delight, “I’ve grown taller!” Mommy said, “Yes! Our family has grown taller these two months too. Mommy and Daddy learned to say sorry, and you learned to tell God the truth. God helps our whole family grow together!”
sprout.ask: In these two months, what do you think has become different in our family?
sprout.do: Measure everyone’s height on the door frame or wall, draw a line and write the date, and beside it stick a small note about one way “our family has grown.”

soldier.story: When doctors give a health check, they measure height and weight, listen to the heartbeat and test the blood, not to scare people but to find problems early and take care of them. Our family needs a health check too. These eight weeks we have learned that the family is God’s design; children are treasures God has entrusted to Mom and Dad; faith is to be passed down from one generation to the next; our family is to serve God together; Jesus is the King of our home; we should not compare but see each other’s hearts; and when we do wrong, we say sorry. Now we will see where our family is healthy and where it needs God’s healing.
ask: Of the things we learned in these eight weeks, which do you remember best?
What do you think is the healthiest thing about our family? And what needs the most improvement?
soldier.do: Do a “kids’ family health check.” Draw eight hearts on a sheet of paper, one for each week’s theme. Let your child score each heart with a smiley, neutral or sad face, then pray together for the heart with the sad face.

youth.talk: This is the eighth week we have walked together. Honestly, we aren’t sure whether you have felt any change, and perhaps at times it seemed we had only changed our way of talking. So we would like to ask for your help: use your eyes to give our family a health check. What you observe may be more accurate than what we see ourselves. We will take what you say seriously, and choose one thing from it to change in a concrete way.
ask: In these eight weeks, which change in Mom and Dad do you think is real? Which is still only talk?
If our family were a patient, where do you think it most needs healing right now?
youth.do: Parent and child each fill in a family health check (eight areas, 1 to 5 each), compare answers, and choose one area for the whole family to work on next week. Ask the child to be the “inspector” and report back at the weekend.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for being with our family these eight weeks and helping us grow together. Heal the places in our family that need healing, and lead us to keep following Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

8.memT: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

mem.t: I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.

sat.t: Family Day: A Walk Among the Vines
sat.d: Take the whole family for a walk in a park, an orchard or your neighbourhood, and find a big tree (a grapevine is even better). Ask the children to observe: where are the branches joined? Where do the leaves get their water? Pick up a small twig that has already fallen to the ground, still with leaves, and take it home. Put it on the windowsill and watch how it changes over the coming week. Back home, draw a grapevine together: write “Jesus” on the trunk, write a family member’s name on each branch, and draw the fruit you hope each branch will bear. Finally, read John 15:5 together and pray for each “branch.”

sun: As we enter the “life” stage, what kind of branch do you feel you are, in your connection with the Lord: tightly joined, loosely hanging, or about to snap?
In the busyness of raising children, what most often pulls you away from Jesus’ feet? In which season did you experience the fruit of remaining in the Lord?
What small “remaining in the Lord” rhythm will you set for next week? Whom can you invite to practice with you and remind one another?

lessons.title: I Am the Vine, You Are the Branches
lessons.theme: The fruit of the family comes from the parents’ connection with the Lord

v: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer.
Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.
You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.
Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me.
I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.

lessons.still: Imagine you are a small branch, resting lightly on the vine. No effort, no performance, only being joined. Say to the Lord, “Lord, today I come first to be joined to you.” Stay quietly for a while.
teach: In the first eight weeks we changed our thinking: the family belongs to God, and parents are stewards. From this week we enter the “life” stage, and ask a deeper question: now that our thinking has changed, where does the power come from? Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches.” A branch bears fruit not by straining but by being joined to the vine. The sap flows from the root to the branch, and the fruit grows naturally.

Many parents work hard to help their children bear good fruit: courtesy, responsibility, love for God. We buy parenting books, attend seminars and set rules, but often the harder we try, the more exhausted we become, and the more our children resist. Jesus puts it plainly: “apart from me you can do nothing.” Not “do less,” but “do nothing.” Parents who have left the vine often have nothing left to give their children but their own anxiety and tiredness.

A family is like a tree, and the parents’ spiritual life is the branch that connects to the root. When parents remain in the Lord, his life flows through them into the home: patience, gentleness and joy are no longer performances squeezed out but fruit that grows naturally. This is “life first, then relationships, then ministry”: first take care of the parents’ own connection with God, then the relationship with the children, and only then all the methods of parenting.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is first with God, then with myself, then with others, then with tasks. Parents most often turn this upside down: first the tasks (homework, housework), then people (the child’s feelings), and God last of all. To remain in the Lord is to put the order right: the first connection to make is with the vine.
q: Who is God? — Jesus is the true vine, and the Father is the farmer. What new thing does this show you about God’s role in your home?
Who am I? — These days, am I more like a branch tightly joined to the vine, or a branch desperately trying to bear fruit on its own?
How should I respond? — At what time, and in what way, will I first go back to the vine for five minutes today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus himself is the example of remaining in the Father. He said, “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” If the Son of God does not rely on himself but is always connected to the Father, he invites us to be connected to him in the same way, and to let his life become our life.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the true vine and I am a branch. I admit that I often try to bear the fruit of a good parent by myself, and grow more tired. Today I come back to you first. Let your life flow into me, and then through me to my children. Apart from you I can do nothing; in you I want to bear much fruit. Amen.
acts: Today, before your children get up or after they fall asleep, set aside five minutes to read only John 15:1–5 and do nothing else.
Write: “Apart from the Lord, I can’t ____.” Fill in the parenting difficulty you most often try to tough out on your own.
Change your phone wallpaper to a reminder: “Connect first, then do.”
lessons.noon: “I am the vine. You are the branches.” — Lord, right now I come back to you, and let your life flow into me.

fam.key: We are joined to Jesus.

lamb.do: Let your child hold your finger tightly, and gently wrap his little hand with yours, and rock them slowly together.
lamb.say: You are joined to Mommy, and together we are joined to Jesus.

sprout.story: Xiaofang found a broken branch in the park, still with green leaves on it. She took it home and put it in a vase. After a few days the leaves turned yellow and the branch dried up. Xiaofang felt so sad. “Why isn’t it green any more?” Daddy said, “Because it left the tree, so it can’t drink water. Jesus says he is the tree and we are the branches. As long as we stay joined to Jesus, we will always have life!”
sprout.ask: How can we stay joined to Jesus?
sprout.do: Play “Tree and Branches” as a family. Dad or Mom stands in the middle as the tree, and the children are branches holding the tree’s hands. When you let go, you “wither” and crouch down; when you hold hands again you “come alive” and jump up.

soldier.story: When Jesus spoke with his disciples, he used a picture of a vine: I am the vine and you are the branches; a branch cannot bear fruit by itself, but must be joined to the vine. Think of a phone. A phone is amazing: it can take photos, go online and play games. But when the battery is dead, it can do nothing, and must be plugged in to charge. Our lives are like that too. However clever or capable we are, we need to stay joined to Jesus, and receive love, joy and strength from him. Jesus says apart from him we can do nothing.
ask: When do you feel most like a “dead phone”?
What can you do each day to “charge up” with Jesus?
soldier.do: This week choose a fixed time each day (for example before school or at bedtime) to read one Bible verse and say one prayer. Color in one battery bar on a “charging chart” each day, and see if you can fill it by the weekend.

youth.talk: We used to try very hard to be “good parents.” We read many parenting articles and made many rules for you, but often the harder we tried, the more tired we became, and our relationship with you did not get better. This week we read Jesus saying, “apart from me you can do nothing.” We realized that the problem may not be our methods but that our own connection with God had been cut. So from now on, we want to take care of our own relationship with God first.
ask: What do you think a Christian being “connected to God” looks like in everyday life?
What is your own relationship with God like right now? What would you like to change? (You may choose not to answer.)
youth.do: Parents invite their child to be an observer for a week: “If you see us becoming less impatient, or becoming impatient again, please tell us.” Let your child be a witness to your remaining in the Lord.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the vine and we are the branches. Help us to stay joined to you every day, and to receive love and strength from you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Martha’s Kitchen
lessons.theme: What kind of parent am I: anxious and troubled about many things

v: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.still: Listen to the voices in your heart right now: how much is still undone? What will I cook later? What is due at school tomorrow? Lay these voices before the Lord one by one, and then be quiet and listen to him calling your name.
teach: Martha opened her home to receive Jesus, and that was a beautiful thing. She was warm, capable and responsible, the kind of person who keeps a home in good order. But the Bible says she “was distracted with much serving.” In the end she rushed up to Jesus and complained: “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone?” Busyness turned her love into resentment, and her service into blame.

Many parents live in Martha’s kitchen. In a two-income family the morning is like a battle: lunchboxes, the school bus, work; and in the evening, homework, bath time and bedtime. Jiaxin, who works in Singapore, said she serves her family every day, yet often feels no one cares about how hard she works, and in the end her temper lands on the children. We think that if only we get everything done, the home will be well, but we forget that a frantic heart pulls down the temperature of the whole home.

Jesus gently called her name twice: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed.” Jesus did not say that cooking was wrong; he said the order was wrong. Mary chose to sit at Jesus’ feet, and that was “the good part.” Today let the Holy Spirit shine his light on us: what kind of parent am I? A Martha who only rushes about the kitchen while her heart grows more tangled, or a Mary who sits at the Lord’s feet first and then rises to serve?
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Martha put ministry first, and even her relationships were hurt. Mary took care of life first, so that her serving had a source. Using your heart and relying on the Holy Spirit brings joy; using your head and relying on yourself brings worry. If parents stay often at the Lord’s feet, even the busyness of the kitchen can become worship.
q: Who is God? — Jesus gently called Martha’s name twice. How does he see your busyness and weariness?
Who am I? — What kind of parent am I? This week, in what matter was I frantic inside and in the end took out my resentment on my family?
How should I respond? — Tomorrow, how long am I willing to sit at the Lord’s feet before the busyness begins?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ schedule was fuller than any parent’s: healing the sick, driving out demons, teaching, with crowds so big that he and his disciples had no time even to eat. Yet he was never frantic, because he always withdrew first to a quiet place to be with the Father. He did not blame Martha; he invited her: the one thing needed has been prepared for you too.
lessons.pray: Lord, I am that Martha, rushing about in the kitchen. I am anxious and troubled about many things, and I often bring weariness and resentment to my children and spouse. Please call my name gently, and let me stop and sit at your feet. I am willing to choose the good part, and let you be my source. Amen.
acts: List the three things that make you frantic today and ask the Lord: which can I put down, postpone, or ask someone to help with?
Before you start the housework today, sit down and read Luke 10:41–42, and be quiet for one minute.
Say to your family, “I’ve been too frantic lately. If I’ve lost my temper with you, I’m sorry.”
lessons.noon: “but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” — Lord, in the middle of my busyness, I choose you first.

fam.key: Sit at Jesus’ feet first.

lamb.do: Put down what is in your hands, hold your child and sit quietly for one minute. Don’t look at your phone; just look at him and pat him gently.
lamb.say: Let’s stop first and be with Jesus.

sprout.story: Jesus came to Martha and Mary’s house. Martha was busy in the kitchen cooking, setting out bowls and wiping the table, sweating all over. Her sister Mary sat beside Jesus and listened carefully to him. Martha got cross and ran to ask Jesus to tell her sister to help. Jesus told her gently, “Martha, you are too busy and too worried. Sitting down to listen to me is the best choice.”
sprout.ask: When do you like best to be quiet with Jesus?
sprout.do: Make a little “Jesus Time” corner with a small cushion and a children’s Bible. Each day let your child sit there while Mom or Dad reads a short story.

soldier.story: Jesus visited Martha’s home. Martha wanted to look after Jesus well, so she cooked many dishes and rushed in and out, but her sister Mary sat at Jesus’ feet, listening to his teaching. The busier Martha got, the angrier she became, and she ran to complain to Jesus. Jesus answered, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed.” Have you ever had this experience: homework, tutoring, activities and competitions come one after another, and you are so busy you forget to pray, and even snap at your family? Jesus says that however busy we are, we must first choose the most important thing: being with him.
ask: Do you think Martha did something wrong? What was her real problem?
What has been the busiest thing for you this week? Have you forgotten Jesus because of being busy?
soldier.do: This week, set a family “one thing needed” time: five minutes after dinner every day, when everyone puts down phones and homework, reads a verse together and prays one sentence each in turn.

youth.talk: We have noticed that our home lately looks a lot like Martha’s kitchen: everyone is busy, you with exams and activities, we with work and housework, and we pass one another by, and when we do speak it is often to rush or remind. This week we read how Jesus said to Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. We want to admit first that we often treat tasks as more important than you, and even more important than God.
ask: What do you think is the most “Martha’s kitchen” thing about our family?
In your busy life right now, what could “sitting at Jesus’ feet” look like for you?
youth.do: Each person looks over this week’s schedule and drops or reduces one thing that is not “the one thing needed,” keeping that time for God or family. Parents go first.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, we are often very busy. Remind us that the most important thing is to be with you. Help us to sit at your feet first every day. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: A Tree Planted by the Streams
lessons.theme: I believe: the fruit of the family comes from the parents’ roots

v: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
but his delight is in the LORD’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.
He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
“Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, and whose confidence is in the LORD.

For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.

lessons.still: Imagine a tree with its roots sunk deep in the soil beside a stream. The sun outside is fierce, yet its leaves stay green. Quietly think of yourself as that tree, and say to the Lord, “Lord, I want to put down roots in you.”
teach: Psalm 1 describes a blessed man: “his delight is in the LORD’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.” He “will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither.” This tree does not go looking for water itself; it is planted beside the streams. Parents’ spiritual life is the same: it is not held up by willpower but by letting ourselves be planted beside God’s word and drinking every day.

Jeremiah says that the one who trusts in the LORD “will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes.” The seasons of parenting often bring heat: the night a child is sick, the clashes of adolescence, money pressures, the exhaustion of caring for aging parents. Grandma Chen in Ipoh, who looks after her grandchildren while caring for her husband after his stroke, said that in her driest days she got through by reading one verse of a psalm every morning. When roots go deep, a year of drought does not make the tree wither.

Today we move from knowing to conviction: the fruit of the family comes from the parents’ roots. We often want to repair our children’s fruit directly, their temper, attitude and habits, but neglect our own roots. Of course the children’s fruit also depends on their own choices, but the spiritual climate of a home often begins to change from the parents’ roots. Write your declaration: I believe that if my life is rooted in the Lord, our family will bear his fruit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The five-fold change from the inside out: thinking, life, living, relationships and ministry. After our thinking has changed, the next thing is to put roots down into life. Roots lie underground, unseen, yet they determine everything above. A parent’s devotion is like roots, and the atmosphere of the home is like leaves; what children can see is often the fruit of roots that parents cannot see.
q: Who is God? — God is the stream that never runs dry, and he himself plants those who trust in him. In which dry season have you experienced his refreshing?
Who am I? — Where are my roots now: in God’s word, in others’ approval, or in my child’s performance?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe my roots …; I believe our family’s fruit …
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, each of his three replies began, “It is written.” His roots went deep into the Father’s word, so that in hunger, temptation and pressure he could still stand. He also invites us, as he did, to meditate on God’s word day and night, and not to fear when the heat comes.
lessons.pray: Lord, I want to be a tree planted by the streams. I admit that I often want to fix my children’s fruit directly and neglect my own roots. I believe that my life must be rooted in you, and I believe that you will bear your fruit in our home through my life. Keep my leaf green in the heat and drought. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations: I believe my roots will go down into …; I believe God will bring forth in our family …; I believe in the season of drought …
Choose the verse that moved you most this week, copy it on a sticky note, put it beside the kitchen or bathroom mirror, and read it three times a day.
Notice the moments today when you want to “fix your child’s fruit,” and stop first to ask: have my roots had a drink today?
lessons.noon: “He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither.” — Lord, let my roots drink their fill of your living water today.

fam.key: When roots go deep, the fruit is sweet.

lamb.do: Let your child help water a small pot plant at home. Hold his little hand and slowly pour the water into the soil together.
lamb.say: The little tree drinks water and grows, and you will grow in God’s love too.

sprout.story: In the garden there were two little trees. One grew beside a small stream and could drink water every day; the other grew in sandy ground and was often thirsty. When summer came, the sun was big and hot. The leaves of the little tree in the sand dried up, but the little tree by the stream was still green, and it even bore sweet fruit! Grandma said, “When we read the Bible and pray every day, it is like the little tree drinking water. Our hearts will be green and sweet.”
sprout.ask: How do you think we can let our hearts “drink water”?
sprout.do: Put a mung bean or red bean on damp cotton wool, give it a little water each day and read a verse, and watch how its roots grow.

soldier.story: Psalm 1 says that the person who loves God’s word and meditates on it day and night is like a tree planted by streams of water, which bears fruit in its season and whose leaf does not wither. Did you know that some big trees send their roots very deep and very wide? When a typhoon comes, a tree with shallow roots is blown over at once, but a tree with deep roots stands firm. Our lives are the same. When we face exam stress at school, a misunderstanding with friends, or a really bad mood, what we depend on are the roots we have put down ordinarily: reading God’s word, talking with God, and believing his promises.
ask: How deep do you think your “roots” are now?
When pressure comes like a typhoon, how do you usually face it?
soldier.do: This week read one verse of Psalm 1 each day and draw a tree. Each day you read, draw the roots a little longer, and at the weekend see how deep your roots have grown.

youth.talk: We often put our attention on you: your marks, your habits, your attitude. But this week we read that whether a tree’s fruit is good depends on where its roots are. We began to reflect that maybe we should first check our own roots, and not keep pruning your branches. We want you to know that from now on we will put our own relationship with God first.
ask: Where in daily life do you think a person’s “roots” show?
What area of your life feels most like “drought” right now?
youth.do: Parent and child each choose a psalm (for example Psalm 1 or 23), read it every day this week, and at the weekend swap and share which line watered you like water.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, make us like trees planted by the streams, drinking your word every day and bearing sweet fruit. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Prayer Before Dawn
lessons.theme: In the gaps of parenting, make a place for the Lord

v: Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.
Simon and those who were with him searched for him.
They found him and told him, “Everyone is looking for you.”

lessons.still: Whether it is early morning, your lunch break or late at night, this moment can be God’s time. Take three deep breaths, and each time say in your heart, “Lord, I am here.” You need not say more.
teach: In Mark chapter 1, Jesus had an extremely busy day: teaching in the synagogue, driving out an unclean spirit, healing Peter’s mother-in-law; and in the evening, the whole city gathered at the door and he healed many who were sick. But “early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.” After the busiest of days, the first thing he did was not to catch up on sleep or plan the schedule but to return to the Father.

Many parents say: I would like to have devotions too, but my children are too small and work is too busy; there is simply no time. In fact, remaining in the Lord does not have to wait for a long quiet stretch. It can begin in the gaps of parenting: five minutes before the children wake, a verse meditated on while feeding the baby, a prayer while waiting for the school bus, a psalm heard while washing up. Jianhua, a father in Taipei, turned the MRT carriage of his daily commute into his “deserted place.”

Today’s practice is to set a small “remaining in the Lord” rhythm for yourself: a fixed time, a fixed place, a simple way. It need not be perfect; it only needs to begin. When the disciples found Jesus they said, “Everyone is looking for you.” Your children, your work and your housework will keep looking for you too; because everyone is looking for you, you need all the more to be found by the Lord first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. Remaining in the Lord is not one more item on the to-do list but letting the Lord be the beginning of the day. First God, then myself, then others, then tasks. Give the first five minutes to the Lord, and the whole day ahead will be different.
q: Who is God? — Even the Son of God needed to be alone with the Father in his busiest time. How does this change how you see your own needs?
Who am I? — I often use “no time” as my excuse, but what really keeps me from drawing near to God?
How should I respond? — Write down your “remaining in the Lord” rhythm: what time? what place? what will I do?
lessons.jesus: All his life Jesus practiced connection with the Father: he prayed at his baptism, prayed all night before choosing his disciples, went up the mountain alone to pray after feeding the five thousand, prayed in Gethsemane, and prayed even on the cross. His strength did not come from a schedule but from the Father’s presence. He is the best example of parents remaining in the Lord.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you rose and prayed before dawn, but I often let my children, my phone and my to-do list take the first moment of my day. Today I am willing to make a place for you, beginning with five minutes. Meet me in the gaps of parenting, and let me be found by you first before I respond to everyone’s needs. Amen.
acts: Set a fixed five minutes of “remaining in the Lord”: tomorrow, get up a little before your children, or after they sleep, and read a passage from John 15.
Choose a corner at home as your “deserted place”: a chair, a Bible and a pen.
Practice a “prayer on the way out” as a family: every time you leave home today, say together, “Lord, go with us.”
lessons.noon: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.” — Lord, in the middle of my busyness, I also want to come before you first.

fam.key: Every day, say good morning to Jesus first.

lamb.do: When your child wakes in the morning, first hold him and whisper a prayer toward the light from the window, before changing the diaper or feeding him.
lamb.say: Good morning, darling! Good morning, Jesus!

sprout.story: It was still dark, the rooster had not crowed yet, and everyone was asleep. Jesus quietly got up and went to a quiet place to talk with his heavenly Father. Later his friends found him and said, “Everyone is looking for you!” Jesus had already finished talking with the Father, his heart was full of strength, and he set out with his friends to go and help more people.
sprout.ask: What is the first thing you want to say to Jesus when you get up in the morning?
sprout.do: Teach your child a “good-morning prayer” gesture: open both hands wide like the sun and say, “Good morning, Jesus! Be with me today.” Do it as a family every morning.

soldier.story: Jesus spent a super-busy day in Capernaum: teaching in the synagogue, driving out an unclean spirit, healing Peter’s mother-in-law; and in the evening the whole city crowded around the door, bringing the sick to be healed. The next day, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went to a quiet place alone to pray. When the disciples found him they said, “Everyone is looking for you.” Think about it: if you were Jesus and had been so tired the day before, would you choose to sleep a bit longer, or to pray? Jesus knew that the busier he was, the more he needed to be with the Father, because strength comes from the Father.
ask: Why did Jesus get up early to pray when he was so busy?
At what time in your day is it best to talk quietly with God?
soldier.do: Design your own “five-minute morning prayer” with Mom and Dad: one verse, one thank you, one prayer for the day. Do it for five days in a row and tick it on the calendar each day.

youth.talk: You may think that getting up early for devotions is something only older people do, and honestly we often fail at it too. We used to think we needed a long stretch of quiet time before it counted as devotions, so we kept putting it off. This week we read how Jesus got up before dawn to pray at his busiest, and we decided to begin small: five minutes a day. We won’t require you to do the same, but you are welcome to join us, or to tell us your own way.
ask: In your generation, what are good ways of drawing near to God (for example a Bible app, worship songs, journaling)?
If you were to design your own “five minutes,” how would you arrange it?
youth.do: This week invite your child to pick one day when they and a parent get up ten minutes earlier, drink something hot and read a passage together, without talking about homework.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for teaching us to speak with our heavenly Father first. Help us to say good morning to you first every day, and to be with you all day long. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Remain in My Love
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: has remaining in the Lord flowed into love at home?

v: Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love.
If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, even as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.
I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.
“This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.

lessons.still: Recall the moments you spent with the Lord this past week, perhaps many, perhaps few. There is no need to blame yourself; just tell him honestly, “Lord, this is what my week looked like.” Then be still, and hear him say that he loves you.
teach: Jesus said, “Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love.” Remaining in the Lord is not a set of spiritual techniques but dwelling in a love. As the Father loved Jesus, so Jesus loves us. Only when parents are first filled with this love can they avoid loving their children with an empty heart.

Then Jesus said, “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.” This is the test of remaining in the Lord. We may have devotions every day and still be cold to our children and sharp with our spouse; that connection may have stayed only in the head. A true connection must send the sap all the way to the tips of the branches: to the dinner table, the homework desk and the bedside at bedtime. Jesus also said this is so “that my joy may remain in you”; a home that remains in the Lord slowly gains a little more joy.

This week we saw the vine and the branches, Martha’s kitchen, the tree by the streams, and prayer before dawn. Today, review two things honestly. First, did I come back to the vine this week? Second, did the love I received from the Lord flow to my family? We do not need a good score, only a next step. The adjustment is often small: get up five minutes earlier tomorrow, or hold your child a little longer tonight at bedtime.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. If our life is truly renewed by the Lord, it must flow into our relationships; if it cannot flow out, go back to the source and connect again. The 920 life: every family member is our “2,” and living out the “0” of the self-emptied life bears the “9” fruits of the Spirit.
q: Who is God? — Jesus loves us as the Father loved him. Where did you feel this love this week?
Who am I? — How many times did I come back to the vine this week? Did the love I received from the Lord flow to my family?
How should I respond? — What one thing will I adjust next week? How can remaining in the Lord flow more naturally into our home?
lessons.jesus: Jesus did not only tell us to remain in his love; he himself kept the Father’s commandments and remained in the Father’s love. He also lived this love among his disciples: washing their feet, bearing with their weakness, and in the end laying down his life for them. Love flows from the Father to Jesus, and from Jesus to us. This is the life of the vine.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for inviting me back to you again and again this week. I admit that some days I forgot to stay connected, and sometimes I received your love but did not let it flow to my family. Fill me again, so that I remain in your love and love my children and spouse as you love me. Help me to keep practicing next week. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: how many times this week did we each connect with the Lord? What effect did that have on the atmosphere at home? (Single parents can talk with a spiritual companion.)
Ask your child, “This week, have Mom or Dad been more like Jesus? More patient, or just as impatient?” Only listen; do not defend yourself.
Write down one concrete adjustment for next week, for example: fix your devotion time to the ten minutes before your children get up.
lessons.noon: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.” — Lord, let your love flow from me to my family today.

fam.key: Jesus loves me, and I love my family.

lamb.do: Hold your child, first kiss his forehead, then take his little hand and let him touch the face of Dad, Mom or a big brother or sister.
lamb.say: Jesus loves you, and we love you too.

sprout.story: A hose carries water from the tap to the garden. When the tap is turned on, the water flows into the hose, and from the hose onto the flowers, and the flowers drink their fill. Mommy said, “Jesus’ love is like water. It flows from Jesus into our hearts, and from our hearts onto other people. If the hose gets knotted, the flowers can’t get any water!”
sprout.ask: Who did you let Jesus’ love flow to this week?
sprout.do: Play “Love Hose” with a length of wool: start with a paper that says “Jesus,” and pass it from person to person. Everyone who gets the wool says “I love you” and passes it to the next family member.

soldier.story: Jesus said: I love you as the Father loves me, so remain in my love; and love one another as I have loved you. It is like a relay race. The Father hands the baton of love to Jesus, Jesus hands it to us, and we hand it to the people around us. If the baton stops in our hands, the race stops. This week we learned to stay connected to Jesus, and now we check: have we passed Jesus’ love on? Have we been a bit more patient and gentle with our little brothers and sisters, our parents and our classmates?
ask: When was the time this week you were most connected with Jesus?
Did you pass Jesus’ love on to anyone this week? Whom would you like to pass it to next week?
soldier.do: Hold a family meeting. Each person shares one thing from this week where “love flowed out” and one where “love got stuck,” and then you choose one act of love to do together next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we began to spend a little time each day drawing near to God. Some days we managed it, and some days busyness interrupted us again. We want to ask you an honest question: did you feel we were a little different this week? If not, please tell us straight. Jesus says that when we truly remain in him, love flows out. If it cannot flow out, it means we still need to return to the source.
ask: Was there a moment this week at home when you felt loved?
Where do you think love gets “stuck” in our family?
youth.do: Parents apologize to the child for one moment this week when love did not flow out, and then ask the child for a small suggestion for next week, which the whole family will carry out.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for loving us. Help us to remain in your love always, and pass your love on to our family and friends. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

9.memT: I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.

mem.t: but those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.

sat.d: This Saturday, deliberately have a “slow day” as a family. Set no alarm in the morning, and make a simple breakfast together. In the afternoon, take a walk at a nearby park or by the sea, with no rushing and no tutoring. Ask everyone to do one small thing that helps them “renew their strength”: taking a nap, drawing, kicking a ball or listening to worship songs. In the evening, lie on the living-room floor with the big light off and one small lamp on, and take turns saying, “Today the time I felt most relaxed was …” Finally, read Isaiah 40:31 together and pray for one another.

sun: Lately, what has tired you most: your body, your emotions, or your spirit? When did you feel you could not go on?
In the busiest season of parenting, what small ways have you found to draw near to God? Is there any difficulty your group could help with together?

Next week, how will you arrange a real “rest awhile” for yourself? Is there a tired parent in your group whom you could help concretely (for example by helping with school pick-ups or bringing a meal)?

lessons.title: Mount Up with Wings Like Eagles
lessons.theme: The God who never grows weary gives strength to weary parents

v: Haven’t you known? Haven’t you heard? The everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint. He isn’t weary. His understanding is unsearchable.
He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might.
Even the youths faint and get weary, and the young men utterly fall;
but those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.

lessons.still: If you are tired right now, admit that you are tired. Let your shoulders drop and your breathing slow. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I am tired. You never faint and you are never weary. Please come and hold me up.”
teach: “Even the youths faint and get weary, and the young men utterly fall.” Isaiah is honest: human strength has limits. A new parent gets up to feed the baby for the third time in a night; two-income parents help with homework after work; parents of a child with special needs never get a vacation all year round. Tiredness is not a sign of weakness but the reality of being human. The Bible does not ask us to pretend we are not tired.

But the prophet turns our eyes from ourselves to God: “The everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint. He isn’t weary.” We run out of battery; he does not. We fall asleep; “he who keeps you will not slumber.” The better news is: “He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might.” God is not only a God who never tires; he is willing to share his strength with the tired.

“But those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength.” Waiting is not passively sitting around. It is like an eagle waiting for a rising current of warm air: it does not flap frantically but spreads its wings and rides the current upward. Parents’ strength is the same: not held up by coffee and willpower, but by turning to God in our weariness and letting his strength carry us. In the busiest season of parenting, waiting on God may be just one deep breath and one short prayer, yet it can renew our strength.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Use your heart and rely on the Holy Spirit; do not use your head and rely on yourself. Parents who use their head and rely on themselves try to prop everything up and control everything, and end up drained. Parents who use their heart and rely on the Holy Spirit admit their limits, hand their burdens to the God who never grows weary, and renew their strength. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on your own strength.
q: Who is God? — God never faints and is never weary, and he gives power to the weary. What does this God mean to you right now?
Who am I? — Where is my greatest weariness at present: body, emotions or spirit? What do I usually rely on to keep going?
How should I respond? — At what moment today can I stop and wait on God for one minute?
lessons.jesus: Jesus knows what weariness is like. He was “tired from his journey” and “sat down by the well”; in the stern of the boat during the storm, he slept on a cushion. The Son of God took a human body and accepted human limits. So he fully understands tired parents: he will not scold you for being tired, he will only invite you to come near.
lessons.pray: Everlasting God, you never faint and are never weary, but I am often so tired that I cannot speak. I admit that I often prop up this family with my own strength until I have no patience and no joy. Today I come to wait on you. Give power to me in my weariness, increase strength in me in my weakness, so that I mount up with wings like eagles, run and not be weary, walk and not faint. Amen.
acts: At your most tired moment today, stop and take three deep breaths. Each time, say, “Lord, I wait for you.”
Copy Isaiah 40:31 onto a card and put it by your bed or your baby’s crib.
Tonight go to bed thirty minutes earlier than usual, and treat sleep as part of receiving God’s grace.
lessons.noon: “but those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength.” — Lord, I am tired, and right now I wait for you.

fam.key: When I am tired, God gives me strength.

lamb.do: Hold your child and spread your arms wide, swaying slowly from side to side like an eagle spreading its wings to fly in the sky.
lamb.say: God gives us strength, and we fly up high like eagles!

sprout.story: A little eagle was learning to fly. It flapped its wings as hard as it could until it was so, so tired, but still could not fly high. Mother Eagle said, “Child, spread your wings and wait a moment. The wind will lift you up.” The little eagle spread its wings, and when a wind came, it floated easily up into the sky! The Bible says that people who wait for God will get new strength like eagles too.
sprout.ask: When you are tired, how can you ask God for strength?
sprout.do: Play “Eagles Fly” as a family. Everyone spreads their arms, and when Mom or Dad says, “The wind is coming!”, everyone slowly “flies” around the living room, saying, “Wait for God, and get strength!”

soldier.story: The book of Isaiah says that even the youths faint and get weary, and the young men utterly fall, but those who wait for the LORD will mount up with wings like eagles. Eagles are clever birds. They find rising currents of warm air, and just by spreading their wings they can be carried very high, without having to flap hard all the time. We often get very tired too, with exams, matches, music practice and arguments with friends. If we only struggle on our own, we soon run out of strength. But if we learn to stop when we are tired, pray to God and trust him, God will give us new strength.
ask: When were you last very tired? Was it your body that was tired, or your heart?
What do you think “waiting on God” could look like in your life?
soldier.do: Make an “eagle card”: write Isaiah 40:31 on it and keep it in your schoolbag or pencil case. This week, whenever you feel tired, take it out, read it once and pray to God.

youth.talk: We want to be frank about something: lately we have been really tired, with work, housework and caring for the older generation, sometimes so tired that we speak to you with no patience. This is not your fault. It is that we have not looked after ourselves well and have not leaned on God well. This week we read in Isaiah that even the youths faint and get weary. We guess you are tired too, just in different places.
ask: What has tired you most lately: schoolwork, friendships, or something else?
When you are very tired, how do you wish your family would treat you?
youth.do: Parent and child each name “the thing that tires me most,” then think together of a concrete way to lighten the other’s load a little, and do it this week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you never get tired. When we are tired, please give us strength, so we can fly high like eagles. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Elijah Under the Juniper Tree
lessons.theme: What kind of parent am I: when I am drained, God lets me eat and sleep first

v: But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree. Then he requested for himself that he might die, and said, “It is enough. Now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.”
He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!”
He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again.
The LORD’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.”
He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, God’s Mountain.
