lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to gently show you: are you standing on the mountaintop right now, or sitting under the juniper tree? You need not pretend to be strong. Tell him how you really are at this moment. He will not scold you.
teach: Elijah had just seen God send down fire in a great victory on Mount Carmel, yet the next moment, because of Jezebel’s threat, he fled all the way into the wilderness, sat under a juniper tree and said, “It is enough. Now, O LORD, take away my life.” This was the moment a great man of God ran dry. A great low after a great high, a collapse under long-term pressure: many parents know it. The first months after a baby is born, the year a child was diagnosed, the season of moving house or changing jobs, when it seems that everything is finished.

The most moving part is God’s response. He did not preach first, nor scold Elijah for lack of faith. He let him sleep, then sent an angel to touch him and say, “Arise and eat!” After he had eaten, God let him sleep again. The second time the angel said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” God took care of Elijah’s body first, and then dealt with his spirit. God “knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.” Sometimes the most spiritual thing is to have a good meal and a good sleep.

Today let the Holy Spirit shine his light on us: what kind of parent am I? One who keeps propping everything up and never admits to being tired, or one who is already sitting under the juniper tree feeling that all is lost? Both need God’s care. If you have long-term insomnia, a low mood that will not lift, or, like Elijah, thoughts of not wanting to live, please tell someone you trust and your pastor at once, and seek professional help. This is not weak faith; it is one of the ways God cares for you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled parents think they must be able to do everything, and dare not even admit tiredness, which is really trying to take God’s place. Let people be people and let God be God: to admit you are limited, that you need to eat, to sleep and to be helped, is to return humbly to the human place. God cared for Elijah, and he cares for you.
q: Who is God? — At Elijah’s lowest moment, God first gave him bread and water and let him sleep. What kind of God does this show you?
Who am I? — What kind of parent am I: the one who never admits tiredness and keeps pushing on, or the one already drained and feeling it is all over?
How should I respond? — What are the “bread and water” God needs to prepare for me first today? Whose help am I willing to accept?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane Jesus said, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death.” He did not pretend to be strong. He told his disciples and the Father honestly of his pain, and afterward “an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.” Jesus has been through the deepest valley a human can know, so he can sit beside you under your juniper tree.
lessons.pray: Lord, you see me sitting under the juniper tree. I admit that I am already very tired, and sometimes even feel it is all over. Thank you for not scolding me but preparing bread and water for me. Please care for my body and heal my heart, so that I am willing to admit my needs and accept help. The journey is too great for me; please add to my strength yourself. Amen.
acts: Have a proper meal today: sit down and eat slowly, not standing up and not while scrolling on your phone.
Find someone you trust (your spouse, a friend or your group leader), tell them how tired you really are, and ask them to pray for you.
If your tiredness has lasted a long time and is affecting your sleep and emotions, arrange today to talk with your pastor or a professional.
lessons.noon: “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” — Lord, thank you for caring for me when I am at my most tired.

fam.key: God takes care of my body and my heart.

lamb.do: When your child is tired and wants to sleep, don’t hurry to put him down. Hold him and rock him gently, hum a slow song, and let him fall asleep peacefully in your arms.
lamb.say: If you’re tired, sleep. God will take care of you, and Mommy is right here.

sprout.story: Elijah was God’s prophet. One day he walked a very, very long way, and was so tired that he sat down under a tree and said he did not want to walk any more. He lay down and fell asleep. After a little while an angel touched him gently and said, “Get up and eat!” Elijah looked, and beside him were a warm cake and a jar of water. He ate until he was full, and slept again, and the angel came and gave him food again. Later Elijah had strength, and he stood up and kept on walking. God takes such good care of people!
sprout.ask: When you are tired, how do you want Mom and Dad to take care of you?
sprout.do: Play “Angel Delivery.” Take turns being the angel, gently pat a family member who is lying down and say, “Get up and eat!” and then bring a cookie and a cup of water.

soldier.story: Elijah had just been through a great victory: he had prayed on Mount Carmel, and God sent fire down from heaven. But Jezebel, the wicked wife of King Ahab, threatened to kill him. Elijah was so frightened that he ran into the wilderness, sat under a juniper tree and said to God, “It is enough. Now, O LORD, take away my life.” He was tired and sad, and did not want to do anything. God did not scold him. He let him sleep, then sent an angel with bread and water, saying, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” God knows that people get tired and sad. He cares for our bodies and for our hearts too.
ask: Why do you think Elijah felt so low after the big victory?
When you are very tired or sad, whom can you talk to?
soldier.do: This week, each night at bedtime, tell Mom and Dad, “Today my feeling is …” and describe it with the weather (sunny, cloudy or rainy). Then pray together.

youth.talk: Elijah was a mighty prophet in the Bible, yet there were times when he was so tired that he said, “It is enough.” We want you to know that being tired, sad, or even feeling you cannot go on, does not mean your faith is poor. The way God cared for Elijah was very practical: he let him sleep, let him eat, and walked with him. If one day you feel this way too, we hope you will tell us. We will stay beside you, and we will find help together.
ask: Is there a friend around you who seems very tired or low? How could you walk with him?
How well do you think our family does at “admitting we’re tired”? Does everyone dare to say it?
youth.do: Agree on a “code word” as a family: whenever anyone feels they cannot go on, they just say the code word, and everyone else stops what they are doing to be with them and listen. If your child or you ever have thoughts of hurting yourself, please seek help from your pastor and professionals immediately.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for caring for us when we are tired, giving us food and letting us sleep. Help us to be willing to say so when we are tired, and to look after one another. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: My Grace Is Sufficient for You
lessons.theme: I believe: my weakness is the doorway for God’s power

v: He has said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.
Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.

lessons.still: Think of the weakness you least want others to see: perhaps your temper, your impatience, or your sense of powerlessness. Do not rush to hide it. Place it gently in the Lord’s hands, and hear him say, “My grace is sufficient for you.”
teach: Paul had a thorn in his flesh. He begged the Lord three times to take it away, but the Lord answered, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” God did not remove the thorn, but he gave Paul a new way of seeing: weakness was no longer only a flaw to be hidden but became a doorway for the power of Christ.

Parents are most afraid of admitting weakness. We want always to have the answers in front of our children, always to have strength, always to be steady in our emotions. But the reality is that we get tired, we get things wrong, we fall apart. Xiaowen, a single mother, once thought she had to be both father and mother alone, and must never let her child see her cry. Then one day she wept while praying in front of her daughter, and her ten-year-old hugged her and said, “Mom, God will help us.” That day she found that weakness can be the place where children come to know God.

Paul says, “For when I am weak, then am I strong.” This is not a slogan; it is the logic of the cross: on the weakest of crosses, Jesus accomplished the greatest salvation. Today we move from knowing to conviction: I believe God’s grace is sufficient for me; I believe my weakness will not destroy this family but will let my children see God’s power.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your viewpoint. From the human viewpoint, weakness is failure; from God’s viewpoint, weakness is a doorway for grace. From the temporary viewpoint, a tiring season seems as if it will never pass; from the eternal viewpoint, God is shaping you in this season. The focus is not on your own strength but on the power of Christ.
q: Who is God? — God says, “My grace is sufficient for you.” What does that mean to you at this moment?
Who am I? — What weakness do I least want my children to see? Why am I so afraid?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe God’s grace …; I believe my weakness …
lessons.jesus: Jesus hung on the cross, the weakest and most failed moment in human eyes: mocked, abandoned, unable to save himself. Yet it was there that God’s great power accomplished salvation. Jesus’ cross tells us that God’s greatest power is often displayed in what looks like the weakest place.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for saying, “My grace is sufficient for you.” I admit that I often fear showing weakness in front of my children, and push on until I am exhausted. Today I declare: I believe your grace is sufficient for me, and I believe your power is made perfect in my weakness. Let the power of Christ rest on me, and let my children see your strength through my weakness. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations: I believe God’s grace …; I believe my weakness …; I believe that in this tiring season …
Today, say honestly to your children once, “Mom/Dad is very tired today. Let’s ask God to help us together.”
List one thing you have been pushing through that you actually need help with, and ask a family member or friend to help today.
lessons.noon: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” — Lord, in my weakness, show your power.

fam.key: I am weak, but God is strong.

lamb.do: When your child falls while learning to walk, help him up first, then take his hand and walk a few more steps with him.
lamb.say: It’s all right to fall. God will lift you up, and I’ll hold your hand.

sprout.story: Xiaokai was learning to ride a bike and kept falling off. He cried, “I can’t do it, I’m so silly!” Grandpa came over, held the back of the seat and said, “It’s all right if you can’t do it yet. Grandpa is behind you, holding you.” Xiaokai tried again, and this time he rode so far! It turned out Grandpa had been holding him from behind all the time. The Bible says that when we feel we are not good enough, God is behind us, holding us.
sprout.ask: When do you feel “I can’t”? Whom do you want to ask for help then?
sprout.do: Play “Hold Me Up.” One person walks with eyes closed while another holds them gently by the side, from the living room to the bedroom. Then swap.

soldier.story: Paul was a great apostle, but he had a “thorn,” perhaps an illness or another trouble, that made life hard for him. He begged God three times to take it away. But God said to him, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Paul understood that he did not need to pretend to be great, because it was precisely when he could not do something that God’s power showed best. It is like an empty cup, which is the only kind that can be filled with water. When we admit we are not enough, God can pour his strength into us.
ask: Is there something you feel you can never do well, however hard you try?
If God’s power is made perfect in your weakness, how can you see your weak points?
soldier.do: Write down one thing you feel weak in, and next to it write “God’s grace is sufficient for me.” Pray about it once a day. This week, ask Mom and Dad to share their weaknesses too.

youth.talk: You may often feel that we ought to be parents who can do everything, and we have thought so ourselves, so we have seldom let you see our weakness. But honestly, there are many things we cannot do: we cannot control our temper, we do not know how to help you, and the pressure of work sometimes takes our breath away. Paul says God’s power is made perfect in weakness. We want to learn to be more real in front of you, and we also want to hear about your weaknesses.
ask: In your circle of friends, is it easy to admit weakness? Why or why not?
Is there something you have been pushing through that you actually wish someone would help you with?
youth.do: Parents first share one weakness they are going through and how they are learning to depend on God, then invite the child to share (without pressure), and then lay hands on one another and pray.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, there are times when we cannot do it. Thank you for saying your grace is sufficient for us. When we are weak, please hold us up with your strength. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Come Away and Rest Awhile
lessons.theme: In the busiest season, learn Jesus’ rhythm of rest

v: The apostles gathered themselves together to Jesus, and they told him all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught.
He said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
They went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.
He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus sitting beside you, looking at your crowded calendar and the pile of housework, and quietly inviting you to come away with him to a quiet place and rest awhile. Do not rush to answer. Let this invitation stay in your heart for a moment.
teach: The apostles came back from their mission and excitedly reported to Jesus. Jesus did not arrange the next round at once, but said, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” Mark adds, “For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.” No time even to eat: it sounds like a description of parents today. Jesus saw it, and he himself invited his disciples to rest.

Isaiah describes God: “He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.” God is especially tender with the ewes who are nursing their young. He does not hurry them but gently leads them. This is God’s promise to parents in the season of raising children: he knows you cannot go fast now, and he is willing to match your pace.

Today’s practice is to deliberately arrange a “rest awhile” for yourself in the busiest season. Husband and wife can take turns, giving each other an hour or two alone each week. You can ask grandparents or brothers and sisters from church to look after the children for half a day. When the children nap, don’t rush to do housework; first lie down and read a psalm. Rest is not laziness but obedience to Jesus’ invitation. A parent who has rested can give the children a home with warmth.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks. Parents often sacrifice themselves to get things done, and sacrifice their relationship with their children as well. Jesus let his disciples rest because he valued people more than work. Use your heart and rely on the Holy Spirit: giving your heart to God in rest bears more fruit than pushing on in weariness.
q: Who is God? — He is the good shepherd who gently leads those who have their young. How does he see the pace you are going at now?
Who am I? — Do I often feel that resting is a waste of time? Where does that thinking come from?
How should I respond? — How will I concretely arrange a “rest awhile” this week? Whose help do I need?
lessons.jesus: Jesus himself had a rhythm of rest: he slept in the boat, ate at friends’ homes, and often withdrew to the mountain or the wilderness. He was not a machine that could not stop, but a Son of Man who walked with the Father and knew when to work and when to rest. He invited his disciples to rest, and he invites you today, when you are tired.
lessons.pray: Good shepherd Jesus, thank you for seeing my busyness, when I have no time even to eat, and thank you for gently leading me without hurrying me. I admit that I often treat rest as a luxury, and so bring weariness and anger to my family. Today I respond to your invitation. I am willing to set aside time to rest awhile for myself, and to ask others for help. Renew me in the quiet. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse (or a trusted family member or friend) and arrange one to two hours of time alone for yourself this week.
Today when your child naps or after he goes to sleep at night, rest for fifteen minutes first, and then do the housework.
Practice “ten quiet minutes” as a family: turn off the TV and phones, lie down, listen to one worship song, and do nothing else.
lessons.noon: “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” — Lord, I respond to your invitation and rest awhile in you.

fam.key: Jesus asks us to rest awhile.

lamb.do: Before your child’s nap, lie down with him, rest your hand lightly on his tummy, and rise and fall with his breathing.
lamb.say: We’re resting together, and Jesus is here too.

sprout.story: The shepherd had many sheep, and one of them was a mother sheep who had just had a lamb. She walked very, very slowly. The other sheep had run ahead, and the mother sheep was worried. The shepherd came back, picked up the lamb, and said to the mother sheep, “Don’t hurry. We’ll go slowly.” The Bible says God is like this good shepherd, who carries the lambs in his arms and gently leads the mother sheep.
sprout.ask: How do you think God would hold you?
sprout.do: Play “Shepherd and Lamb” as a family. One person is the shepherd and carries or leads a family member who is the lamb, slowly to the “green pasture” (a floor mat) at the other side of the living room, and everyone lies down to rest for one minute.

soldier.story: The disciples went out to tell the good news and heal the sick, and when they came back they were both excited and tired. But so many people were looking for Jesus that they had no time even to eat. So Jesus said, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” And they went by boat to a quiet place. Jesus knew that even the most capable people need rest. If a phone has all its apps running at once, it slows down, gets hot, and finally crashes. People are the same: if we keep busy and never rest, our tempers get worse and our hearts grow tired.
ask: When do you think you most need to “rest awhile”?
For you, what is real rest? Is it playing on your phone, or something else?
soldier.do: This week choose one evening for a “screen-free rest night”: turn off all screens, and play board games, go for a walk or chat together, and finish with a prayer.

youth.talk: Jesus once said to his disciples, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile,” because they had no leisure even to eat. This sounds very much like our family: everyone is busy, and even eating a meal together is hard. We would like to ask you how you feel about the pace of life now. Is there something we could cut down together? We also want to learn to truly rest, and not just scroll on our phones.
ask: Do you think scrolling on your phone counts as rest? What kind of rest really restores your strength?
What kind of “rest awhile” time would you like our family to have each week?
youth.do: Parent and child plan a “rest awhile” slot for this week (such as two hours on Sunday afternoon). The child decides how to spend it, and the parents take part throughout, with nothing else scheduled.

fam.pray: Good shepherd Jesus, thank you for inviting us to rest. Help us not to be too busy, to rest awhile with you often, and to look after one another. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: New Every Morning
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: a fresh start in God’s loving kindness

v: It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
“The LORD is my portion,” says my soul. “Therefore I will hope in him.”

lessons.still: Think back over this week’s weariness and grace. At what moment were you so tired you wanted to give up? At what moment did you feel God holding you up? However this week has gone, remember: tomorrow morning his loving kindness will be new again.
teach: Lamentations is one of the saddest books in the Bible. The writer weeps amid the ruins, feeling forgotten by God. But in the middle of chapter 3 he suddenly says, “It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” In the most exhausted and desperate time, he took hold of one truth: God’s loving kindness comes again each morning.

This week we learned that the God who never grows weary gives strength to the weary; that under the juniper tree God first let Elijah eat and sleep; that God’s grace is made perfect in our weakness; and that Jesus invites us to come away and rest awhile. Today review honestly: did I admit my tiredness this week? Did I accept help? Did I wait on God in the gaps of busyness? Or did I walk the old road of propping everything up by myself?

Zhiwei and Meiling, a two-income couple in Kuala Lumpur, took turns this week for the first time to give each other two hours of “time off.” Meiling said that she read psalms for half an hour in a café, and when she got home even her tone of voice with the children was different. An adjustment need not be big; it only needs to be concrete. A tiring season does not pass overnight, but God’s loving kindness is new every morning, and we can make a fresh start in him every day.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjust and repeat. What tired parents need most is not more self-blame but a fresh start in God’s loving kindness. Proud parents will not admit they are tired; humble parents dare to say, “I need help.” Humility draws out humility: when parents learn to rest, children also learn to look after their own hearts.
q: Who is God? — God’s loving kindness is new every morning, and great is his faithfulness. Where did you experience his faithfulness this week?
Who am I? — This week did I admit my weariness, accept help and wait on God? Or did I go back to propping everything up by myself?
How should I respond? — What one thing will I adjust next week? For example a fixed time to rest, going to bed earlier, or asking for help.
lessons.jesus: On the morning of Jesus’ resurrection, the women came to the tomb with sorrow and weariness, and found the stone already rolled away. That was the newest morning in human history. Because of Jesus, every morning can be a fresh beginning; yesterday’s tiredness and failure are not today’s final word.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that your loving kindness is new every morning. This week I had weakness and weariness, and also some moments of renewed strength, and all of them were your grace. I admit that I often still prop everything up by myself. Please forgive me, and help me next week to be more willing to wait on you, more willing to rest, and more willing to accept help. The LORD is my portion, so I will hope in him. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: when were we each most tired this week? How can we share the load? (Single parents can talk with a spiritual companion or family member.)
Ask your child, “This week, when Mom/Dad was tired, were they harsher with you? Have I been more like Jesus?” Just listen; do not defend yourself.
Write down next week’s adjustment, for example: a two-hour rest slot once a week, or in bed by eleven every night.
lessons.noon: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” — Lord, thank you that your loving kindness is new again today.

fam.key: Every morning, God’s love is new.

lamb.do: When your child wakes up in the morning, open the curtains to let the sunshine in, and hold him as you look at the sky outside together.
lamb.say: Good morning! God’s love is new again today.

sprout.story: Xiaoqi quarreled with her brother yesterday and even tore his drawing, and she felt so sad at bedtime. In the morning the sunshine came into the room, and Mommy said, “Good morning! We told God sorry for yesterday already, and today is a new day!” Xiaoqi ran to her brother and said, “Brother, shall we draw a new picture together today?” Her brother smiled and nodded.
sprout.ask: If today is a new day, what good thing do you want to do?
sprout.do: Make a “New Morning” card. Each person draws a sun and writes “Today is a new day,” sticks it by the front door, and touches it each time they go out.

soldier.story: The writer of Lamentations saw his city destroyed and was heartbroken, feeling as if there was no hope left at all. But he remembered one thing: God’s loving kindness and mercies never end, and they are new every morning. Just as the sun rises every day, whatever happened yesterday, God’s love comes again today. This week we learned that when we are tired we can ask God for strength, we can rest, and we can ask for help. Now let’s check: this week when you were tired, did you remember God? Did you rest well?
ask: Which day this week was the most tiring for you? How did you get through it?
Next week, how would you like to look after your body and your heart?
soldier.do: Hold a family meeting. Each person shares one “renewed strength” experience from this week and one thing to improve next week (such as going to bed earlier), writes them on a paper and sticks them up. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we tried to learn to rest, admit we are tired, and ask for help. A few times we managed it, and a few times we went back to our old ways and were so busy that we lost our temper with you. Lamentations says God’s loving kindness is new every morning, which comforts us greatly: we do not have to give up because we did not do well, but can start again every day. We would also like to hear how your week has been.
ask: This week, do you think the pace of our family has been a little better? Where is it still too rushed?
Did you get good rest this week yourself? What do you need us to cut back on for you?
youth.do: Parents and child together decide on one “whole family rest” adjustment for next week, such as no talk about homework after ten at night, or no alarm on Saturday morning. Write it down and stick it on the fridge.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that your love is new every morning. Help us to start again each day, to lean on you when we are tired, and to look after one another. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

10.memT: but those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.

mem.t: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.

sat.t: Family Day: The Imperfect Food Party
sat.d: Cook one “imperfect dish” together as a family. Let the children lead: pancakes, fried eggs or wrapping dumplings. Crooked shapes and burned edges are all fine; the point is to make it together and laugh together. As you eat, each person shares one thing: “This week I wasn't perfect, but God still loves me.” Mom and Dad go first. After the meal, lie down on the floor together, close your eyes and listen to a quiet hymn. Finally, Dad or Mom reads Matthew 11:28 and blesses each person: may you come to Jesus and find rest.

sun: What does the “perfect parent” look like in your mind? Where did that standard come from? What burden has it put on you?
Jesus says his yoke is easy and his burden is light. In what recent situation have you experienced the lightness that comes from living from the heart by the Spirit?
Which burden that does not belong to you do you want to lay down this coming week? How can you help another parent in your group be set free from the pressure to be a “perfect parent” too?

lessons.title: Come to Me
lessons.theme: Jesus invites weary, burdened parents to find rest

v: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

lessons.still: Count the burdens you are carrying right now, one by one: the children's homework, the family finances, your marriage, the expectations you place on yourself... Then imagine Jesus stretching out his hand and saying to you, “Come to me.” Gently set them all down.
teach: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.” These words are printed on countless cards and hung on countless walls, yet we often read them too fast. Jesus is not inviting people who have everything under control. He is inviting the weary and burdened: the mother who works all day and worries about her children, the father still doing the accounts late at night, the grandparents helping to raise their grandchildren. He says, “Come to me.”

A parent's burdens come in two kinds. Some God has truly entrusted to us: loving our children, raising them, teaching them to know God. Others we, or our culture, have added: that our children must win from the starting line, that good parents never lose their temper, that everything about our children is our responsibility. The second kind is often the heaviest, because it has no end. These are exactly the loads Jesus wants to lift from us.

Then Jesus says, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me.” A yoke is the wooden frame that lets two oxen pull the plow together. Jesus does not say you will never carry anything again. He says: share the yoke with me. He takes the heavy side and sets the direction. “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” Rest is not running away from responsibility; it is carrying it in a different way, walking side by side with Jesus.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Laying down the burden of being a “perfect parent” is laying down the self-ruled life that tries to take God's place. Parents are not their children's savior; Jesus is. Let people be people and let God be God. We do our part in the family and leave the results to God, and our hearts will find rest.
q: Who is God? — Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him. How does he see the burden you carry right now?
Who am I? — Of the burdens I am carrying, which has God entrusted to me? Which have I, or others, added?
How should I respond? — Which burden that doesn't belong to me will I give to Jesus today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus says, “I am gentle and humble in heart.” He is not a harsh taskmaster telling us to try harder. He is a gentle companion who is willing to share the yoke with us. On the cross he took up the heaviest burden in the world, our sin, so that in him we could find true rest.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I am the one who is weary and burdened. I carry my children's future, my family's needs, and many expectations I have added myself, and I am so tired. Today I accept your invitation and come to you. Please lift off the loads that are not mine. Teach me to take your yoke and learn from you, and let me find rest in you. Amen.
acts: Draw two columns on a sheet of paper: “What God has entrusted to me” and “What I have added myself.” Write each of your burdens in the right column.
Pray over each item in the “added myself” column: “Lord, I give this to you.”
Say one sentence to your spouse or child today: “I don't have to be a perfect parent. Jesus will help us.”
lessons.noon: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.” — Lord Jesus, I have come. Please give me rest.

fam.key: Come to Jesus and you will find rest.

lamb.do: Lie down on the sofa or bed with your child resting on your chest, listening to your heartbeat. Rest together quietly.
lamb.say: It's so cozy in Mommy's arms, and so cozy in Jesus' arms too.

sprout.story: Little Bear went to school carrying a great big heavy backpack. It was packed with books, toys, stones and lots and lots of other things. Walking along, Little Bear got so tired that he could not take another step. Papa Bear came over and said, “Come, let's take out what you don't need, and Papa will carry the heavy things.” Little Bear's backpack was suddenly light! Jesus says the same: if you are tired, you can come to him, and he will help us.
sprout.ask: Is there something heavy in your heart that you would like Jesus to carry for you?
sprout.do: Play “Unpack the Backpack”: let your child walk once around the room with a backpack holding a few books, then take the books out one at a time. With each book, say, “Jesus, this one is for you!” Feel how the backpack gets lighter.

soldier.story: Long ago, farmers plowed their fields with oxen. They put a wooden frame called a yoke on the necks of two oxen so they could pull together. Usually an experienced old ox was paired with a young one. The old ox pulled harder and led the way, and the young ox learned how to walk. Jesus says, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me.” He is willing to pull with us and take the heavy side. That is why he says his yoke is easy and his burden is light.
ask: What is the heaviest “burden” you feel right now?
If Jesus carried it with you, what do you think would be different?
soldier.do: Every evening this week, write one thing that feels heavy on a little slip of paper and put it into a “trust box.” Then pray together: “Jesus, we'll carry this one together.”

youth.talk: We want to share something we have discovered. We always thought good parents had to be responsible for everything about you: your grades, your future, your faith, even your moods. That burden has made us tired, and it has made us manage you too much. This week we read that Jesus says all who are weary and burdened can come to him. We are learning that some burdens aren't ours to carry; they are meant to be given to God.
ask: What burdens do you feel you are carrying that aren't yours to carry?
Which of our expectations of you feels the heaviest?
youth.do: Each of you writes down one burden you want to give to Jesus. Read Matthew 11:28–30 together, pray for each other's burdens, and agree to remind one another this week by asking, “Have you given it to Jesus?”

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that when we are tired we can come to you. We give you our heavy things. Please give our hearts rest. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: The Yoke of the Perfect Parent
lessons.theme: What kind of parent am I? Begun in the Spirit, but trying to finish by myself

v: For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them.
Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on the “good parent checklist” in your heart. How many items are on it? Which one makes you blame yourself most often? Sit quietly and let him lay the whole list open before you.
teach: Jesus rebuked the Pharisees: “They bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them.” Faith had become an endless string of rules. Many parents today carry a bundle of burdens too: perfect family photos on social media, the ten rules of the parenting experts, the expectations of our elders, the model families at church. We tie them up and lay them on our own shoulders, and on our children's.

Paul asked the Galatians, “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” We are saved by grace, yet we often try to become perfect parents by our own effort. Guoqiang, a deacon at a church in Johor Bahru, says that what wears him out most is not raising his children, but needing everyone to see that his children look like a deacon's children. He realized he had been fathering with his head and his willpower, and only rarely from the heart by the Spirit.

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you: what kind of parent am I? Perfectionist parents often share a few marks. When our child makes a mistake, we feel we have failed. We cannot bear a messy home. We are hard on ourselves and on our children. We seldom enjoy the present moment because we are always worrying about the next step. Perfectionism looks very spiritual, but it is really trying to finish in the flesh. Jesus has not called us to be perfect parents. He has called us to be parents held up by grace.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself; the heart brings joy, the head brings worry. Perfectionism is head-and-self living at its extreme: calculating, comparing, controlling, and never enough. Returning to grace means admitting that our family's fruit does not depend on my being perfect, but on the Holy Spirit working in our home.
q: Who is God? — God lets us begin in the Spirit and be completed by the Spirit. What does he really expect of you?
Who am I? — Am I a perfectionist parent? Which item on my “good parent checklist” makes me blame myself most?
How should I respond? — Which demand on that checklist, one that doesn't come from God, will I cross out today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never asks people to become perfect before they come to him. He accepted Peter who stumbled, Thomas who doubted, and the Samaritan woman who came with her past. On the cross he said, “It is finished!” The perfect One has accomplished everything for us, and we no longer need to complete it by ourselves.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, shine your light on me. I admit that I began by grace but I often try to be a perfect parent by my own effort. I have laid many burdens on my own shoulders and on my children's, and our home is full of tension. Forgive me, and bring me back to grace. Help me to live from the heart by you, and no longer from the head by myself. Amen.
acts: Write down the “good parent checklist” in your heart. With a red pen, cross out the items God has not asked of you.
Allow one corner of your home to stay messy today. Don't tidy it, and tell yourself, “This is fine too.”
When your child makes a mistake, first tell yourself, “My child's mistake doesn't mean I have failed.” Then deal with the problem.
lessons.noon: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” — Holy Spirit, today I won't rely on myself. I will rely on you.

fam.key: We aren't perfect, but God loves us.

lamb.do: When your child gets food all over their face and clothes at mealtime, don't rush to wipe it. Smile at them, take a photo, and then gently clean them up.
lamb.say: It's okay to get messy. You're learning, and God loves you.

sprout.story: When Meimei drew, if she made even one small mistake she would crumple up the paper and start again, until at last she cried, “I can't draw anything right!” Grandma took out an old, old picture. It was a wobbly sun that Meimei's mom had drawn as a little girl. Grandma said, “Your mom drew it just like this when she was small. I've kept it all this time because I love it so much.” Meimei smiled through her tears, smoothed out the paper she had just crumpled, and gave it to Grandma.
sprout.ask: When you draw or do something wrong, do you get very cross? How can Mommy and Daddy help you?
sprout.do: Draw “wobbly pictures” as a family: everyone closes their eyes and draws an animal. When you finish, look at them together and laugh, then stick them on the wall with the title “Not perfect but very lovable.”

soldier.story: In Jesus' day the Pharisees made up a great many rules. They even laid down how far you could walk on the Sabbath and exactly how to wash your hands before eating. They tied up a huge pile of burdens and put them on other people's shoulders, but they would not lift a finger to help. Jesus did not like this at all. Paul also reminded the believers in Galatia: you began to trust God by the Spirit, so why are you now trying to become perfect by your own effort? Sometimes we are very hard on ourselves too: I must get a hundred percent, I must never make mistakes, I must make everyone like me. God wants us to work hard, but he doesn't want us tied up by “perfect.”
ask: Is there something you are very hard on yourself about, where you must be perfect?
If you can't be perfect, do you think God will still love you?
soldier.do: This week choose one thing you usually demand perfection from yourself in. Try letting “eighty percent is good enough” be okay, and then tell your family how it felt.

youth.talk: We've realized we may be perfectionists. We want the house to be tidy, we want you to behave well in front of others, and we want to look like a good family at church. This week we read that Jesus rebuked those who laid burdens on other people's shoulders. It stung, because we seem to have put that kind of burden on you. We want to ask: do you ever feel you have to be perfect in this family to be accepted?
ask: Where do you think our family demands perfection the most? How does that make you feel?
Do you tend toward perfectionism yourself? Where is it most obvious?
youth.do: Parents apologize to their child for one “demand for perfection” family rule, and together with your child change or remove one rule that makes it hard to breathe.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us even though we aren't perfect. Please help us not to be too hard on ourselves or on others, and to grow slowly together by the Holy Spirit. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Like a Weaned Child
lessons.theme: I believe: I don't have to be perfect, and I can rest in God's arms

v: LORD, my heart isn’t arrogant, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me.
Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.
Israel, hope in the LORD, from this time forward and forever more.

lessons.still: Picture a child who has been fed and is resting peacefully against his mother, not fussing, not crying, not grabbing. Rest in God's arms in the same way and say to him, “Lord, I want my heart to be calm and quiet.”
teach: David wrote a very short psalm: “LORD, my heart isn't arrogant, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me.” He was a king, yet he admitted that some things are beyond his ability. Perfectionist parents often want to control everything: their children's future, what others think, every variable. David's rest begins with admitting that he is not God.

Then he says, “Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother.” A nursing baby leans on his mother to get something, and may cry and grasp. A weaned child leans on his mother simply because he loves to be there. This is a picture of mature faith: not coming to God for what we can get from him, but simply resting in his presence.

Hebrews says, “There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God.” It also says that whoever enters his rest has “rested from his works.” A parent's rest doesn't come because all the problems at home have been solved. It comes because we have stopped trying to make everything complete by ourselves. Today, write your own declaration: I believe I don't have to be a perfect parent; I believe I can be like a weaned child, resting in God's arms.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on yourself, others or circumstances. The perfectionist's focus is whether I am doing well enough; the focus of rest is what Jesus has already accomplished. Turn from a temporary view to an eternal view: my child's whole life is in God's hands, and I only need to be faithful today.
q: Who is God? — God is like a mother who lets us rest securely in her arms. When did you last rest in God's arms like that?
Who am I? — Do I come close to God mostly to ask for things, or simply because I love being with him?
How should I respond? — Write your own “I believe” declaration: I believe I don't have to...; I believe I can...
lessons.jesus: In the storm the disciples panicked, but Jesus was asleep on a cushion at the back of the boat. His rest was not because the waves were small, but because he trusted the Father completely. He also said to his disciples, “Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you.” Jesus has given his rest to us as well.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, my heart is so often arrogant, wanting to hold on to great matters and things too wonderful for me. Today I declare: I believe I don't have to be a perfect parent; I believe I can rest calm and quiet in your arms like a weaned child. Help me to rest from my own works and enter your rest, and let my children see this peace in me. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations: I believe I don't have to...; I believe I can...; I believe my children are in God's hands...
Take five minutes today to ask for nothing and simply sit quietly before God, enjoying his presence.
List one thing you have been trying to control that is really beyond your ability. Pray Psalm 131:1 over it and give it to God.
lessons.noon: “Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother.” — Lord, today let me rest in your arms.

fam.key: In God's arms I feel safe.

lamb.do: After your child has eaten, let them rest against you. Don't rush to put them down or go and do something else. Gently pat their back and quietly stay with them.
lamb.say: Tummy full, safe in Mommy's arms, and safe in God's arms too.

sprout.story: When a baby is hungry, he cries “waa, waa” for milk. But when the baby grows a little and is full, he lies quietly in his mother's arms, with no fussing at all, just because he loves to be with Mommy. King David said that before God he was like that child, with a heart at peace. We don't always have to ask God for things. We can just lean on him and say, “God, I love being with you.”
sprout.ask: Whose arms do you love to lean on most? Why?
sprout.do: Play “One Quiet Minute” as a family: sit close together, close your eyes and be quiet for one minute, imagining you are resting in God's arms. When it is over, say together, “God, I love being with you!”

soldier.story: David was the king of Israel. He had to run the country, lead armies and deal with many hard things. Yet he wrote a very short psalm that says: my heart is not proud, and I don't force myself to do things that are too big and too hard; my heart is calm and quiet, like a weaned child resting against his mother. Even someone as capable as David found his greatest strength not in his cleverness but in being quiet before God. When we worry about exams, friends or things at home, we can learn from David, give the things that are too big to God, and let our hearts grow quiet.
ask: Have you been worried lately about something “too big and too hard”?
What do you think helps your heart become calm and quiet?
soldier.do: Every night this week before bed, spend one quiet minute without speaking. Tell God about one worry, then say, “God, I give this to you.”

youth.talk: We used to think that being good parents meant planning every step for you: what school, what friends, what path. But Psalm 131 says there are great matters and things too wonderful for us that we are not meant to control. We want to learn to be quiet before God, and we also want to tell you: your future is in God's hands, not entirely in ours. This makes us feel lighter, and we hope it will make you feel lighter too.
ask: Is there anything about your future that worries you? What is it?
When you feel very anxious, what helps you calm down?
youth.do: Each of you writes an “I believe” card. Parents write “I believe your future is in God's hands.” The child writes one thing they want to give to God. Swap cards and pray for each other.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for holding us like a mother. Please keep our hearts at peace, and help us love to rest in your arms. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Not by Might, but by My Spirit
lessons.theme: Living from the heart by the Spirit: in moments of conflict, pause, pray, listen, act

v: Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, “This is the LORD’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says the LORD of Armies.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to remind you of the moment today when conflict is most likely: rushing out the door in the morning, homework in the evening, or dragging feet at bedtime. Before that moment arrives, invite him now: “Holy Spirit, please remind me when the time comes.”
teach: Zerubbabel led the people returning from exile to rebuild the temple. The work was huge and the opposition fierce, and it seemed impossible to finish. Through Zechariah God said to him, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.” Building God's temple is like this, and building a family is like this too. The very things parents most often use to get results are might and power: volume, authority, reasoning, rewards and punishments. They have their uses, but they cannot change a heart.

Paul says, “If we live by the Spirit, let's also walk by the Spirit.” Living from the heart by the Spirit can be very practical at home. When your child talks back, drags their feet or cries, and you feel your anger rising, try four steps. Pause: stop for three seconds and say nothing. Pray: say in your heart, “Holy Spirit, help me.” Listen: notice what the Spirit reminds you of, and listen for the need behind your child's behavior. Act: respond according to that prompting. This is not a technique; it is handing authority back to the Holy Spirit again and again.

Daniel, a father in Singapore, says that the first time he tried pausing for three seconds, his son was slamming the door hard. In those three seconds a thought came to him: he isn't challenging you; he's afraid of tomorrow's exam. Instead of shouting, he knocked on the door and said, “Shall I help you get ready?” Living from the head, we see only behavior. Living from the heart by the Spirit, we see the person. Today, put it into practice once at home.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself. With the head, we want to win, to argue, to fix it right now. With the heart, we first come back to the Holy Spirit and let him lead. One of the three foundations is that the Holy Spirit is my guide. When parents are guided by the Spirit first, the home changes from a tug of war over power into a flow of grace.
q: Who is God? — The Holy Spirit is the God who makes things happen. When have you experienced his guidance?
Who am I? — When conflict happens at home, which “might” and “power” do I rely on most?
How should I respond? — In which moment most likely to cause conflict will I practice “pause, pray, listen, act” today?
lessons.jesus: After Jesus was baptized, the Spirit descended on him like a dove. His whole life was led by the Holy Spirit: he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, and he preached and cast out demons in the Spirit's power. If the Son of God depended on the Spirit, how much more should we, limited parents? Jesus also promised that the Father would give us another Helper to be with us forever.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, I admit that I often rely on might and power to run this home: raising my voice, giving big lectures, controlling my children with rewards and punishments. Today I want to rely on you. In moments of conflict, remind me to pause first, pray to you first, listen for your voice first, and then act as you lead. Since I live by you, I want to walk by you. Amen.
acts: In the moment today when conflict is most likely, practice the four steps “pause, pray, listen, act,” and write down in the evening what happened.
Write “pause, pray, listen, act” on a sticky note and put it on the fridge or your child's bedroom door.
Agree on a family signal (for example, a pause hand sign) that anyone can use when they feel close to anger, so everyone pauses for three seconds.
lessons.noon: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.” — Holy Spirit, today at home I rely on you.

fam.key: When you feel angry, stop and pray first.

lamb.do: When your child cries and fusses, stop first and take three deep breaths. Then pick them up and hum a familiar song in a gentle voice.
lamb.say: Let's stop for a moment. The Holy Spirit will help us.

sprout.story: Xiaoxiang's block tower fell down. He was so angry that he wanted to throw the blocks on the floor. Mommy taught him a bit of magic: “Let's be a traffic light! Red light: stop! Yellow light: tell Jesus, please help me! Green light: think about what to do next.” Xiaoxiang tried it once: red, yellow, green. Then he said, “I'm going to build an even taller one!”
sprout.ask: When you feel cross, how can you be a traffic light?
sprout.do: Make a little “traffic light” card: write “Stop” on red, “Pray” on yellow and “Think, then do” on green. Put it where your child can see it, and practice together as a family.

soldier.story: The Israelites came back from Babylon to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple. But the work was big, enemies kept making trouble, and everyone was discouraged. So God said to Zerubbabel, who led them: not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit. It means the most important strength is not how strong or clever you are, but the help of the Holy Spirit. It's the same at home and at school. When we are angry or arguing, we often want to win by being loud, or by using fists or words. But the Holy Spirit can help us solve problems in another way.
ask: When did you last get angry? How did you try to “win” then?
If next time you stopped and asked the Holy Spirit for help, do you think the result would be different?
soldier.do: This week practice “pause, pray, listen, act”: each time you are about to get angry, stop for three seconds, say a short prayer in your heart, think about the other person's need, and then decide what to do. Each time you manage it, draw a dove on your card.

youth.talk: We want to be honest. When we have conflicts with you, what we often use is “might”: I'm the adult, so what I say goes. Or “power”: a long explanation to try to convince you. As a result you want to talk less and less. This week we read in Zechariah: not by might, nor by power, but by God's Spirit. We want to try something. Next time we have a conflict, we'll stop and pray first, and then talk with you.
ask: When we have a conflict, what makes you most uncomfortable?
What do you think would be different about a parent who relies on the Spirit when we argue?
youth.do: Agree on a “pause rule” together: when either of you feels about to lose control, you can say, “I need ten minutes.” Each of you calms down and prays, then comes back to talk after ten minutes. Try it at least once this week.

fam.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for helping us. When we are angry, please remind us to stop and pray to you first, and then act in love. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Lying Down in Green Pastures
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: Did I enter the Lord's rest this week?

v: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing.
He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.
He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.

lessons.still: Imagine the good shepherd leading you to a green meadow with a quiet stream beside it. He doesn't push you to do anything; he just lets you lie down. In this meadow, slowly look back over the week.
teach: David says, “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.” Notice that the shepherd “makes” the sheep lie down. Sheep lie down only when they are not afraid, not hungry and not fighting. The good shepherd first deals with the sheep's fears and needs, and then they can truly rest. A parent's rest is also given by the Shepherd, not squeezed out by force.

This week we heard Jesus invite the weary and burdened to come to him. We saw the yoke of perfectionism, learned to rest in God's arms like a weaned child, and practiced relying on the Holy Spirit in conflict. This is also the third week of the unit “Parents Abiding in the Lord,” a journey from the vine and the branches, through finding strength in weariness, to today's rest. Please review honestly: this week, did I lay down one burden that is not mine? Was there one conflict where I stopped first and responded by the Spirit?

“He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake.” Adjusting is not about becoming a perfect parent, which is exactly what we set down this week. It is about letting the good shepherd keep guiding us. Xiuqin, a grandmother in Tainan who looks after two grandsons, says her biggest change this week was that she stopped worrying when they didn't finish their meals, and began to enjoy mealtimes with them. Small changes like that are the beginning of rest.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the way every change must travel, but review is not another kind of perfectionism. Review by the Spirit means letting the Spirit point out one or two things and then adjusting with grace. People matter more than tasks: more important than getting everything right is that the people in our home find rest in love.
q: Who is God? — The LORD is my shepherd, and he makes me lie down in green pastures. Where did he give you rest this week?
Who am I? — This week, did I lay down a “perfect parent” burden? Did I respond by the Spirit in a conflict?
How should I respond? — What is the one thing I will adjust next week? How can I bring a little more rest into our home?
lessons.jesus: Jesus says, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” He doesn't only lead us to green pastures; he paid with his own life for us. Because he gave his life, we no longer have to earn acceptance by ourselves, and we can truly lie down in him. He is both the source of our rest and its guarantee.
lessons.pray: Good Shepherd Jesus, thank you for leading me to green pastures this week. I admit I still often carry burdens that are not mine, and still often live from the head by myself. Thank you that at some moments you restored my soul; that was all your grace. Please keep guiding me in the paths of righteousness next week, and make our family a home of rest. Amen.
acts: Talk as a couple for ten minutes: what burden did each of us lay down this week? Which burden do we still need to give to God together? (Single parents can talk with a spiritual companion.)
Ask your child, “This week, did you feel Daddy/Mommy was a bit more relaxed? A bit more like Jesus?” Just listen, and don't defend yourself.
Write down one adjustment for next week, for example: stop for three seconds first in every conflict, or let go of one perfectionist demand each day.
lessons.noon: “He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.” — Good Shepherd, today let me rest in you.

fam.key: Jesus is my good shepherd.

lamb.do: Spread a green blanket or bath towel on the floor as the “green pasture.” Lie down with your child, look at the ceiling, and gently stroke their head.
lamb.say: Jesus is the good shepherd. He lets us have a good rest.

sprout.story: Little Lamb Baa-Baa followed the shepherd all day long and got very, very tired. The shepherd led her to a green meadow with a clear little stream beside it. The shepherd said, “Baa-Baa, when you've eaten your fill, lie down and rest. I'm here to protect you.” Baa-Baa drank the water, ate the grass, lay down comfortably and soon fell fast asleep. Jesus is our good shepherd. He takes care of us and lets us have a good rest.
sprout.ask: When do you feel most comfortable and most safe?
sprout.do: Act out “The Good Shepherd and the Little Lambs” as a family: one person is the shepherd and leads the “lambs” once around the house. At last you come to the “green pasture” (the sofa or a floor mat), everyone lies down, and the shepherd gently prays for each little lamb.

soldier.story: When David was young, he was a shepherd, and he knew that sheep get nervous easily. If there are wild animals nearby, flies buzzing around, or other sheep pushing for the grass, the sheep dare not lie down. The good shepherd has to deal with these problems first, and then the sheep can lie down in peace in the green pasture. That's why David said, the LORD is my shepherd, and he makes me lie down in green pastures. This week we learned that Jesus invites the tired to come to him, and he helps us carry our burdens. We don't have to be perfect, and we can rely on the Holy Spirit. Now let's check: this week, did you let Jesus be your good shepherd?
ask: Was there something this week that made you very nervous, and that you later gave to Jesus?
Which worry will you give to the good shepherd next week?
soldier.do: Hold a family meeting. Each person shares one “burden I put down this week” and one “thing I want to give to Jesus next week.” At the end, say Psalm 23:1–3 together from memory. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: All this week we've been learning one thing: we don't have to be perfect parents, and we can give our burdens to Jesus. To be honest, it's harder than we thought, because we're used to controlling everything. A few times we managed to stop first, and a few times we went back to our old ways. We'd like to hear what you noticed: has our home been a bit more relaxed this week? Or do you feel there was no difference?
ask: This week, did you feel we asked less of you to be “perfect”?
What do you think our family needs to do to be more like “still waters”?
youth.do: Parents apologize to their child for a moment when they fell back into perfectionism or control. Then together choose a “rest action” for the whole family next week, for example a walk together on Sunday evening without talking about homework.

fam.pray: Good Shepherd Jesus, thank you for taking care of us and leading us to green pastures to rest. Please keep leading us, and fill our home with peace. In Jesus' name, amen.

11.memT: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.

mem.t: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

sat.t: Family Day: Our Family's New Tradition
sat.d: Sit down together as a family. Parents begin by sharing one thing: “Something beautiful from my childhood home that I want to pass on,” such as Grandma's soup or Dad's goodnight stories. Then share one more: “Something I want to stop with my generation,” told in a way the children can understand. Then invent together a “new tradition” that belongs to your family: a pancake breakfast once a month, a blessing at bedtime, or a weekend prayer walk will all do. Write it on a card, give it a name, and try it for the first time today.

sun: Think back to the family you grew up in. Which pattern (a way of speaking, handling conflict or showing love) have you unknowingly brought into your present family?
In what moment this week did “in Christ, a new creation” become real to you? Where does it still feel hard?
How will you walk alongside a parent in your group who is facing pain from their family of origin? What first step will you take next week for a new tradition?

lessons.title: In Christ, a New Creation
lessons.theme: My past has shaped me, but it does not define me

v: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.
But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation;

lessons.still: Be still and remember the home you grew up in: the dining table, the living room, a particular voice. Don't judge anything; just say to the Lord, “Lord, you know my past, and you live in my present.” Let those words slowly settle your heart.
teach: Every parent walks into marriage and parenting carrying an “invisible suitcase.” In it are the things our family of origin gave us. Some are treasures: the taste of a bowl of soup, a blessing at bedtime. Some are burdens: the sound of shouting, the silence of the cold war, the threat “If you fail, don't come home.” Often we don't mean to, yet on some tired evening we hear our parents' tone of voice come out of our own mouths.

Paul says, “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” This doesn't mean the past never happened, or that we should pretend we were never hurt. It declares a new identity: I am no longer only the child of such-and-such a family; in Christ I have a new source. It is like a transplanted tree whose roots are set in new soil, so that from now on it draws new nourishment.

Paul goes on: “All things are of God.” New life doesn't come from gritting our teeth and vowing, “I will never be like my parents.” Many people make that vow and end up living as the very person they didn't want to become. The power to change comes from God, who has reconciled us to himself through Christ and who, bit by bit, renews the reactions deep inside us. Our part is to open the suitcase and lay it before him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your concepts and you change your life. Our family of origin gave us our first set of ideas about what a family is, but it is not the final standard; Scripture is. Moving from “this is how I was raised” to “in Christ I am a new creation” is turning from the human viewpoint to God's viewpoint, and it is where change begins.
q: Who is God? — God makes all things new, and through Christ he has reconciled us to himself.
Who am I? — In my suitcase, which treasure do I want to pass on? Which burden do I want to set down?
How should I respond? — Which reaction that I brought from my family of origin am I willing to bring before God today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus' family tree includes Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Uriah, full of imperfect stories. The Son of God did not choose a “clean” family. He entered a broken family line himself and opened a new way from within it. He is not ashamed of our past; he works in the middle of it.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you know my past and are not ashamed of my family. I lay before you both the treasures and the burdens I brought from my family of origin. Thank you that in you I am a new creation. Please keep what is beautiful, heal what is wounded, and renew the way I speak and react to my children. Amen.
acts: Draw two columns on a sheet of paper: “What I want to pass on” and “What I want to set down.” Write one or two things in each.
Copy 2 Corinthians 5:17 onto your phone wallpaper or a sticky note.
Say to your child today one sentence you longed to hear as a child but never did.
lessons.noon: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” — Lord, right now I don't live by my past; I live by you.

fam.key: In Jesus, we are all new.

lamb.do: Dress your child in a clean new outfit, then lift them up and twirl them around.
lamb.say: New clothes! Jesus makes us new too.

sprout.story: A little caterpillar crawled slowly every day and thought he was very ugly. One day he wrapped himself in a little house and slept quietly. Many days passed, and the little house opened, and out flew a beautiful butterfly! He was still the same little creature, but he had become new. The Bible says Jesus makes our hearts new too.
sprout.ask: What do you think Jesus will make new in us?
sprout.do: Crawl along the floor like caterpillars as a family, count “One, two, three,” then open your arms like butterfly wings and fly once around the room.

soldier.story: Paul used to be called Saul. He was fierce and went everywhere arresting Christians. Then Jesus met him on the road to Damascus, and his life changed completely. The man who arrested Christians became the boldest preacher of Jesus. Later he wrote, “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” He didn't pretend the past hadn't happened, but he knew Jesus had given him a brand-new beginning.
ask: What do you think is the difference between a “new creation” and “just behaving a bit better”?
Is there something you would really like to start over?
soldier.do: Write on a piece of paper one thing you'd like to “start over,” fold it and give it to Dad or Mom, and ask them to pray for you this week.

youth.talk: You may have noticed that when Dad or Mom gets angry, some of the words sound just like what Grandpa and Grandma used to say. To be honest, we've noticed it too. We each brought good things from our own homes, and some bad habits as well. The Bible says that in Christ we can be new creations. We are learning how not to pass the bad parts on to you.
ask: What do you think is the best thing our family has received from the generation before?
Is there a way of speaking that you wish would stop in our family?
youth.do: Parents begin by sharing a story from their own family of origin, then ask your child which family tradition they most want to keep.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for making us new in you. Please help us keep what is good and give you what is not. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Whose Shadow Do I Carry?
lessons.theme: Seeing the patterns passed down from the previous generation

v: Isaac lived in Gerar.

The men of the place asked him about his wife. He said, “She is my sister,” for he was afraid to say, “My wife”, lest, he thought, “the men of the place might kill me for Rebekah, because she is beautiful to look at.”
Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age, and he made him a tunic of many colors.
His brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, and they hated him, and couldn’t speak peaceably to him.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to open an old photo album for you and show you yourself. Ask him, “Lord, which of the ways I am in front of my children did I actually learn from the generation before?” Don't hurry to defend yourself; let him point it out gently.
teach: Twice, when in danger, Abraham told people, “She is my sister,” using a lie to protect himself. Years later his son Isaac came to Gerar, felt the same fear, and said exactly the same thing: “She is my sister.” Isaac wasn't there to hear his father lie, yet when the pressure came he automatically took his father's path. Family patterns are often not taught but “caught”, like an accent: we can't hear it in ourselves, but others know at once.

In the next generation it becomes worse. Scripture says, “Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob.” Favouritism took root in this family. When Jacob grew up, he too “loved Joseph more than all his children” and made him a tunic of many colors. As a result, his brothers “hated him, and couldn't speak peaceably to him.” Behind one coat lay three generations of unresolved favouritism. A child who is favored often grows up to become a favoring parent.

We see these patterns not to blame the previous generation. Our parents carried their own wounds too, and did their best with what they had. The purpose of revelation is to let us honestly admit, “This reaction is something I brought.” For example: irritation the moment a child cries, explosion the moment a child talks back, coldness the moment a child fails a test. Stop and ask, whose voice is this? Seeing is the beginning of change; what is not seen will only be replayed.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Deal with the parents' own hearts first, then with the children's behavior. A self-ruled parent sees only the child's problem; a humble parent is willing to admit, “The very thing in my child that drives me up the wall may be the thing in me that hasn't been healed.” Let God be God, and let the Holy Spirit do the work of shining his light.
q: Who is God? — God sees the weakness of three generations and still walks faithfully with this family.
Who am I? — In what situation do I most often say or do the “previous generation's version”?
How should I respond? — Write down one family pattern you want to hand over to God.
lessons.jesus: Jesus' family tree is full of imperfect people, yet he was willing to be born into it. He did not point a finger at this family from outside; he came in himself and brought salvation through this bloodline. He sees everything we have brought from the previous generation, and still says, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.”
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for shining your light on me so gently. I admit that some of my reactions do not come from you, but from old wounds and habits. I don't want to blame anyone; I only want to hand it to you honestly. Please break those unhealthy patterns in my generation, and let my children see what you are like. Amen.
acts: Recall the last time you lost control with your child and write down: “Who does this remind me of? What was I afraid of at that moment?”
Watch today whether you are showing special favor to one child, and give another child some time that is just theirs.
If you carry memories of violence or serious harm from your family of origin, please seek professional counseling and the company of your church pastor.
lessons.noon: “Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob.” — Lord, make my love impartial, like your love.

fam.key: Every one of us is a treasure.

lamb.do: Sing each child's name in turn in the same little song, and give a kiss to whoever's name you've just sung.
lamb.say: You are a treasure, your big brother and sister are treasures too, and everyone is a treasure.

sprout.story: Joseph's father gave him a beautiful coat of many colors, but his brothers didn't get one. The brothers felt so sad that they stopped saying kind words to Joseph. The home began to be unhappy. Mommy said, “In our family everyone is a treasure. Mommy and Daddy love each one of you, and God loves each one of you too.”
sprout.ask: If you were one of Joseph's brothers, how would you feel inside?
sprout.do: Everyone finds a piece of clothing or a scarf to wear as a “coat of many colors.” Take turns walking around once while everyone claps and says, “You are a treasure!”

soldier.story: Joseph's father Jacob loved him dearly and gave him a coat of many colors, but he gave nothing like it to his other sons. The more the brothers saw it, the angrier they got, until they even sold Joseph to Egypt. In fact, Jacob had been the favored child once himself: his father Isaac loved his brother Esau more, while his mother loved Jacob more. Favouritism passed from grandfather to father to the next generation, and filled the brothers with hatred. The habits of a family often pass down from generation to generation.
ask: Do you ever feel someone in our family is favored? You can say so honestly.
What do you think would help favouritism stop in our family?
soldier.do: Write a little card to a brother or sister about one thing you admire in them, and give it to them at dinner.

youth.talk: The Bible has a family like this: the grandfather lied and the father lied the same way; the grandfather played favorites and the father played favorites, until the brothers turned against each other. As we read it, we were startled too, because some habits we don't like in ourselves were passed down to us from the generation before. We want to ask you honestly: have there been times when you felt compared or not favored?
ask: Do you think we've compared you and your brothers and sisters without realizing it?
Is there a sentence you really don't want to hear again?
youth.do: Parents spend ten minutes alone with each child and ask only one question: “Have we ever made you feel compared?” Write down what they say without defending yourself, and find an opportunity to apologize afterward.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving each one of us equally. Please help our family not to compare or play favorites, and to treasure one another. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: It Stops With Me
lessons.theme: I believe: the blood of Christ can break old patterns

v: knowing that you were redeemed, not with corruptible things like silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers,
but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ,
“What do you mean, that you use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge’?
“As I live,” says the Lord GOD, “you shall not use this proverb any more in Israel.

lessons.still: Imagine a long chain stretching from your grandparents and parents all the way to you and your children. Stand in the middle of the chain and say to the Lord, “Lord, please work here.” Be quiet, and wait for his peace.
teach: The Israelites had a proverb: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.” It meant that when one generation does wrong, the next is doomed to suffer and no one can escape. Many Chinese parents carry a similar sense of fate: “People in our family just have bad tempers,” “My mom was like this, and I can't change either.” It is as if life were a track already laid, and we can only drive along the ruts of the generation before, with even our children's future decided. This sounds humble, but it really lets the past sit on the throne.

But God says, “You shall not use this proverb any more in Israel.” God does not deny that family influence is real, but he refuses to let it be the last word. Every person belongs directly to God and can choose again before him. My family of origin influences me, but it does not decide me. Meiling, who grew up in Malaysia, says, “I thought I was destined to be as cold as my mother, until I found that God had never said that about me.”

Peter goes deeper: you were redeemed “from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers”, not with silver or gold, “but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ.” The price has been paid. It is like a train switched onto a different track at a junction: the rails are the same rails, but from then on the direction is different. Conviction is admitting that this chain can be broken in my generation by the blood of Christ. Today, write your own “I believe.”
