lessons.light: 321 Light: A shift of viewpoint, from “fate” to “redemption”, from the human viewpoint to God's viewpoint. The self-ruled parent says, “This is just how I am”; the self-emptied parent says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” This is not denying the past; it is letting Jesus reign over the past.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who, by the blood of Christ, redeems people from the useless way of life handed down from their fathers.
Who am I? — Is there a fatalistic phrase in my heart, “That's just how our family is”?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe this pattern can stop in my generation, because...
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the lamb without blemish or spot. The blood he shed on the cross not only forgives our personal sins, it also redeems us from the useless way of life handed down from our fathers. He carried the burden we couldn't carry, so that our children wouldn't have to carry it either.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for redeeming me with your precious blood from the useless way of life handed down from my fathers. I will no longer say, “That's just how I am.” I believe that in you I can have new reactions; I believe my children don't have to repeat my wounds. Please work in my generation, so that blessing replaces curse, and love replaces fear. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” statements: I believe I am no longer bound by...; I believe my children can...; I believe the blood of Jesus...
Find one fatalistic phrase you often say, and replace it today with a sentence of faith.
Tell your spouse or a spiritual companion the “I believe” you wrote, and ask them to pray for you.
lessons.noon: “…you were redeemed, not with corruptible things like silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers.” — Lord, I believe in your precious blood, which brings a new beginning in my generation.

fam.key: Jesus gives us a new beginning.

lamb.do: Wrap your child in a soft blanket and rock them gently, then open the blanket and say good morning to them with a smile.
lamb.say: A new day has begun, and Jesus is with us.

sprout.story: Xiaoling's picture accidentally got dirty, and she cried so sadly. Grandma brought a fresh white sheet of paper and said, “Shall we draw a new one?” Xiaoling wiped her tears and drew an even prettier picture. Grandma said, “Jesus is like a fresh white sheet of paper he gives us. If we get it wrong, we can start again.”
sprout.ask: What would you like Jesus to help you start over today?
sprout.do: Give your child a fresh sheet of paper and ask them to draw a “new beginning.” When it's done, the whole family prays for them.

soldier.story: Long ago the Israelites had a saying, which meant roughly: if the father eats sour grapes, the son's teeth are set on edge. In other words, when a father does wrong, the son can't escape it either. But God said, stop using this saying! Every person can come directly to God and choose to follow him. It is like a relay race: if the runner before you ran in the wrong direction, the one who takes the baton can turn around and run toward the right finish line. Jesus died for us to give us this kind of new direction.
ask: Do you think a person can change a bad habit that has been passed down in the family? Why?
What good thing do you want to “take the baton” for in our family and pass on?
soldier.do: Play “the baton” as a family: use a pen as the baton, and when you pass it to the next person, say, “I want to pass on ____.”

youth.talk: You may have heard adults say, “People in our family all have bad tempers,” or “It's genetic, you can't change it.” We used to say it too. But the Bible says the blood of Christ redeems us from the useless way of life handed down from our fathers. We want to admit to you that some bad patterns are not yet fully broken in us, but we believe they can stop with this generation.
ask: Have you ever heard the phrase “That's just how our family is”? How did it make you feel?
Do you believe people can really change? Have you seen an example?
youth.do: Parent and child each write one “I believe” declaration, swap and read them, and remind each other this week.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for shedding your blood for us so that we can have a new beginning. Please help us pass on what is good and stop what is bad. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Turning Hurt Into Blessing
lessons.theme: Like Joseph, letting grace flow from the scars

v: Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

lessons.still: Breathe slowly. Remember a family member who once hurt you. You don't have to force yourself to forgive; just say to the Lord, “Lord, this wound is in your hands.” Let the Holy Spirit stay here with you for a moment.
teach: Joseph's family of origin was almost a family tragedy: a father who played favorites, jealous brothers, being sold as a slave, and years of wrongful imprisonment. By any normal reasoning he had every reason to pass the hurt on. But when his brothers knelt before him, he said, “Don't be afraid, for am I in the place of God?” He did not take the judge's seat. He returned to his place as a human being and let God be God. A man with great power chose to lay power down. This is humility.

Joseph went on: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” This is not brushing it aside with “It doesn't matter.” The harm was real. It is that he saw how God can weave other people's evil intent into his plan to save lives. He even named his son Manasseh, saying, “God has made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house.” The “forget” here is not amnesia, but a wound that no longer rules him.

The step of practice is to turn scars into blessing. Joseph “comforted them, and spoke kindly to them,” and promised to provide for their little ones. Today you can choose one small thing too: say to your child a sentence you longed to hear as a child, and replace the shouting of those days with gentleness. Forgiving does not mean pretending nothing happened, nor going back into an unsafe relationship. If the harm was serious and involved violence or abuse, please find professional counseling and a church pastor to walk with you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to your proper place. Joseph had the power to take revenge, yet said, “Am I in the place of God?” People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than being right. Pride stirs up pride, and hurt passes from generation to generation; humility stirs up humility, and blessing can pass from generation to generation too.
q: Who is God? — God can turn people's evil intent into good, and bring about a plan that saves lives.
Who am I? — Am I still holding the right to judge a family member, and refusing to hand it to God?
How should I respond? — What “kind word” will I speak to my child today, giving them a blessing I didn't receive as a child?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was rejected by his own people and betrayed by his disciple, yet on the cross he prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing.” He bore the deepest hurt and poured out the greatest blessing. His scars became the source of our healing.
lessons.pray: Lord, you know the wounds I brought from home, and you see how deep they go. I don't want to pass them on to my children. Give me strength to be like Joseph and not sit in the judge's seat; and heal me, so that I can bless my children with gentle words. Where it is needed, please prepare people I can trust to walk with me. Amen.
acts: Say to each child today a blessing you longed to hear as a child, for example, “I'm proud of you.”
Write a letter you won't send to a family member who hurt you, and when you've written it, entrust it to God.
Do one small good deed together as a family for an elderly person or a neighbor.
lessons.noon: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” — Lord, turn my scars into blessings for my children.

fam.key: We use love instead of hurt.

lamb.do: When your child falls or cries, pick them up first, gently pat their back, and speak only when they have quietened down.
lamb.say: It hurts! Mommy gives you a cuddle, and Jesus gives you a cuddle too.

sprout.story: Joseph's brothers were very unkind to him once and sold him to a faraway place. Many years later Joseph became an important official, and the brothers, hungry, came to him to buy grain. The brothers were so afraid, thinking Joseph would take revenge. But Joseph wept and hugged them, saying, “Don't be afraid. I will take care of you!” Joseph used love instead of anger.
sprout.ask: If someone is unkind to you, how can you be like Joseph?
sprout.do: Play “Hugs of Love” as a family: act out a small “I'm sorry” moment, and the person who was apologized to opens their arms, says “I forgive you,” and gives a hug.

soldier.story: Joseph was sold by his brothers, then spent many years as a slave and a prisoner in Egypt for something he hadn't done. Later he became prime minister and was in charge of the food for the whole country. When his brothers came to buy grain and found that their younger brother was the prime minister, they were so frightened they knelt on the ground. Joseph could have taken revenge, but he told them: you meant to harm me, but God turned it into good, so that many people could stay alive. He even promised to look after the brothers' children. Joseph turned the hurt he had suffered into a blessing for others.
ask: Do you think it was easy for Joseph to forgive his brothers? What helped him do it?
Does forgiving someone mean that what they did was not serious? Why?
soldier.do: Think of someone who once made you sad and pray a blessing for them. If you need to, ask Dad or Mom to help you work it through.

youth.talk: Joseph's family was actually a mess: his father played favorites, and his brothers almost killed him. Yet later he said to his brothers, “Am I in the place of God?” We were deeply moved reading this, and we struggled too, because there are parts of our relationship with the previous generation that we haven't fully let go. Forgiving doesn't mean that what happened was fine, or that we must let ourselves be hurt again. It means not letting the hurt keep ruling us.
ask: What do you think is the difference between forgiving and “pretending nothing happened”?
Is there something you feel we (your parents) did to hurt you that hasn't been properly dealt with?
youth.do: Parents first admit to your child one thing you handled badly in the past and apologize. If your child is willing, think together of a small action to mend the relationship.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you turn bad things into good, as you did for Joseph. Please help us use love instead of anger and blessing instead of hurt. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Do Not Remember the Former Things
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: forgetting what is behind, pressing on to what is ahead

v: “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old.
Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Think back over this week. Was there a moment when you noticed you did not react in the old pattern, even just once? Ask the Holy Spirit to help you see that new shoot, and also the places that still need adjusting.
teach: God said to the exiled Israelites, “Don't remember the former things, and don't consider the things of old.” Then right away: “Behold, I will do a new thing.” He will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. For a parent carrying scars from a family of origin, this is a great comfort: God doesn't only mend the past, he opens up a new road. A wilderness will not become a garden overnight, but once there is a road you can walk out of it a step at a time, and once there are rivers, dry ground slowly turns green.

Paul also says, “One thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before.” Behind him lay both glory and shame, for he had persecuted the church. He was neither tied down by past glories nor crushed by past guilt; he ran straight toward the goal. The purpose of review is not to dig up old accounts, but to see the direction clearly and run the next step. A runner who glances down at his feet now and then does it to run more steadily, not to stop on the spot.

This week, perhaps you stopped just once before shouting, or said “I'm sorry” to your child for the first time. Don't despise it: the first trickle of water in a desert is the beginning of a river. Also honestly note the places that have not changed, and write down one specific, doable adjustment. Change comes through repetition, often two steps forward and one step back. What matters is that the direction is right, and that you are not walking alone.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the second half of the eight steps. Patterns from our family of origin often need many repetitions before they change, so don't give up after one failure. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on the past or your own failures, but on the new thing he is about to do.
q: Who is God? — God makes a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, and does new things.
Who am I? — In what moment this week did I not react in the old pattern? In what moment did I fall back on the old road?
How should I respond? — What is one specific action I will adjust next week?
lessons.jesus: When Peter failed, Jesus did not dig up old accounts. He only asked him three times, “Do you love me?” and entrusted him, “Feed my lambs.” He let Peter start out again from his failure. He treats you the same way today, as you review yourself.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for being with me this week as I faced everything my family of origin gave me. I offer you the new shoots I have seen, and I hand over the places that haven't changed yet. Please keep doing new things in our family, and make a way in the wilderness. I want to forget what is behind, press on to what is ahead, and follow you. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: which old pattern did each of us see in ourselves this week? What new change?
Ask your child, “This week, were Daddy/Mommy a little more like Jesus? What still needs to change?”
Write down one specific adjustment for next week and stick it on the fridge.
lessons.noon: “Behold, I will do a new thing.” — Lord, please do a new thing in our family, and in me.

fam.key: God is doing something new in our family every day.

lamb.do: Take your child to a window or the balcony and show them the sky, the leaves or a little flower. Point them out.
lamb.say: Look, how beautiful God's world is! God gives us something new every day.

sprout.story: Jiahao planted a seed in the garden and went to look at it every day, but nothing happened. He was so disappointed. One morning he shouted, “Mommy, come quick!” A tiny green shoot had poked up out of the soil. Mommy said, “Look, God is doing something new. It's small, but it will grow!”
sprout.ask: Where do you think you've grown a tiny bit this week?
sprout.do: Plant a bean or mung bean together as a family, put it on the windowsill, and look every day to see if a new shoot has come up.

soldier.story: Paul used to persecute Christians, and later became an apostle who spread the good news. He wrote, “One thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before. I press on toward the goal.” He didn't let past mistakes drag him back, and he didn't let past successes make him proud. It's like a race: if you keep looking back, you run slowly or even fall. You must look at the finish line and run forward a step at a time.
ask: Was there something you did better this week than last week?
What “goal” do you want to work toward next week?
soldier.do: Hold a family meeting. Each person shares one “place I became new this week” and one “thing I want to work on next week.” Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we talked a lot about our families of origin. Honestly, we've found some patterns in ourselves that go deeper than we thought, and a few times we almost treated you in the old way. But God says, “Behold, I will do a new thing.” We'd like to hear what you've noticed, because you know best whether we were different this week. Whatever you say, we're willing to hear it all the way through before we try to explain.
ask: Did you notice anything different about us this week?
If you could give us one piece of advice, what would it be?
youth.do: As a family, choose one adjustment for next week, for example “pause for ten seconds when angry,” and remind one another.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for doing something new in our family every day. Please help us not to look back but to keep moving forward, each day a little more like Jesus. In Jesus' name, amen.

12.memT: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

mem.t: ‘Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,

sat.t: Family Day: The “Because You Are You” Treasure Box of Love
sat.d: Prepare an empty box and a pile of little cards. Each person writes or draws one card for every family member, each beginning with the words “I love you because you are you, not because...”, for example “not because you scored a hundred.” Little ones can draw a heart or press a handprint, with a parent writing for them. Put all the cards in the box. After dinner, take turns drawing a card, reading it aloud to the person it is for, and giving them a hug. At the end the parents read 1 John 4:19 together. Keep the treasure box in the living room, and whenever anyone feels unloved, they can open it and look.

sun: This week, when you read 1 Corinthians 13 with your own name in it, which line made you stop most?
When is your child most likely to feel that “Mom and Dad's love has conditions”? What makes you think so?
Which picture of “God first loved us” did you experience this week? How would you like to bring that love to another family in your group?

lessons.title: Love Is the Fruit of the Spirit
lessons.theme: Parents abide in the Lord first, and then love grows as fruit in the home

v: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
We love him, because he first loved us.

lessons.still: Imagine you are a branch, resting quietly on the vine. You don't have to strain or perform; you simply let the sap of the vine flow into you. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I come first to be loved by you, and then I will go and love my family.”
teach: For the next nine weeks we will get to know the fruit of the Spirit at home, one at a time. Paul says, “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace...” Notice that “fruit” is singular in the original. It is not nine separate fruits but one cluster of grapes with nine flavors. Nor is it “results we produce”; it is what the Spirit “bears” in those who abide in the Lord. An apple tree doesn't have to grit its teeth to grow apples. It only has to stay connected to its roots and stand in the sunshine.

This is good news for tired parents: the love in our homes is not squeezed out of us by effort. Many parents try very hard to “love their children”, yet they love wearily and resentfully, because they are giving out of their own limited supply. John says, “We love him, because he first loved us.” First to be loved, then able to love; first to be filled, then able to overflow. An empty cup cannot pour out water, but a cup filled to overflowing with God's love needs no effort to spill over to the people around it.

Fruit has another characteristic: it is not for the tree itself to eat, but for the people around it to taste. Our children taste the love that grows in us every day. They may not remember how many lessons we taught, but they will remember what it was like to be near us. So the order for these nine weeks is this: parents bear fruit first, and children learn by following. Love comes first and is the root of the other eight flavors: patience without love turns into suppression, and self-control without love turns into coldness.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The fruit of the Spirit is the overflow of a life, not a parenting technique. The “9” in 920 is the nine fruits, the “0” is the self-emptied life, and the “2” is everyone in the family who is connected to me. The more self-emptied the parents are, the more the family can taste the flavor of Christ.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who loved us first, and who bears fruit in us through the Holy Spirit.
Who am I? — Am I loving my children now with strength I squeeze out of myself, or from love that flows out of God's love?
How should I respond? — Which five minutes will I use today to sit quietly and simply “be loved by God”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love.” The source of Jesus' own love is the Father's love. He often withdrew to quiet places to pray, first being satisfied in the Father's love, then going out to love others. He is our example of one who abides in love and bears the fruit of love.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving me first. I admit that I often love my children with my own strength, and I love wearily and resentfully. Please let me abide in your love first and be filled by you, and then let the Holy Spirit bear real love in me. May my children taste you when they are near me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Take five minutes today to read 1 John 4:19 quietly and say to God, “Thank you for loving me first.”
Write down the nine fruits of the Spirit and stick them on the fridge as a map for the next nine weeks.
Say “I love you” to each child once, with no conditions attached.
lessons.noon: “We love him, because he first loved us.” — Lord, right now let me be loved by you first, and then go and love my family.

fam.key: God loved us first, so we can love.

lamb.do: Let your child lie on your chest and listen to your heartbeat while you gently pat their back.
lamb.say: Listen, thump, thump. Mommy loves you, and God loves you even more.

sprout.story: In the orchard there was a grapevine, and bunches of purple grapes grew on its branches. One little branch said, “I want to grow grapes too!” It tried and tried with all its might, but nothing grew. The vine said, “You don't have to strain. Just stay joined to me.” A few days later, sweet grapes grew on the little branch too.
sprout.ask: What does the little branch have to do to grow grapes?
sprout.do: Count the nine fruits of the Spirit together, holding up one finger for each, and finish by making a heart with your hands.

soldier.story: Paul says the Holy Spirit bears nine fruits in us: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Fruit is not stuck on; it grows. You can stick plastic apples on a tree, and they look just like the real thing, but you can't eat them. A real apple grows because the tree is joined to its roots. Each week from now on we will get to know one fruit, and the first is “love.” Mom and Dad will practice first, and you can check whether we are bearing fruit!
ask: What do you think is the difference between being good “on the outside” and being good because it has “grown”?
Of the nine fruits, which one would you most like more of in our family?
soldier.do: Make a “fruit tree” poster: draw a tree and nine empty fruit circles, and this week color in “love” first.

youth.talk: For the next nine weeks our family will be learning the nine fruits of the Spirit together. Honestly, Mom and Dad are a bit nervous, because this is like inviting you to check on us. We've noticed that we often ask you to be loving and patient without living it out first. The Bible says fruit grows; it isn't acted out. So for these nine weeks we want to start with ourselves.
ask: Which fruit do you think shows most in Mom and Dad? Which is most lacking?
Do you think a person can really stay loving “on their own strength” all the time?
youth.do: Ask your child to give Mom and Dad a score from 1 to 5 for each of the nine fruits. Parents simply say thank you, and score again after nine weeks.

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, thank you for loving us first. Please let the Holy Spirit bear lots and lots of the fruit of love in our family, so that we love one another. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Put My Name in 1 Corinthians 13
lessons.theme: Is my love conditional?

v: Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,
doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;
doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth;
bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.

lessons.still: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 slowly once, then read it a second time with your own name in place of “love.” When you reach a line you can't say, stop there and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you gently.
teach: 1 Corinthians 13 is often read at weddings, but it was first written to a church that was quarreling constantly. Paul says, “Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn't envy. Love doesn't brag, is not proud...” This is not a romantic poem but a mirror. One pastor suggests reading it with your own name in place of “love”: “Zhiming is patient and is kind...” By the third line, many parents can't read on.

At home our love often becomes conditional without our noticing. When the child does well on a test we smile broadly; when grades drop, the dinner table goes quiet. When the child is good we cuddle; when they are fussy we push them away. We never say it aloud, but our children can read it: “I have to perform well to deserve love.” A child who grows up like this may spend a lifetime working to earn love, and may even see God the same way.

Paul says love “doesn't seek its own way.” Behind conditional love there is often the self-ruled life: I need my child to win face for me, I need my child to make me feel like a successful parent. The Holy Spirit's light is not meant to make us blame ourselves endlessly, but to let us see that I need God's love more than I thought. Once we admit it, change begins. A doctor must first find the lesion before treating it, and the Spirit's light is the X-ray before the healing.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self is the root of every problem. Conditional love treats a child as a tool for meeting my needs; unconditional love treats a child as an inheritance God has entrusted to me. When a parent turns from “I need my child to give me face” to “I only want to please God,” love is free.
q: Who is God? — God's love is patient and takes no account of evil, and that is how he loves me.
Who am I? — With my name in 1 Corinthians 13:4–7, which line can I least say? When do I give my children conditional love?
How should I respond? — In which specific moment today will I give my child an “unconditional” response?
lessons.jesus: A rich young man came to ask Jesus the way to eternal life, and went away sorrowful in the end. But Scripture records that before he turned away, “Jesus looking at him loved him.” Jesus' love is not because someone answers correctly or keeps up; it is given before the other person has responded at all.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for shining your light on me through 1 Corinthians 13. I admit that my love is often conditional: when my children do well I am warm, and when they don't I am cold. I admit I need my children to satisfy my need for face. Please forgive me, and heal the wounds this has left in my children's hearts. Let me be loved unconditionally by you first, and then learn to love my children this way. Amen.
acts: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 once with your own name in place of “love,” and circle the line that is hardest.
Notice the moment today when your attitude changed because of your child's performance, and write it down.
When your child does something wrong, first say “I still love you,” and then deal with the matter.
lessons.noon: “Love is patient and is kind.” — Lord, please grow this love in me, instead of my own conditions.

fam.key: No matter what, I love you.

lamb.do: When your child cries or makes a big mess, crouch down first, look into their eyes, and give them a hug.
lamb.say: Even when you cry, Mommy loves you.

sprout.story: Little Bear accidentally knocked over his milk. The floor was wet, and he was so scared that he hid under the table. Mama Bear came over, crouched down and said, “Little Bear, come out.” Little Bear asked in a small voice, “Do you still love me?” Mama Bear hugged him and said, “Of course! I love you when you spill the milk, and I love you when you cry. Let's wipe it up together!”
sprout.ask: When you do something wrong, do you feel Mommy and Daddy still love you?
sprout.do: Play the “I Still Love You” game: your child says something, such as “I broke my toy,” and the parent hugs them and says, “I still love you!”

soldier.story: Paul wrote a famous passage: “Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn't envy. Love doesn't brag, is not proud.” Let's try an experiment: put your own name in place of “love.” For example, “Xiaojie is patient and is kind.” You'll find that some lines are easy to say and some you can't say. Mom and Dad are the same. This passage is like a mirror that shows us we still need God's help.
ask: With your name in it, which line is hardest to say?
Which line do you think our family needs most?
soldier.do: Each person picks one line from 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 and writes it on a card, practices it every day this week, and shares at dinner.

youth.talk: Recently we read 1 Corinthians 13 and tried putting our own names in place of “love.” When we reached “is not provoked” we couldn't read on. We also noticed that when you do well on a test we are especially happy, and when you don't, we turn cold. We don't want you to feel you have to perform to deserve love. If you ever have felt that, we are sorry.
ask: Have you ever felt our attitude toward you depends on your grades or performance?
Do you think “unconditional love” means accepting anything?
youth.do: Parents say to your child, “Even if you achieved nothing, we would still love you the same.” Then ask your child how it felt to hear that.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us just the same whether we are good or not. Please help us love one another this way too. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: God Loved Us First
lessons.theme: I believe: my children don't need to earn my love

v: By this God’s love was revealed in us, that God has sent his only born Son into the world that we might live through him.
In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

lessons.still: Let yourself be like a little child sitting in your heavenly Father's lap. You haven't done anything right yet today, and he already loves you. Receive this love quietly and say to him, “Father, thank you for loving me when I wasn't lovable.”
teach: John says, “In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.” The order of the gospel is clear: God loves first, and we respond afterward. Paul also says, “While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Not after we became good, but when we were least lovable. God's love is the starting point, not the prize.

Many parents themselves grew up in conditional love. Jiahui, who grew up in Penang, says, “My father only patted my shoulder when I came first.” When he became a father, he treated his son the same way without thinking. Then one day he understood that his heavenly Father had never required him to come first before calling him “son.” At that moment he said to his son for the first time, “You don't have to come first. I delight in you anyway.”

Conviction is letting this truth move from the head into the heart: I am loved by God, not because of my performance, so my child doesn't need to earn my love through his performance either. This doesn't mean no rules and no discipline. It means discipline is built on the security of love, and not on withdrawing love to control a child. Today, write your own “I believe,” so that it becomes an anchor you can hold when your child fails and you are disappointed in yourself.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A shift of viewpoint, from “love is a reward” to “love is the source.” When parents receive unconditional love from God, they no longer need their children's performance to prove themselves. This is the self-emptied life: no longer I, but Christ's love living in me.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who sent his Son to die for us while we were still sinners.
Who am I? — Am I still trying in my heart to “earn” God's love? How does this affect the way I love my children?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe God loves me, not because...; I believe my child is loved by me, not because...
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was baptized in the Jordan, he had not yet performed a single miracle or preached a single sermon, and a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” Jesus' ministry began with being loved. He invites us too to receive the Father's delight first, and then go out to love others.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving me while I was still a sinner and sending Jesus to die for me. I believe you love me not because of my performance; I believe my children don't have to earn my love. Please heal the child inside me who has always tried to perform, and let my children feel safe near me and know that they are loved. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write two “I believe” declarations, one about how God loves you and one about how you love your children.
Say one sentence of appreciation to your child today that has nothing to do with grades or performance, for example, “I like being with you.”
Read Romans 5:8 to your spouse, and say to each other, “You don't have to be perfect. I love you anyway.”
lessons.noon: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Father, I believe you loved me first, and I want to love my children this way.

fam.key: I don't have to be good for God to love me.

lamb.do: In the morning, as soon as your child wakes up, before they have done anything, pick them up, kiss them and smile at them.
lamb.say: The moment you woke up, Mommy loved you so much.

sprout.story: Grandpa had a mango tree at his home in Kuala Lumpur. His little granddaughter asked, “Grandpa, why do you love me so much? Is it because I'm very good?” Grandpa smiled and said, “I loved you when you were still in Mommy's tummy. You couldn't do anything then!” The little girl said, “Does God love me like that too?” Grandpa said, “Yes! God loved you even before Grandpa did!”
sprout.ask: When do you think God began to love you?
sprout.do: Take out your child's baby photos and look at them together. Tell them, “You couldn't do anything yet, and we loved you so much.”

soldier.story: The Bible says, “While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Imagine you did something terrible at school and the teacher made you stand in the corner. Then someone walks up and says, “I'll stand for you. You go and rest.” And he knows you did wrong. That is what Jesus did for us. He didn't wait for us to become good before loving us; he died for us when we were still very far from good.
ask: Which makes you want to change more: “be good first, then be loved” or “be loved first, then become good”?
Do you ever feel you have to behave well for Mom and Dad to love you?
soldier.do: Each person writes one sentence: “I believe God loves me because...” but you can't write about anything good you've done, only what God has done.

youth.talk: John says, “Not that we loved God, but that he loved us.” We have been working hard at being good parents, and sometimes working hard at making you a “good child.” But we are slowly discovering that in our own hearts we've been trying to earn God's love too, as if we had to do well enough for God to be satisfied. If we ourselves are like that, no wonder we have treated you the same way. We want to learn together to be loved first.
ask: Among your friends, does anyone feel they have to be outstanding to deserve love?
Where do you think the biggest difference between God's love and human love lies?
youth.do: Parent and child each write down their own “I believe” declaration, read them aloud together, and then pray for each other.

fam.pray: Dear heavenly Father, thank you for loving us first, even when we were not good. We don't have to perform for you, and you still love us. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: The Father Ran and Embraced Him
lessons.theme: Giving love to our child when he is least lovable

v: “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
“But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate;
for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.

lessons.still: Imagine the father standing at the roadside, gazing into the distance day after day. Do you too have a child who makes you wait and worry? Quietly place that child in the heavenly Father's hands, and ask the Lord for a heart that runs.
teach: The prodigal son took his father's wealth, left for a far country and squandered it all. On the road home he prepared a speech: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.” He thought he would have to work to win back a place. But “while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.” In those days, for an elder to hitch up his robe and run along the road was undignified, but this father didn't care about face. He cared about one thing only: his son had come home.

The father did not wait for his son to finish his apology, nor did he hold a review meeting first. He called for the robe, the ring and the sandals. The robe restored honor, the ring restored identity, and the sandals restored his place as a son, because only servants went barefoot. This is the most concrete picture of unconditional love: love comes before performance, and the embrace before the lecture. The line “Make me as one of your hired servants” never got a chance to be said.

Today's practice is to give love to our child when he is least lovable. When your child talks back, makes a mess or disappoints you, “run” first: an embrace, a sentence like “I'm just glad you're home,” and then deal with the consequences. Unconditional love is not the absence of boundaries. The prodigal still faced the wealth he had lost. But he knew that his place in the family had never been taken away. This is the one thing a child most needs to be sure of.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The prodigal's father lost half his property, but he did not lose his son over property. Parents often hurt a child's heart over a broken bowl or a failed test paper. To let Jesus reign is to let love walk ahead of right and wrong.
q: Who is God? — God is the Father who saw his son from far off, was moved with compassion, and ran to embrace him.
Who am I? — When my child disappoints me, am I more like the father who ran, or the father who stood at the door waiting for an apology?
How should I respond? — In which moment today will I “run” to my child?
lessons.jesus: John records that Jesus, “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” That very night he bent down to wash his disciples' feet, even Judas, who was about to betray him. Jesus' love does not ask whether the other person deserves it; he loves to the end.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for running to embrace me when I was far from you. I admit that when my children disappoint me, I often put on a stern face first and wait for them to bow their heads. Please give me that father's heart, so that when my child is least lovable I will give love first, and then walk with him through the consequences. Amen.
acts: Today when your child makes a mistake or gets upset, first give a hug or say “I'm here,” and then deal with the matter.
Choose the child who has been giving you the most headaches lately, take them out alone for a treat they like, and don't talk about the problem.
Tonight at bedtime, say to each child, “No matter what happens, you will always be our child.”
lessons.noon: “While he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.” — Lord, let me run to my child like this too.

fam.key: When you come home, we will hug you.

lamb.do: When your child runs to you, crouch down, open your arms, catch them, pick them up and twirl them around.
lamb.say: You're here! I'm so happy, I love you so much.

sprout.story: A younger son left home and spent all the money his father gave him, and his tummy rumbled with hunger. He thought, “I'll go home and tell Daddy I'm sorry.” He was still very, very far away when his father saw him. His father ran and ran and hugged him tight, gave him beautiful new clothes and threw a big party! Our heavenly Father is just like this daddy.
sprout.ask: If you were the younger son, how would you feel when your daddy hugged you?
sprout.do: Act it out: your child walks slowly across the room from the far side, and the parent sees them from a distance, runs to hug them and says, “Welcome home!”

soldier.story: A younger son took his father's money and left home, and when it was all spent he had to feed pigs, so hungry he wanted to eat what the pigs ate. He decided to go home and even prepared his apology. But while he was still far away, his father ran, hugged him and kissed him, and before the son could finish speaking he told the servants to bring the best robe, a ring and sandals. The father didn't say, “First prove you've changed!” He said, “This my son was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.”
ask: Why did the father hug him first instead of scolding him?
Do you think a person who is loved like this wants to change more, or less? Why?
soldier.do: This week, if someone in the family makes a mistake, practice saying “I still love you” first, and then think together how to put it right.

youth.talk: We've heard the story of the prodigal son many times, but this time we noticed the father especially: he ran along the road. In those days it was shameful for an elder to run, but he didn't care about face. We want to admit to you that when you disappoint us, our first reaction isn't to run to you, but to put on a stern face and wait for you to bow your head first. We want to change.
ask: When you've done wrong, what do you most want Mom and Dad's first reaction to be?
Do you think love and rules can exist together? How?
youth.do: Parent and child agree on a “code word.” When your child feels they have messed up and need to be accepted, they can use it, and the parents give a hug first and then talk.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for being like the daddy who ran, always opening your arms to wait for us to come home. Please help our family to embrace one another like this. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Not in Word Only, but in Deed
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: Did my children taste my love this week?

v: If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.
If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing.
If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.
My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.

lessons.still: Look back over this week. In which moment did your child truly taste love? And in which moment did you do a great deal, yet without love in your heart? Ask the Holy Spirit to go back over it with you slowly, with no hurry to give a score.
teach: Paul says, “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don't have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.” He goes on to say that even giving away all his goods to feed the poor, without love, profits him nothing. These words sting parents. We can drive them to school, cook, help with homework and pay the fees every day, doing a great deal, yet in the child's ears it is only noise, because it has no love in it, only duty, anxiety and resentment. Children can tell. The same bowl of noodles served with a smile and slammed on the table with a sigh tastes completely different.

John is very practical: “Let's not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” Love is not a feeling, nor a slogan, but visible, touchable action. Huimin, in a dual-income family in Singapore, found that what her daughter remembered most was not the gifts she bought, but the evening she put down her phone and listened to her daughter talk about school for half an hour. That half hour cost not a cent, yet it was the clearest proof in her daughter's heart that “I am loved.”

This week we read that love is fruit, looked into the mirror of 1 Corinthians 13, received the truth that God loved us first, and learned from the father who ran to embrace. Today, review honestly: what did my children taste this week, love or noise? Don't condemn yourself; just write down one specific action you can do better next week. Love is fruit that keeps on growing, and today's pruning is so that it bears more next week.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review and adjustment are the pruning that lets the fruit grow. Proud parents ask only “How much have I done for my child?” Humble parents ask “Does my child feel loved?” Ministry cannot replace life, and doing many things cannot replace real love.
q: Who is God? — God's love is not only in words; he proved his love by the action of the cross.
Who am I? — Of the things I did for my children this week, which came from love? Which were only duty or anxiety?
How should I respond? — Next week, which specific action will I use to let my children taste love?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.” He did not love only in words. He loved with three years of walking beside his disciples, one night of foot-washing and one laying down of his life on the cross. His love has deeds and truth, and he waits patiently for us to learn to love this way.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for letting me get to know the fruit of love this week. I admit that I often do a lot without love, and say a lot without doing it. Please forgive me. Thank you also for showing me the moments when my children truly tasted love. Please keep bearing love in me, and next week let my love have more deeds and more truth. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what was the most loving moment in our home this week? What was the moment most like a “clanging cymbal”?
Ask your child, “This week, when did you feel Daddy/Mommy loved you most? Were we a bit more like Jesus?”
Write down one specific act of love for next week, for example, ten minutes of focused time every day without looking at your phone.
lessons.noon: “Let's not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” — Lord, let my love today be seen and touched by my children.

fam.key: Love is something we do.

lamb.do: Play with your child with full attention for ten minutes today. Put your phone in another room and follow their game.
lamb.say: I'm here with you. I love playing with you.

sprout.story: Big Brother Rabbit told his little brother every day, “I love you so much!” But when his little brother wanted to play with his ball, he said, “No!” and his little brother cried. Mommy asked Big Brother Rabbit, “You say you love your little brother, so how can you let him know?” Big Brother Rabbit thought for a moment, rolled the ball to his little brother and said, “Let's play together!” His little brother laughed, because he really felt his brother's love.
sprout.ask: What did you do this week to let someone in the family know you love them?
sprout.do: Play “Acts of Love” as a family: each person does one small thing to help a family member, such as pouring water or fetching slippers, and says “I love you” when finished.

soldier.story: Paul says that even if a person can speak many languages, is very clever, or even gives everything to the poor, without love he is like a loud gong: clang, clang, clang, only noise with no meaning. John also says that love can't be only in words from the mouth; it must be in deeds and truth. It is like saying, “I love Mom so much,” but never helping her. All Mom hears is noise. This week we learned about love. Now let's see whether we have put it into practice.
ask: This week at home, did you love a family member with an action?
Do you think Mom and Dad loved you with actions this week? Which time do you remember most?
soldier.do: Hold a family meeting. Each person shares one “moment this week when I felt loved” and one “thing I want to do next week to love the family with action.” Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: All this week we've been learning about “love.” Looking back, we've done a lot: driving you around, cooking, reminding you about homework, but sometimes inside we were impatient, even resentful. Paul says love-less action is like a noisy gong. We really want to know: from where you stand, was this week love or noise? You can say it straight, and we will listen all the way through first.
ask: Was there anything we did this week that really made you feel loved?
Was there anything we thought was love, but you felt as pressure?
youth.do: Ask your child to write down “the way I would most like you to love me next week” for the parents, and the parents take it seriously and do it.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us with action. Please help us love one another not only with our mouths, but with deeds. In Jesus' name, amen.
